      Companies Act, 2013 and the SEBI ICDR Regulations, we cannot undertake variation in the utilization of the Net
      Proceeds as disclosed in this Updated Draft Red Herring Prospectus-I without obtaining the approval of the
      Shareholders through a special resolution. In the event of any such circumstances that require us to vary the disclosed
      utilization of the Net Proceeds, we may not be able to obtain the approval of the Shareholders in a timely manner, or
      at all. Any delay or inability in obtaining such approval of the Shareholders may adversely affect our business.

      This may restrict our ability to respond to any change in our business or financial condition by re-deploying the

      gaps or failures.

57.   It may be difficult for investors to enforce any judgment obtained outside India against our Company, the Directors
      or the Key Managerial Personnel in India, respectively, except by way of a lawsuit in India on such judgment.

      Our Company is incorporated under the laws of India. Our Company’s assets are located in India and all of our
      Company’s Directors and Key Managerial Personnel are residents of India. As a result, it may not be possible for
      investors to effect service of process upon our Company or such persons in jurisdictions outside India, or to enforce
      against them judgments obtained in courts outside India.

      Recognition and enforcement of foreign judgments is provided for under Section 13 and Section 44A of the Code of
      Civil Procedure, 1908, as amended (the “Civil Procedure Code”). India is not a party to any international treaty in
      relation to the recognition or enforcement of foreign judgments. The United Kingdom, Singapore, United Arab
      Emirates, and Hong Kong, among other jurisdictions, have been declared by the Government of India to be
      reciprocating territories for purposes of Section 44A of the Civil Procedure Code. Section 44A of the Civil Procedure
      Code provides that where a foreign judgement has been rendered by a superior court, within the meaning of such
      section, in any country or territory outside of India which the Government of India has by notification declared to be
      in a reciprocating territory, it may be enforced in India by proceedings in execution as if the judgement had been
      rendered by the relevant court in India. However, Section 44A of the Civil Procedure Code is applicable only to
                                                              55
      monetary decrees not being of the same nature as amounts payable in respect of taxes, other charges of a like nature
      or of a fine or other penalties. A judgement of a court of a country which is not a reciprocating territory may be
      enforced in India only by a suit on the judgement under Section 13 of the Civil Procedure Code, and not by proceedings
      in execution. Under the Civil Procedure Code, a court in India shall, on the production of any document purporting to
      be a certified copy of a foreign judgement, presume that the judgement was pronounced by a court of competent
      jurisdiction, unless the contrary appears on record. However, under the Civil Procedure Code, such presumption may
      be displaced by proving that the court did not have jurisdiction. The Civil Procedure Code only permits the
      enforcement of monetary decrees, not being in the nature of any amounts payable in respect of taxes, other charges,
      fines or penalties.

      Judgments or decrees from jurisdictions which do not have reciprocal recognition with India cannot be enforced by
      proceedings in execution in India. The United States and India do not currently have a treaty providing for reciprocal
      recognition and enforcement of judgments in civil and commercial matters. A final judgement for the payment of
      money rendered by any court in a non-reciprocating territory for civil liability, whether or not predicated solely upon
      the general laws of the non-reciprocating territory, would not be enforceable in India. Even if an investor obtained a
      judgement in such a jurisdiction against us, our officers or directors, it may be required to institute a new proceeding
      in India and obtain a decree from an Indian court. Any such suit must be brought in India within three years from the
      date of the judgement in the same manner as any other suit filed to enforce a civil liability in India.

      However, the party in whose favour such final judgement is rendered may bring a new suit in a competent court in
      India based on a final judgement that has been obtained in the United States or other such jurisdiction within three
      years of obtaining such final judgement. It is unlikely that an Indian court would award damages on the same basis as
      a foreign court if an action were brought in India. Moreover, it is unlikely that an Indian court will award damages to
      the extent awarded in a final judgement rendered outside India if it believes that the number of damages awarded were
      excessive or inconsistent with public policy or Indian law. In addition, any person seeking to enforce a foreign
      judgement in India is required to obtain the prior approval of the RBI under the FEMA to execute such a judgement
      or to repatriate any amount recovered.

58.   We may be affected by competition laws in India, the adverse application or interpretation of which could have an
      adverse effect on our business.

      The Competition Act, 2002, as amended (“Competition Act”), was enacted for the purpose of preventing practices
      that have or are likely to have an adverse effect on competition (“AAEC”) in certain markets in India and has mandated
      the Competition Commission of India (“CCI”) to prohibit such practices. Under the Competition Act, any
      arrangement, understanding or action, whether formal or informal, which causes or is likely to cause an AAEC is
      deemed void and attracts substantial penalties.

      Any agreement among competitors, which directly or indirectly involves the determination of purchase or sale prices,
      limits or controls production, supply, markets, technical development, investment or provision of services may be
      deemed to have an AAEC. Further, agreements among competitors that share the market or source of production or
      provision of services by way of allocation of geographical area, type of goods or services or number of consumers in
      the relevant market or in any other similar way or directly or indirectly results in bid-rigging or collusive bidding is
      presumed to have AAEC. The Competition Act also prohibits abuse of a dominant position by any enterprise. Further,
      the CCI has extra-territorial powers and can investigate any agreements, abusive conduct or combination occurring
      outside India if such agreement, conduct or combination has an AAEC in India.

      The Competition Act also provides that acquisitions of shares, voting rights, assets or control or mergers or
      amalgamations that cross prescribed thresholds and are otherwise not exempt, be mandatorily notified to, and pre-
      approved by, the CCI. The Government of India has enacted the Competition (Amendment) Act, 2023 (“Amendment
      Act”), which has introduced several amendments to the Competition Act, such as expansion of the scope of
      ‘combination’ through introduction of deal value thresholds, which provides that any transaction, in connection with
      acquisition of any control, shares, voting rights or assets of an enterprise, merger or amalgamation, having a deal value
      of more than ₹20,000 million would require an approval from the CCI, if the parties had substantial business operations
      in India. Further, the Competition Commission of India (Combinations) Regulations, 2024, effective from September
      10, 2024, set out detailed procedural guidance for the classification and regulation of ‘combination’ under the
      Competition Act.

      Consequently, agreements entered into by us could be within the purview of the Competition Act. Further, the effects
      of the provisions of the Competition Act on the agreements entered into by us cannot be predicted with certainty at
      this stage. However, since we pursue an acquisition driven growth strategy, we may be affected, directly or indirectly,
      by the application or interpretation of any provision of the Competition Act, any enforcement proceedings initiated by
      the CCI, any adverse publicity that may be generated due to scrutiny or prosecution by the CCI, or any prohibition,
      direction, or substantial penalties levied under the Competition Act, which would result in additional costs for
      compliance as well as adversely affect our business, financial condition and results of operations.

62.   A third party could be prevented from acquiring control over our Company because of anti-takeover provisions
      under Indian law.

      As a listed Indian entity, there are provisions in Indian law that may delay, deter or prevent a future takeover or change
      in control of our Company, even if a change in control would result in the purchase of your equity shares at a premium
      to the market price or would otherwise be beneficial to you. Such provisions may discourage or prevent certain types
      of transactions involving an actual or threatened change in control of our Company. Under the Takeover Regulations,
      an acquirer has been defined as any person who, directly or indirectly, acquires or agrees to acquire shares or voting
      rights or control over a company, whether individually or acting in concert with others. Although these provisions
      have been formulated to ensure that interests of investors/shareholders are protected, these provisions may also
      discourage a third party from attempting to take control of our Company subsequent to completion of this Offer.
      Consequently, even if a potential takeover of our Company would result in the purchase of the Equity Shares at a
      premium to their market price or would otherwise be beneficial to our shareholders, such a takeover may not be
      attempted or consummated because of SEBI Takeover Regulations.

63.   Investors could be subject to Indian taxes arising out of capital gains and stamp duty on the sale of the Equity
      Shares and will be subject to Indian taxes on any dividends.

      Under current Indian tax laws, unless specifically exempted, capital gains arising from the sale of equity shares held
      as investments in an Indian company are generally taxable in India. A securities transaction tax (“STT”) is levied on
      equity shares sold on recognised stock exchange. Any capital gain exceeding ₹125,000, realised on the sale of Equity
      Shares on a recognised stock exchange, held for more than 12 months immediately preceding the date of transfer, will
      be subject to long term capital gains in India, at the rate of 12.5% (plus applicable surcharge and cess). This beneficial
      rate is, among others, subject to payment of STT. Further, any gain realised on the sale of Equity Shares held for more
                                                             58
      than 12 months, which are sold using any platform other than a recognised stock exchange and on which no STT has
      been paid, will be subject to long term capital gains tax in India at the rate of 12.5% (plus applicable surcharge and
      cess).

      Further, any capital gains realised on the sale of Equity Shares held for a period of 12 months or less immediately
      preceding the date of transfer will be subject to short term capital gains tax in India. Such gains will be subject to tax
      at the rate of 20% (plus applicable surcharge and cess), subject to STT being paid at the time of sale of such shares.
      Otherwise, such gains will be taxed at the applicable rates.

      Capital gains arising from the sale of the Equity Shares will not be chargeable to tax in India in cases where relief from
      such taxation in India is provided under a treaty between India and the country of which the seller is resident read with
      the Multilateral Instrument, if and to the extent applicable, and the seller is entitled to avail benefits thereunder.
      Generally, Indian tax treaties do not limit India’s ability to impose tax on capital gains. As a result, residents of other
      countries may be liable for tax in India as well as in their own jurisdiction on a gain realised upon the sale of the Equity
      Shares. No dividend distribution tax is required to be paid in respect of dividends declared, distributed or paid by a
      domestic company after March 31, 2020, and, accordingly, such dividends would not be exempt in the hands of the
      Shareholders both for residents and non-residents. Our Company may or may not grant the benefit of a tax treaty
      (where applicable) to a non-resident shareholder for the purposes of deducting tax at source pursuant to any corporate
      action including dividends.

      The stamp duty for transfer of certain securities, other than debentures, on a delivery basis is currently specified at
      0.015% and on a non-delivery basis is specified at 0.003% of the consideration amount.

      Investors are advised to consult their own tax advisors and to carefully consider the potential tax consequences of
      owning, investing or trading in our Equity Shares. Any dividends paid by an Indian company will be subject to tax in
      the hands of the shareholders at applicable rates. Such taxes will be withheld by the Indian company paying dividends.
      Non-resident shareholders may claim benefit of the applicable tax treaty, subject to satisfaction of certain conditions.
      We may or may not grant the benefit of a tax treaty (where applicable) to a non-resident shareholder for the purposes
      of deducting tax at source pursuant to any corporate action including dividends. Investors are advised to consult their
      own tax advisors and to carefully consider the potential tax consequences of owning Equity Shares.

      Unfavourable changes in or interpretations of existing, or the promulgation of new, laws, rules and regulations
      including foreign investment and stamp duty laws governing our business and operations could result in us being
      deemed to be in contravention of such laws and may require us to apply for additional approvals.

64.   Fluctuations in the exchange rate between the Rupee and other currencies could have an adverse effect on the
      value of the Equity Shares in those currencies, independent of our results of operations.

      Upon listing, the Equity Shares will be quoted in Rupees on the Stock Exchanges. Any dividends in respect of the
      Equity Shares will be paid in Rupees and subsequently converted into the relevant foreign currency for repatriation, if
      required. Any adverse movement in currency exchange rates during the time it takes to undertake such conversion
      could reduce the net dividend received by investors. In addition, any adverse movement in currency exchange rates
      during a delay in repatriating the proceeds from a sale of Equity Shares outside India, for example, because of a delay
      in regulatory approvals that may be required for the sale of Equity Shares, could reduce the net proceeds received by
      investors. The exchange rate between the Rupee and other currencies (such as the U.S. dollar) has changed
      substantially in the past and could fluctuate substantially in the future, which could have an adverse effect on the value
      of the Equity Shares and returns from the Equity Shares in foreign currency terms, independent of our results of
      operations.

65.   Foreign investors are subject to investment restrictions under Indian law that limit our ability to attract foreign
      investors, which could adversely affect the trading price of the Equity Shares.

      Under foreign exchange regulations currently in force in India, transfer of shares between non-residents and residents
      are freely permitted (subject to compliance with sectoral norms and certain other restrictions), if they comply with the
      pricing guidelines and reporting requirements specified by the RBI. If the transfer of shares, which are sought to be
      transferred, is not in compliance with such pricing guidelines or reporting requirements or falls under any of the
      exceptions referred to above, then a prior regulatory approval will be required. Furthermore, unless specifically
      restricted, foreign investment is freely permitted in all sectors of the Indian economy up to any extent and without any
      prior approvals, but the foreign investor is required to follow certain prescribed procedures for making such investment.
      The RBI and the concerned ministries/departments are responsible for granting approval for foreign investment.
      Additionally, shareholders who seek to convert Rupee proceeds from a sale of shares in India into foreign currency
      and repatriate that foreign currency from India require a no-objection or a tax clearance certificate from the Indian
      income tax authorities.

      In addition, pursuant to the Press Note No. 3 (2020 Series), dated April 17, 2020, issued by the Department for
      Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (“DPIIT”), which has been incorporated as the proviso to Rule 6(a) of the
                                                              59
      FEMA Rules, investments where the beneficial owner of the Equity Shares is situated in or is a citizen of a country
      which shares land border with India, can only be made through the Government approval route, as prescribed in the
      Consolidated FDI Policy Circular dated October 15, 2020 (“FDI Policy”) and the FEMA Rules. Subsequently, vide
      Press Note No. 2 (2026 Series), dated March 15, 2026 issued by the DPIIT, and made effective from May 2, 2026,
      being the date of publication of the Foreign Exchange Management (Non-debt Instruments) (Amendments) Rules,
      2026 in the official gazette, the FDI Policy has been further amended to, among other things, define the expression
      “beneficial owner” and to provide that prior approval of the Government of India shall be required only where citizen(s)
      and/or entity(ies) of a country sharing a land border with India hold, directly or indirectly, individually or cumulatively,
      more than 10% of the shares, capital or profits of the investor entity, or exercise control over such investor entity, or
      exercise ultimate effective control over the investee entity. Furthermore, in the event of transfer of ownership of any
      existing or future foreign direct investment in an entity in India, directly or indirectly, resulting in the beneficial
      ownership falling within the aforesaid restriction/purview, such subsequent change in the beneficial ownership will
      also require approval of the Government of India. These investment restrictions shall also apply to subscribers of
      offshore derivative instruments. We cannot assure you that any required approval from the RBI or any other
      governmental agency can be obtained with or without any particular terms or conditions or at all. For further
      information, see “Restrictions on Foreign Ownership of Indian Securities” on page 414.

67.   Investors will not be able to sell immediately on an Indian stock exchange any of the Equity Shares they purchase

      applicable rates if allotment is not made, refund orders are not dispatched or demat credits are not made to investors
      within the prescribed time periods.

68.   Holders of Equity Shares could be restricted in their ability to exercise pre-emptive rights under Indian law and

      existing ownership percentages before the issuance of any new equity shares, unless the pre-emptive rights have been
      waived by adoption of a special resolution by holders of three-fourths of the equity shares voting on such resolution.

      However, if the laws of the jurisdiction the investors are located in does not permit them to exercise their pre-emptive
      rights without filing an offering document or registration statement with the applicable authority in such jurisdiction,

70.   Subsequent to the listing of the Equity Shares on the Stock Exchanges, we could be subject to surveillance
      measures, such as the Additional Surveillance Measures and the Graded Surveillance Measures by the Stock
      Exchanges in order to enhance the integrity of the market and safeguard the interest of investors.

      SEBI and the Stock Exchanges, in the past, have introduced various pre-emptive surveillance measures with respect
      to the shares of listed companies in India (the “Listed Securities”) in order to enhance market integrity, safeguard the
      interests of investors and potential market abuses. In addition to various surveillance measures already implemented,
      and in order to further safeguard the interest of investors, the SEBI and the Stock Exchanges have introduced additional
      surveillance measures (“ASM”) and graded surveillance measures (“GSM”).

      ASM is conducted by the Stock Exchanges on Listed Securities with surveillance concerns based on certain objective
      parameters such as price-to-earnings ratio, percentage of delivery, customer concentration, variation in volume of
      shares and volatility of shares, among other things. GSM is conducted by the Stock Exchanges on Listed Securities
      where their price quoted on the Stock Exchanges is not commensurate with, among other things, the financial
      performance and financial condition measures such as earnings, book value, fixed assets, net-worth, other measures
      such as price-to-earnings multiple and market capitalisation.

      Upon listing, the trading of our Equity Shares would be subject to differing market conditions as well as other factors
      which may result in high volatility in price, and low trading volumes as a percentage of combined trading volume of
      our Equity Shares. The occurrence of any of the abovementioned factors or other circumstances may trigger any of the
      parameters prescribed by SEBI and the Stock Exchanges for placing our securities under the GSM and/or ASM
      framework or any other surveillance measures, which could result in significant restrictions on trading of our Equity
      Shares being imposed by SEBI and the Stock Exchanges. These restrictions may include requiring higher margin
      requirements, limiting trading frequency or freezing of price on upper side of trading, as well as mentioning of our
      Equity Shares on the surveillance dashboards of the Stock Exchanges. The imposition of these restrictions and curbs
      on trading may have an adverse effect on market price, trading and liquidity of our Equity Shares and on the reputation
      and conditions of our Company. Any such instance may result in a loss of our reputation and diversion of our
      management’s attention and may also decrease the market price of our Equity Shares which could cause you to lose
      some or all of your investment.

71.   There is no guarantee that our Equity Shares will be listed on the Stock Exchanges in a timely manner or at all.

      In accordance with Indian law and practice, permission for listing and trading of our Equity Shares will not be granted
      until after certain actions have been completed in relation to this Offer and until Allotment of Equity Shares pursuant
      to this Offer.

      In accordance with current regulations and circulars issued by SEBI, our Equity Shares are required to be listed on the
      Stock Exchanges within such time as mandated under UPI Circulars, subject to any change in the prescribed timeline
      in this regard. However, we cannot assure you that the trading in our Equity Shares will commence in a timely manner
      or at all. Any failure or delay in obtaining final listing and trading approvals may restrict your ability to dispose of
      your Equity Shares.

prior to the filing of the Red Herring Prospectus in accordance with Regulation 41 of the SEBI ICDR Regulations. The relevant
details shall be included in the Red Herring Prospectus. For details in relation to the proposed utilisation of the Gross Proceeds,
please see “Objects of the Offer” beginning on page 95.

Appraising Entity

None of the objects for which the Net Proceeds are proposed to be utilised have been appraised by any agency.

Credit Rating

As this is an Offer of Equity Shares, there is no credit rating required for the Offer.

Debenture Trustees

As this is an Offer of Equity Shares, the appointment of debenture trustees is not required.

Green Shoe Option

No green shoe option is contemplated under the Offer.

Illustration of the Book Building Process

Book building in the context of the Offer refers to the process of collection of Bids from Bidders on the basis of the Red Herring
Prospectus and the Bid Cum Application Forms (and the Revision Forms) within the Price Band and the minimum Bid Lot,
which will be decided by our Company, in consultation with the Book Running Lead Managers, and advertised in all editions
of Financial Express, an English national daily newspaper, all editions of Jansatta, a Hindi national daily newspaper and
Mumbai edition of Navshakti, a Marathi daily newspaper (Marathi being the regional language of Maharashtra, where our
Registered Office is located) at least two Working Days prior to the Bid/ Offer Opening Date and shall be made available to
the Stock Exchanges for the purpose of uploading on their respective websites. The Offer Price shall be determined by our
Company, in consultation with the Book Running Lead Managers, after the Bid/Offer Closing Date. For further details, see
“Offer Procedure” on page 395.

All Bidders (other than Anchor Investors) shall participate in this Offer mandatorily through the ASBA process by
providing the details of their respective bank accounts in which the corresponding Bid Amount will be blocked by the
SCSBs or Sponsor Bank(s), as the case may be. In addition to this, the UPI Bidders may participate through the ASBA
process by either (a) providing the details of their respective ASBA Account in which the corresponding Bid Amount
will be blocked by the SCSBs; or (b) through the UPI Mechanism. Anchor Investors are not permitted to participate in
the Offer through the ASBA process.

In terms of the SEBI ICDR Regulations, QIBs and Non-Institutional Bidders are not permitted to withdraw their Bid(s)
or lower the size of their Bid(s) (in terms of the number of Equity Shares or the Bid Amount) at any stage. Anchor
Investors are not allowed to withdraw their Bids after the Anchor Investor Bidding Date. RIBs and Eligible Employees
bidding in Employee Reservation Portion bidding in the Retail Portion can revise their Bids during the Bid/ Offer Period
and withdraw their Bids until Bid/ Offer Closing Date. Except for Allocation to RIBs, Non-Institutional Bidders and the
Anchor Investors, allocation in the Offer will be on a proportionate basis. Further, allocation to Anchor Investors will
be on a discretionary basis and allocation to the Non-Institutional Investors will be in a manner as may be introduced
under applicable laws.

Each Bidder will be deemed to have acknowledged the above restrictions and the terms of the Offer, by submitting their
Bid in the Offer.

The process of Book Building under the SEBI ICDR Regulations and the Bidding Process are subject to change from
time to time and the Bidders are advised to make their own judgment about investment through this process prior to
                                                                      79
submitting a Bid in the Offer.

The Bidders should note that the Offer is also subject to obtaining (i) the final approval of the RoC after the Prospectus is filed
with the RoC; and (ii) final listing and trading approvals of the Stock Exchanges, which our Company shall apply for after
Allotment as per the prescribed timelines in compliance with the SEBI ICDR Regulations.

For further details, see “Terms of the Offer”, “Offer Structure” and “Offer Procedure” on pages 384, 390 and 395, respectively.

   i. Pursuant to Regulations 14 and 16 of the SEBI ICDR Regulations, an aggregate of 20% of the post-Offer Equity Share
      capital of our Company held by our Promoters, shall be locked in for a period of three years, or any other period as
      prescribed under the SEBI ICDR Regulations, as minimum Promoters’ contribution (“Minimum Promoters’
      Contribution”) from the date of Allotment and the shareholding of our Promoters in excess of 20% of the post-Offer
      Equity Share capital shall be locked in for a period of one year from the date of Allotment.

   Our Promoters, severally not jointly, have each given their respective consents to include such number of Equity Shares
   held by our Promoters as disclosed above, constituting 20% of the post-Offer Equity Share capital of our Company as
   Minimum Promoter’s Contribution. Our Promoters have agreed not to dispose, sell, transfer, charge, pledge, lien or
   otherwise encumber in any manner the Minimum Promoters’ Contribution from the date of filing this Updated Draft Red
   Herring Prospectus - I, until the expiry of the lock-in period specified above, or for such other time as required under
   SEBI ICDR Regulations, except as may be permitted, in accordance with SEBI ICDR Regulations.

   Our Company undertakes that the Equity Shares that are being locked-in are not ineligible for computation of Promoters’
   contribution in terms of Regulation 15 of the SEBI ICDR Regulations. For details of build-up of shareholding of our
   Promoters, see “– 8. History of the share capital held by our Promoters – a. Build-up of the Equity shareholding of our
   Promoters in our Company” on page 87.

   In this connection, please note that:

   a.      The Equity Shares offered for Minimum Promoters’ Contribution do not include (i) Equity Shares acquired in the
           three immediately preceding years for consideration other than cash and revaluation of assets or capitalisation of
           intangible assets not involved in such transactions, or (ii) Equity Shares that have resulted from bonus issue by
           utilization of revaluation reserves or unrealised profits of our Company or resulted from bonus shares issued
           against Equity Shares, which are otherwise ineligible for computation of Minimum Promoters’ Contribution.

   b.      The Minimum Promoters’ Contribution does not include any Equity Shares acquired during the one year
           immediately preceding the date of this Updated Draft Red Herring Prospectus - I, at a price lower than the price
           at which the Equity Shares are being offered to the public in the Offer.

   c.      Our Company has not been formed by the conversion of one or more partnership firms or a limited liability
           partnership firm and hence, no Equity Shares have been issued in the one year immediately preceding the date of
           this Updated Draft Red Herring Prospectus – I pursuant to conversion from one or more partnership firms or
           limited liability partnerships.

   d.      All the Equity Shares held by our Promoters are in dematerialised form.

   e.      The Equity Shares held by our Promoters and offered for Minimum Promoters’ Contribution are not subject to
           pledge or any other encumbrance with any third party.

   Other lock-in requirements:

           i.         In addition to the 20% of the post-Offer shareholding of our Company held by our Promoters and locked
                      in for three years as specified above, in terms of the SEBI ICDR Regulations, the shareholding of our
                      Promoters in excess of 20% of the fully diluted post-Offer equity share capital shall be locked in for a
                      period of one year from the date of Allotment. The entire pre-Offer Equity Share capital of our Company,
                      held by persons other than our Promoters, will be locked-in for a period of six months from the date of
                      Allotment or such other period as may be prescribed under the SEBI ICDR Regulations. In the event
                      where lock-in of the pre-Offer Equity Share capital of our Company, which is held by persons other than
                      our Promoters, cannot be created under SEBI ICDR Regulations, the relevant Depositories, upon
                      instructions from our Company, shall record such Equity Shares as ‘non-transferable’ for such duration
                      of six months from the date of Allotment in the Offer. Relevant provisions in this regard have been
                      included in the articles of association of our Company. For details, see “Description of Equity Shares and
                      Terms of the Articles of Association” on page 416. However, the above lock-in of Equity Shares shall not

                                                                     89
                      be applicable for (i) the Equity Shares offered pursuant to the Offer for Sale, and (ii) any Equity Shares
                      transferred to and held by employees (whether currently employees or not) of our Company in accordance
                      with ESOP Scheme. Further, any unsubscribed portion of the Offered Shares will also be locked in, as
                      required under the SEBI ICDR Regulations. As on the date of this Updated Draft Red Herring Prospectus
                      - I, our Company does not have shareholders that are VCFs, Category I AIFs, Category II AIFs or FVCIs.

              ii.     As required under Regulation 20 of the SEBI ICDR Regulations, our Company shall ensure that the
                      details of the Equity Shares locked-in are recorded by the relevant Depository.

              iii.    In terms of Regulation 22 of the SEBI ICDR Regulations, the Equity Shares held by our Promoters, which
                      are locked-in pursuant to Regulation 16 of the SEBI ICDR Regulations, may be transferred to and among
                      the members of our Promoter Group or to any new promoter of our Company, subject to continuation of
                      the lock-in in the hands of the transferees for the remaining period (and such transferees shall not be
                      eligible to transfer until the expiry of the lock-in period) and compliance with the Takeover Regulations,
                      as applicable.

              iv.     Pursuant to Regulation 21(a) of the SEBI ICDR Regulations, the Equity Shares held by our Promoters,
                      which are locked-in for a period of three years from the date of Allotment (as mentioned above) may be
                      pledged as collateral security for loans granted by scheduled commercial banks, public financial
                      institutions, NBFC-SI or housing finance companies, provided that such loans have been granted by such
                      bank or institution for the purpose of financing one or more of the objects of the Offer and pledge of the
                      Equity Shares is a term of sanction of such loans.

              v.      Pursuant to Regulation 21(b) of the SEBI ICDR Regulations, the Equity Shares held by our Promoters
                      which are locked-in for a period of one year from the date of Allotment may be pledged only with
                      scheduled commercial banks, public financial institutions, NBFC-SI or housing finance companies as
                      collateral security for loans granted by such banks or public financial institutions, provided that such
                      pledge of the Equity Shares is one of the terms of the sanction of such loans.

                      Provided that the lock-in of Equity Shares shall continue post the invocation of the pledge referenced
                      above in (iv) and (v), for the relevant lock-in period with the transferee and such transferee shall not be
                      eligible to transfer them till the lock-in period stipulated in these regulations has expired.

              vi.     Pursuant to Regulation 22 of the SEBI ICDR Regulations, (a) the Equity Shares held by our Promoters,
                      which are locked-in may be transferred to and among the members of our Promoter Group or to any new
                      promoter of our Company and (b) the Equity Shares held by any person other than our Promoters and
                      locked-in for a period of six months from the date of Allotment in the Offer may be transferred to any
                      other person holding the Equity Shares which are locked-in, subject to continuation of the lock-in in the
                      hands of transferees for the remaining period (and such transferees shall not be eligible to transfer until
                      the expiry of the lock-in period) and compliance with the Takeover Regulations.

     Lock-in of the Equity Shares to be allotted, if any, to the Anchor Investors

     50% of the Equity Shares allotted to Anchor Investors under the Anchor Investor Portion shall be locked-in for a period of
     90 days from the date of Allotment and the remaining Equity Shares allotted to Anchor Investors under the Anchor Investor
     Portion shall be locked-in for a period of 30 days from the date of Allotment.

Fresh Issue

Requirement of Funds

We are a financial technology company focused on digital gifting, consumer spend management, and rewards & loyalty platforms.
Our platforms comprise yayyy.shop (our direct-to-consumer (“D2C”) digital gifting marketplace), SpendPro (a D2C spend
management platform), and RewardOn (our business-to-business-to-consumer (“B2B2C”) rewards and loyalty platform). We also
offer technical and platform development services to businesses, which we have branded as “DevStack” (business-to-business
“B2B”).

We act as a program manager, business correspondent and distribution agent for non-reloadable prepaid payment instruments
(“PPIs”) with a maximum value of ₹10,000 issued by banks and RBI licensed issuers (which we refer to as “PPI Issuers” and such
cards, “Prepaid Cards”) and act as a distribution agent for non-reloadable brand gift cards (PPIs) issued by merchants (which we
refer to as “Gift Cards”). We refer to these activities as our “PPI Program Management and Distribution” business. We offer
consumer spend management through our SpendPro platform to our users of the Prepaid Cards.

Our Rewards and Loyalty business comprises: (i) reward points and our own reward points card, the “yayyy Reward Points Card”,
which can be purchased directly through our digital gifting marketplace on the yayyy.shop website and mobile application and used
to redeem Gift Cards and Prepaid Cards available on our marketplace; and (ii) our RewardOn platform, a comprehensive, end-to-
end digital rewards and incentives platform that enables corporate customers to design, manage, and distribute reward points to user
beneficiaries which can be redeemed digitally through a configurable rules engine integrated with a customised catalogue of Gift
Cards, Prepaid Cards and the yayyy Reward Points Card. We refer to these activities as our “Rewards and Loyalty” business.

Our business model is built around technology infrastructure that enables enterprises, our ecosystem partners who act as referral
agents and distribution partners (“Ecosystem Partners”) and users who transact across our platforms. Our business strategy
includes, (i) continuing to expand our user base across all of our offerings (ii) enhancing our technology and infrastructure, (iii)
enhancing our existing products and develop new products and services to address a broader set of use cases (iv) increase the
number of our business partnerships and alliances to expand our offerings and (v) enhancing the visibility of the “Paramotor” brand.
For further details, see “Our Business” on page 210.

As the adoption of digital gifts, rewards, Prepaid Cards and fintech software continues to grow, we believe that expenditure towards
customer acquisition, retention and brand and business promotion initiatives, technology development initiatives, cloud
infrastructure services and IT assets, and office infrastructure will be critical to support the expansion of our platform ecosystem
and increasing transaction volumes across our offerings. For further details, see “Our Business – Market Opportunities” on page
226.

Our Company proposes to utilise the Net Proceeds towards the following objects:

    1.   Expenditure towards customer acquisition, retention and brand and business promotion initiatives;
    2.   Investment in technology development initiatives, cloud infrastructure services and IT assets;
    3.   Investment in office infrastructure; and
    4.   General corporate purposes.

(collectively, referred to herein as the “Objects”)

of our brand name and creation of a public market for the Equity Shares in India. The main objects and objects incidental and
ancillary to the main objects set out in the Memorandum of Association of our Company enable us: (i) to undertake our existing

Such initiatives are particularly intended to support our D2C platform yayyy.shop and the Rewards and Loyalty Business by driving

historical expenditure towards customer acquisition and retention incentives disclosed below.

 A. Customer acquisition and retention incentives

We propose to utilise ₹3,200.00 million out of the Net Proceeds towards customer acquisition and retention incentives designed to
increase user acquisition and retention, enhance engagement levels among existing users and increase transaction volumes across
our digital platforms.

We earn revenue from (i) acting as a program manager, business correspondent and distribution agent for Prepaid Cards from our
share of interchange fees generated on spends on Prepaid Cards at merchant outlets (ii) commission income from Gift Card
Aggregators for facilitating the distribution of Gift Cards to users. Therefore, our revenue from operations is linked to the transaction
volumes of users of the Prepaid Cards and Gift Cards for our PPI Program Management and Distribution business. We also generate
(i) Platform Fee/Service Fee i.e. revenue from providing technical and platform development services to businesses, under
“DevStack” (ii) revenue from offering our RewardOn platform to corporate customers and reward points or our own reward points
card, the “yayyy Reward Points Card”, directly to users through our digital gifting marketplace. Therefore, for our DevStack and
Rewards and Loyalty Business, our revenue from operations is dependent on corporate customer acquisition, platform adoption,
and transaction and redemption activity across our rewards ecosystem.

We plan to increase the amount we spend on (a) customer acquisition incentives paid to Ecosystem Partners for referring users and
corporate customers to our offerings (b) incentives offered to users to promote usage of the Prepaid Cards, Gift Cards, and reward
points we offer, drive issuance and spending volumes, and increase overall monetisation per user.

Cashbacks, instant incentives, and funded promotional rewards act as a major demand and revenue driver in India’s digital gift card
ecosystem. Attractive discounts, cashback offers, user rewards and bonus value on digital gift cards act as a strong demand driver
among both consumers and corporates. Further, companies are increasingly adopting a referral led growth layer alongside their
D2C channels. While mobile apps, websites, and digital campaigns enable direct acquisition and engagement, referral networks /
agents including affiliates, influencers, content platforms, and digital partners help expand reach and accelerate user acquisition.
Referral partners often bring access to high-intent consumer segments, resulting in improved conversion rates and more efficient
acquisition. While referral incentives are typically paid to ecosystem partners, a portion of these incentives is often indirectly passed
on to end users through promotional benefits such as cashback, discounts, or bonus rewards, thereby improving customer acquisition
efficiency and enhancing value perception, while also maintaining partner engagement. (source: F&S Report, page 46)
We plan to collaborate with additional Ecosystem Partners to extend our reach to additional corporate clients and expand our reach
to additional users for the Prepaid Cards and Gift Cards. To expand the number of our Ecosystem Partners, we plan to undertake
                                                                   98
focused research and development initiatives, identify and target Ecosystem Partners in existing and new segments whose offerings
can be enabled and offered on our Gift Card and Prepaid Card infrastructure, allowing us to leverage such partners’ existing
capabilities, distribution strengths and established user bases. In addition, we plan to onboard Ecosystem Partners in complementing
businesses by offering a white-label rewards and loyalty platform, enabling them to launch and manage customised rewards
programmes under their own brand using our technology stack, without significant incremental infrastructure investments by such
partners. We will offer this product through our DevStack business. For further details, see “Our Business – Our Strategies –
Continue to expand our user base across all of our offerings” on page 222.

We have historically paid customer acquisition incentives to Ecosystem Partners for our PPI Program Management and Distribution
Business and our Rewards and Loyalty Business. However, as mentioned above, we expect to incur such incentives for our
DevStack business as well. In terms of our existing arrangements with Ecosystem Partners,

1.   the incentives payable to Ecosystem Partners for the referral or distribution of our Gift Cards and Prepaid Cards are typically
     structured as a variable consideration, linked to factors such as number of customers/users onboarded, the interchange fee
     earned, load value, or transaction volume on the underlying card.
2.   In respect of referrals for our Rewards and Loyalty Business and DevStack business, the incentive is typically structured as a
     consideration linked to number of customers/users onboarded or a mutually agreed case-to-case revenue share on amounts
     earned by the Company from the referred corporates.

The incentive structure may have to be revised from time to time, to reflect changing commercial objectives.

Our agreements with Ecosystem Partners are non-exclusive referral and distribution arrangements and we retain the right to enter
into similar agreements with other parties. No minimum referral volumes or minimum commission payments are committed to any
Ecosystem Partner, and the applicable commission structure may be revised, at our sole discretion or in certain cases, by mutual
agreement. The agreements are generally valid for an initial term and renew automatically unless terminated, with termination
possible by either party on written notice in the event of breach, insolvency, cessation of business, or regulatory non-compliance.

Historical expenditure on customer acquisition and retention incentives

In the context of our PPI Program Management and Distribution Business and our Rewards and Loyalty Business, incentives are
typically in the nature of customer acquisition incentives paid to Ecosystem Partners to refer users and corporate customers to our
offerings, as well as customer acquisition and retention incentives offered to users to promote purchase of Gift Cards and Prepaid
Cards and redemption of reward points on our platforms. Such incentives typically include reward points credited to user wallets
and discounts on purchase of Gift Cards on the yayyy.shop website and mobile application. The Gift Cards can be purchased directly
or through redemption of reward points or our ‘yayyy Reward Points Card’. Our ‘yayyy Reward Points Card’ in turn can be either
purchased directly or procured by beneficiaries through our RewardOn platform. From time to time, we also run special incentives
for festive occasions like Diwali such as additional discounts on Gift Cards or gifts offered to first few purchasers on such occasions.
These incentives are intended to contribute to an increase in the number of users transacting on our platforms, encourage purchases
of Gift Cards and Prepaid Cards, and drive engagement, transaction volumes as well as value and increase user retention across our
platforms. Such incentives are recognised as expenses in the statement of profit and loss in accordance with applicable accounting
standards.

(1) Total transacting users refers to the number of users who have completed at least one transaction within the period/year.
(2) User retention rate refers to the percentage of transacting users in a given year who had also transacted in the immediately preceding year. This metric is only
evaluated on an annual basis.
(3) The average revenue per transacting user is calculated as revenue from operations divided by total transacting users. We consider total revenue from operations
to be a more meaningful metric than average revenue per transacting user. Revenue from our Rewards and Loyalty Business and DevStack is recognised on a gross
basis while Program Fee revenue is recognised on a net basis in accordance with Ind AS 115, and a single user journey may simultaneously generate both gross

                                                                                100
and net inflows across business verticals, making per-user metrics less meaningful in our view. Further, under the RBI regulatory framework governing PPIs, we
receive only a consolidated share of interchange from PPI issuers and do not have access to card-level or user-level spend data.
(4) Average user acquisition and retention expenses per transacting is calculated as user acquisition and retention expenses divided by total transacting users. We
consider user acquisition and retention expenses as a percentage of revenue from operations to be a more meaningful metric than average user acquisition and
retention expenses per transacting user. User acquisition and retention expenses may be incurred at an offering/platform/distribution-channel level and may not be
attributable to specific users, and expenditure incurred in a period may result to users acquired or retained in a different period.
(5) Includes certain amounts paid to certain related parties for referral and distribution services. For further details, see “Restated Financial Information – Notes
to Restated Financial Information - Note 42 - Related Party Disclosures” on page 309. All such payments were made on an arms’ length basis and no portion of
the Net Proceeds are proposed to be paid to such related parties.

Proposed utilisation of Net Proceeds

The proposed expenditure is expected to support the growth of our digital ecosystem. Higher customer acquisition, retention and
engagement levels are expected to contribute to increased transaction volumes across our offerings. We expect such increase to lead
to improved revenues and strengthen our overall ecosystem economics. While the actual impact on revenue and margins will depend
on user adoption levels, transaction behaviour, the commercial terms across our offerings, and other market conditions, we believe
that the calibrated deployment of customer acquisition and retention incentives will support scaling of transaction volumes across
our offerings.

 B. Brand and Business Promotion Initiatives

We propose to utilize ₹350.00 million out of the Net Proceeds towards brand and business promotion initiatives aimed at supporting
customer acquisition, retention and engagement across our platforms. Our consumer-facing platforms, SpendPro and yayyy.shop,
are D2C in nature. As a financial technology company focused on digital gifting, consumer spend management, and rewards &
loyalty platforms, brand visibility and platform awareness are important drivers for expanding our user base and strengthening
engagement across our ecosystem. Investments in structured marketing initiatives are therefore expected to support the expansion
of our platform ecosystem by improving brand awareness and visibility, strengthening enterprise adoption and encouraging greater
participation by users across our products and services. Further, our revenue is linked to user activity and transaction volumes across
our platforms, and these initiatives are intended to support increased engagement.

Historical expenditure on brand and business promotion initiatives

Our historical brand and business promotion expenditure has been funded from internal accruals and may not be fully reflective of
our future growth plans and new developments in relation to this object. We have predominantly outsourced our marketing function.

We have engaged third-party agencies to assist us in our efforts to increase brand awareness through media publications and for
providing services pertaining to search engine optimization, website content review and optimization, digital clean-up and accuracy
enhancement, social media and performance marketing services, and contextual online monitoring. For instance, in the past, we
engaged The Blind Spot Media, to provide organic public relations, news and press dissemination services to help build media
authority and search engine visibility. Further, we also engaged Alphacret Studio to provide services pertaining to social media
content creation and performance marketing. Some of the key initiatives we have recently undertaken include developing the
corporate brand identity by way of product catalogues, website optimisation and continuing to engage in customer communication
initiatives. Further, to support the launch of academic-industry collaboration through a memorandum of understanding with a
university to establish a multi-faculty, multi-department hub within institutional premises, we entered into arrangement with third
parties for press release and social media carousel.

Examples of our past brand and business promotion initiatives include social media content and advertisements for our offerings
such as yayyy.shop, communication campaigns around occasions such as Women’s Day, New Years’, informational blog posts on
our Company’s website and outdoor advertising of our offerings. We have participated in and were one of the platinum sponsors of
an industry-focused event titled the Global Fintech Fest, 2026 where we undertook activities such as establishing a dedicated booth,
                                                                                101
display of product launch videos and distribution of branded merchandise. We also participated in a fintech focused event titled
“Afinatics 3.0” held at Chitkara University, Punjab, India as an “Industry Partner”.

Our brand and business promotion initiatives are designed to support both corporate customer outreach and user engagement.
Typically, while corporate customers access our platforms through direct relationships and Ecosystem Partners, users are
onboarded, in part, through digital engagement initiatives such as social media advertisements and promotional campaigns.

2.   Investment in technology development initiatives, cloud infrastructure services and IT assets

We propose to utilise ₹940.00 million out of the Net Proceeds over the current and next two Fiscals towards investment in
technology development initiatives, cloud infrastructure services and IT assets. We intend to utilise the aforementioned amount
towards (a) investments in cloud infrastructure services and IT assets and (b) investment in technology development initiatives.

We consider our technology platform to be a key enabler of our business strategy and growth. Our core offerings, including
SpendPro, RewardOn, yayyy.shop and DevStack, are built on technology platforms conceptualised, designed and developed
primarily in-house. These platforms enable us to provide tailored solutions across our ecosystem for rewards, consumer spend
management, digital gifting and technical and platform development services.

The proposed expenditure represents a significant increase compared to our historical expenditure towards technology development
initiatives, cloud infrastructure services and IT assets and is not derived from or anchored to our historical expenditure. The proposed
expenditure from the Net Proceeds is expected to support the continued expansion of our platform ecosystem and enable us to

                                                                       103
accommodate new use cases and higher transaction volumes, support integrations with enterprises and Ecosystem Partners and
enhance the security and reliability of our systems.

The increase in the number of total transacting users from 43,269 in Fiscal 2025, to 1,575,830 in Fiscal 2026, and from 107,403 in
the three-month period ended June 30, 2025 to 634,316 in the three-month period ended June 30, 2026, necessitated immediate
scaling of cloud infrastructure as also reflected in our historical expenditure towards cloud infrastructure and hosting services. In
line with the expansion of our Rewards and Loyalty Business, yayyy.shop website and DevStack business which were launched in
Fiscal 2026 and the proposed deployment of Net Proceeds towards objects such as customer acquisition, retention and brand and
business promotion initiatives, we expect to incur higher expenses in the future. Further, particularly for our DevStack business, we
require additional personnel for our IT and product development team to support project delivery. The proposed expansion is also
intended to support our future technology roadmap and ongoing operations for our existing offerings such as yayyy.shop, SpendPro,
and RewardOn.

For risks involved, see “Risk Factors – 9. We intend to utilise a portion of the Net Proceeds to fund investments in technology
development initiatives and cloud infrastructure services, the outcome of which cannot be ascertained.” on page 29.

We propose to utilise ₹240.00 million out of the Net Proceeds towards cloud infrastructure services, and IT assets in the manner set
herein. Such utilisation is expected to support engineering, product development, cybersecurity, our platform operations, technology
roadmap and sales functions.

Historical expenditure on cloud infrastructure and hosting services

Our historical expenditure towards cloud infrastructure and hosting services availed is set out below:

During Fiscal 2024, our platform operated primarily as a single-vertical business focused on our Program Fee business model, that
required low base cloud container resources to support the limited user base in these periods. In Fiscals 2025 and 2026, user volumes
expanded to 43,269 and 1,575,830 respectively compared to 18,248 in Fiscal 2024, driving a corresponding increase in application
logging and data records, thereby increasing annualized cloud infrastructure and hosting services expenses to ₹0.46 million and
₹2.61 million in Fiscals 2025 and 2026 respectively, compared to ₹0.24 million in Fiscal 2024.

During Fiscal 2026 and the three-month period ended June 30, 2026, our expenditure towards cloud infrastructure and hosting
services increased to ₹2.61 million and ₹2.35 million respectively, compared to ₹0.46 million in Fiscal 2025, primarily due to the
scale-up in platform activity and user adoption from 1,575,830 users and 634,316 users for Fiscal 2026 and three months ended
June 30, 2026 respectively, compared to 43,269 users in Fiscal 2025. In particular, the launch of our digital gifting marketplace on
yayyy.shop website and mobile application (available on a well-known marketplace) and the launch of our Rewards and loyalty
business propelled the number of transacting users on our platforms to 1.58 million and 0.63 million during Fiscal 2026 and the
three-month period ended June 30, 2026, respectively, from 0.04 million in Fiscal 2025, which resulted in higher requirements for
investments in cloud infrastructure services. Since our platforms are built as a secure, multi-tenant, API-driven infrastructure that
manages our catalogue of Gift Cards (234 as of June 30, 2026), Prepaid Cards and the yayyy Reward Points Card, the volume of
data records, file micro-storage layers, and computing engine uptime increased. We expect these requirements to continue to
increase to support our existing transacting users and further increases in transaction volumes.

 B. Investment in technology development initiatives

We propose to utilise ₹700.00 million over the current and next two Fiscals towards investment in technology development
initiatives by way of retaining and recruiting additional personnel for our IT and product development teams on a full time and
permanent basis. Our technology development initiatives have historically been undertaken through a mix of relatively lean internal
IT and product development teams, supplemented by selective engagements of external technical development and project-based
service providers. To meet the evolving requirements of our customers and continue enhancing our platforms, we require additional
specialised personnel skilled in product development, engineering and platform management.

Historical expenditure towards our technology development initiatives

As of August 31, 2026 our IT and product development function comprised of 12 employees. The function is led by our Chief
Technology Officer, Mohit Juneja, who has been associated with our Company since January 22, 2026. Through a combination of
internal and external resources, we developed SpendPro (our D2C spend management platform), yayyy.shop (our D2C digital
gifting marketplace), and RewardOn (our B2B2C rewards and loyalty platform). These platforms are integrated with relevant third-
party systems for issuance, redemption, and settlement, enabling real-time synchronization and automation across the value chain.

Through our DevStack business, which we launched in the first quarter of Fiscal 2026, we offer technical and platform development
services designed for the creation of customised enterprise software applications. For instance, we entered into a platform
enhancement and modernisation engagement for an Indian company providing corporate expense management segment (the
“Client”) while maintaining continuity of live operations. The scope included technology architecture modernisation, automation
enablement using AI-based components, improving integrations with other applications, API enhancements, mobile app
development, and enhancement of risk management, compliance, analytics and security features. For more details, see “Our
Business – Our Products and Services - DevStack” and “Our Business – Technology, Research and Development” on pages 230 and
232 respectively.

maintenance of our technology platforms.

3.   Investment in office infrastructure

We propose to utilise ₹380.00 million out of the Net Proceeds towards setting up eight new office premises on lease in Mumbai,
Chandigarh Capital Region, Delhi NCR, Bengaluru, Chennai, Hyderabad, Kolkata and Pune in India. While the proposed
expenditure is not derived from or anchored to our historical expenditure, these locations represent key commercial centres, talent
hubs and enterprise clusters which we believe are important for supporting the anticipated expansion of our business operations
including through accessing relevant talent pools and expanding our workforce, augmenting our customer base, enhancing customer
servicing and support functions, and strengthening relationships with enterprise clients and Ecosystem Partners. For risks involved,
see “Risk Factors – 8. We intend to utilise a portion of the Net Proceeds to fund investment in office infrastructure. If we are unable
to find suitable locations or if the lease or license payments for these locations are in excess of our estimates, our business financial
condition, results of operations and cash flows may be adversely affected” on page 28.

4.   General corporate purposes

We propose to utilise a portion of the Net Proceeds aggregating up to ₹[●] million towards general corporate purposes, in
accordance with applicable provisions of the SEBI ICDR Regulations, provided that the amount utilised towards general
corporate purposes shall not exceed 25% of the Gross Proceeds. Further, we shall not utilise the amount of Net Proceeds
proposed to be utilized towards general corporate purposes for purposes towards the other identified objects of the Offer in (1)
to (3) above.

The funds utilised towards general corporate purposes may include, among other things, funding of organic growth
opportunities (such as expenses pertaining to expansion into new geographies, launch of new product verticals, or investments
necessitated due to regulatory requirements, among others), inorganic growth opportunities such as undertaking strategic
acquisitions of complementary businesses, technologies, or platforms that may be identified and evaluated post-listing, meeting
our working capital requirements and inventory build-up (such as funding receivables or procurement of PPIs), insurance
premiums, repairs and maintenance, payment of taxes, duties, statutory dues, employee and other personnel expenses (other
than those pertaining to our IT and product development teams), and other similar expenses incurred in the ordinary course of
our business or towards any exigencies, subject to compliance with applicable laws. A portion of such funds may also be
deployed towards general administrative expenses including legal, consultancy and compliance costs, and meeting
contingencies, other operational requirements such as overhead expenses and any other purpose, as may be approved by our
Board or a duly constituted committee thereof from time to time, subject to compliance with applicable law, including
provisions of the Companies Act. The utilisation of funds towards general corporate purposes will be determined by our Board
of Directors or a duly constituted committee thereof, based on our business requirements from time to time, in accordance with
applicable laws.

Monitoring of utilization of funds

In terms of Regulation 41 of the SEBI ICDR Regulations, our Company shall appoint a Monitoring Agency to monitor the

₹1,000.00 million. Our Audit Committee and the Monitoring Agency will monitor the utilisation of the Gross Proceeds, and
the Monitoring Agency shall submit the report required under Regulation 41(2) of the SEBI ICDR Regulations, on a quarterly
basis, until such time as the Gross Proceeds have been utilised in full. Our Company undertakes to place the report(s) of the
Monitoring Agency on receipt before the Audit Committee without any delay. Our Company will disclose the utilisation of the
Gross Proceeds, including interim use under a separate head in its balance sheet for such Fiscal periods as required under the
SEBI ICDR Regulations, the SEBI Listing Regulations and any other applicable laws or regulations, clearly specifying the
purposes for which the Gross Proceeds have been utilised, till the time any part of the Gross Proceeds remains unutilised. Our
Company will also, in its balance sheet for the applicable Fiscal periods, provide details, if any, in relation to all such Gross
Proceeds that have not been utilised, if any, of such currently unutilised Gross Proceeds. Our Company shall, for the purpose

each object of the Offer until the Gross Proceeds have been utilised in full. Further, our Company, on a quarterly basis, shall
include the deployment of Gross Proceeds under various heads, as applicable, in the notes to our quarterly results. Our Company
will indicate investments, if any, of unutilised Gross Proceeds in the balance sheet of our Company for the relevant Fiscal
periods subsequent to receipt of listing and trading approvals from the Stock Exchanges. In the event that a portion of the Gross
Proceeds is utilized towards acquisitions, strategic partnerships or any inorganic growth initiatives, details in such regard, will
be published on the website of our Company and disclosed to the Stock Exchanges in accordance with Regulation 30 and
Schedule III of the SEBI Listing Regulations, as applicable.

Pursuant to Regulation 18(3) and Regulation 32(3) of the SEBI Listing Regulations, our Company shall on a quarterly basis
disclose to the Audit Committee the uses and application of the Gross Proceeds. The Audit Committee shall make
recommendations to our Board for further action, if appropriate. Our Company shall, on an annual basis, prepare a statement
of funds utilised for purposes other than those stated in this Updated Draft Red Herring Prospectus – I and place it before our
Audit Committee. Such disclosure shall be made only until such time that all the Net Proceeds have been utilised in full. The
statement shall be certified by the Statutory Auditor and such certification shall be provided to the Monitoring Agency. Further,
in accordance with Regulation 32 of the SEBI Listing Regulations, our Company shall furnish to the Stock Exchanges on a
quarterly basis, a statement indicating (i) deviations, if any, in the utilisation of the Gross Proceeds from the objects of the Offer
as stated above; and (ii) details of category wise variations in the utilisation of the Gross Proceeds from the objects of the Offer
as stated above. In the event that a portion of the Gross Proceeds is utilized towards acquisitions, strategic partnerships or any
inorganic growth initiatives, details in such regard, will be published on the website of our Company and disclosed to the Stock
Exchanges in accordance with Regulation 30 and Schedule III of the SEBI Listing Regulations, as applicable.

                                                                 123
                                                 BASIS FOR OFFER PRICE

The Price Band and Offer Price will be determined by our Company, in consultation with the BRLMs and in accordance with
applicable laws, on the basis of assessment of market demand for the Equity Shares offered through the Book Building Process
and on the basis of quantitative and qualitative factors as described below. The face value of the Equity Shares is ₹10 each and
the Offer Price is [●] times the Floor Price and [●] times the Cap Price, and Floor Price is [●] times the face value and the Cap
Price is [●] times the face value. Investors should also see “Risk Factors”, “Summary of Restated Financial Information”, “Our
Business”, “Restated Financial Information”, and “Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results
of Operations” beginning on pages 20, 65, 210, 271 and 323, respectively, to have an informed view before making an
investment decision.

Qualitative Factors

We believe that some of the qualitative factors and our strengths which form the basis for computing the Offer Price are as
follows:

    1.   Digital direct to consumer ecosystem powering retail consumption through prepaid spends, gifting and rewards

Prepaid cards, including reloadable and non-reloadable variants, have become integral to modern consumer behaviour, with
total prepaid transactions in India estimated to reach 2.0 billion in Calendar Year 2025 and ₹700.9 billion in terms of transaction
value reflecting broad adoption across categories such as retail, travel, and everyday purchases (source: F&S Report, page 16).
Growth is expected to remain consistent over the next five years, with total prepaid transactions in India projected to reach 4.5
billion and ₹1,028.9 billion in value by Calendar Year 2030, reflecting strong acceptance of the prepaid card model (source: F&S
Report, page 16). From Calendar Year 2025 to Calendar Year 2030, India’s digital gift card market is projected to grow at a
robust CAGR of 17.4%, reaching USD 33.65 billion by Calendar Year 2030 (source: F&S Report, page 22).

    2.   Large and growing retail end user base with strong retention rates

We have built a large retail transacting user base, with transacting users increasing from 107,403 for the three months period
ended June 30, 2025 to 634,316 for the three months period ended June 30, 2026, and from 18,248 for Fiscal 2024 to 1,575,830
for Fiscal 2026, representing a CAGR of 829.28%.

    3.   Technology platforms driving scalable enterprise solutions

Our Company has built and operates in-house, microservices-based technology platforms designed to handle high volumes of
digital transactions and support enterprise-grade B2B use cases.

    4.   Ability to grow and sustain partnerships

We have grown our partnerships (which are our PPI Partners and the Gift Card Aggregators we act as distribution agents for
(collectively “Partners”)) from two Partners at March 31, 2024 to 11 Partners as at June 30, 2026 with no discontinuance of
any partnership.

    5.   Strong financial performance and financial metrics

Our revenue from operations increased from ₹209.16 million for the three months period ended June 30, 2025 to ₹2,527.65
million for the three months period ended June 30, 2026, an increase of 1,108.49%. Our EBITDA increased from ₹123.35 million
for the three months period ended June 30, 2025 to ₹326.19 million for the three months period ended June 30, 2026, an increase
of 164.44%. Our profit after tax for the period/year from continuing operations increased from ₹92.25 million for the three
months period ended June 30, 2025 to ₹238.05 million for the three months period ended June 30, 2026, an increase of 158.05%.

Notes:
(1) Revenue from operations for the period/year as appearing in the Statement of Profit and Loss in the Restated Financial Information
(2) EBITDA is an acronym for earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation, which has been calculated by adding (i) finance
      costs, (ii) total tax expenses and (iii) depreciation and amortisation expense, and subtracting other income from profit after tax from
      continuing operations for the period/year (“EBITDA”).
(3) EBITDA Margin is EBITDA expressed as a percentage of revenue from operations (“EBITDA Margin”).
(4) Profit after tax for the period/year from continuing operations as appearing in the Statement of profit and Loss in the Restated Financial
      Information.
(5) PAT Margin is profit after tax for the period/year from continuing operations expressed as a percentage of revenue from operations (“PAT
      Margin”).
(6) Current Ratio is calculated as total current assets divided by total current liabilities.
(7) Net Capital Turnover Ratio is calculated as revenue from operations (from continuing operations) divided by Working Capital. Working
      Capital is calculated as current assets minus current liabilities (“Working Capital”).
(8) Return on Equity is calculated as Profit/(loss) for the period/year from continuing operations divided by Average Total Equity. Average Total
      Equity is calculated as total equity as at the beginning of the period/year plus total equity as at the end of the period/year, divided by two
      (“Average Total Equity”).
(9) Reward points business refers to revenue from our Rewards & loyalty business. This revenue is recognised on a gross basis.
(10) Program Fees refers to revenue from our PPI Program Management and Distribution business. This revenue is recognised on a net basis.
(11) Platform Fee/Service Fee refers to revenue from providing technical and platform development services to businesses, which we have branded
      as “DevStack”. This revenue is recognised on a gross basis.
(12) User Retention Rate refers to the percentage of transacting users in a given year who had also transacted in the immediately preceding year.
      This metric is only evaluated on an annual basis.
(13) Total transacting Users refers to the number of users who have completed at least one transaction within the period/year .
(14) The average revenue per transacting user is calculated as revenue from operations divided by total transacting users. We consider total
      revenue from operations to be a more meaningful metric than average revenue per transacting user. Revenue from our Rewards and Loyalty
      Business and DevStack is recognised on a gross basis while Program Fee revenue is recognised on a net basis in accordance with Ind AS
      115, and a single user journey may simultaneously generate both gross and net inflows across business verticals, making per-user metrics
      less meaningful in our view. Further, under the RBI regulatory framework governing Prepaid Payment Instruments, we receive only a
      consolidated share of interchange from PPI issuers and do not have access to card-level or user-level spend data.
(15) User acquisition and retention expenses for the period/year as appearing in the Statement of Profit and Loss in the Restated Financial
      Information. Includes certain amounts paid to certain related parties for referral and distribution services. For further details, see “Restated
      Financial Information – Notes to Restated Financial Information - Note 42: Related Party Disclosures” on page 309. All such payments were
      made on an arms’ length basis and no portion of the Net Proceeds are proposed to be paid to such related parties.
(16) User acquisition and retention expenses as a percentage of revenue from operations refers to user acquisition and retention expenses divided
      by revenue from operations.
(17) Average user acquisition and retention expenses per transacting user refers to total user acquisition and retention expenses divided by total
      transacting users. We consider user acquisition and retention expenses as a percentage of revenue from operations to be a more meaningful
      metric than average user acquisition and retention expenses per transacting user. User acquisition and retention expenses may be incurred
      at an offering/platform/distribution-channel level and may not be attributable to specific users, and expenditure incurred in a period may
      result to users acquired or retained in a different period.
