G. Description on the historic use of the KPIs by our Company to analyse, track or monitor the operational
   and/or financial performance of our Company

    In evaluating our business, we consider and use certain KPIs, as presented above, as a supplemental measure to review
    and assess our financial and operating performance. The presentation of these KPIs are not intended to be considered
    in isolation or as a substitute for the Restated Financial Information. We use these KPIs to evaluate our financial and
    operating performance. Some of these KPIs are not defined under Ind AS and are not presented in accordance with
    Ind AS. These KPIs have limitations as analytical tools. Further, these KPIs may differ from the similar information
    used by other companies and hence their comparability may be limited. Therefore, these metrics should not be
    considered in isolation or construed as an alternative to Ind AS measures of performance or as an indicator of our
    operating performance, liquidity, profitability or results of operation. Although these KPIs are not a measure of
    performance calculated in accordance with applicable accounting standards, our Company’s management believes that
    it provides an additional tool for investors to use in evaluating our ongoing operating results and trends and in
    comparing our financial results with other companies in our industry because it provides consistency and comparability
    with past financial performance, when taken collectively with financial measures prepared in accordance with Ind AS.

    Investors are encouraged to review the Ind AS financial measures and to not rely on any single financial or operational
    metric to evaluate our business. See “Risk Factors – 48. This Updated Draft Red Herring Prospectus – I contains non-
    GAAP financial measures and other selected statistical information related to our operations and financial
    performance. These non-GAAP measures and statistical information may vary from any standard methodology that is
    applicable across the industry, and therefore may not be comparable with financial or statistical information of similar
    nomenclature computed and presented by other industry peers.” on page 52.

b.          Comparison of our KPIs:

We are a financial technology company focused on digital gifting, consumer spend management, and rewards & loyalty platforms.
Our Company does not have a direct peer for comparison that is listed. We have determined the peers of our Company to include
companies that are operating in the same or closely related business segment(s). Additionally, the listed industry peers have also
been selected considering that:

     •      Pine Labs Limited (“Pine Labs”) is a prominent player in the digital gift card market (operates Woohoo) alongside our
            Company (operates yayyy.shop) (source: F&S Report). In addition to the other services offered, Pine Labs also offers
            prepaid and gift card issuance and processing solutions, loyalty and rewards management platform (source: F&S Report)
            which is closely related to digital gifting, and rewards & loyalty platforms provided by our Company;

     •      Zaggle Prepaid Ocean Services Limited (“Zaggle”) is a prominent player in the Rewards & Loyalty market (source: F&S
            Report). We are also leveraging loyalty platforms and marketplaces (source: F&S Report) by offering RewardOn
            (enterprise and channel loyalty solutions) and yayyy.shop (consumer-focused rewards and gifting marketplace.
            Additionally, Zaggle is a financial technology and SaaS-based spend management company focused on corporate
            payments, prepaid card solutions, employee expense management, rewards and incentives (source: F&S Report) closely
            related to rewards and loyalty solutions provided by our Company; and

     •      Capillary Technologies India Limited (“Capillary”) is a prominent player in the Rewards & Loyalty market (source: F&S
            Report). We are also leveraging loyalty platforms and marketplaces (source: F&S Report) by offering RewardOn
            (enterprise and channel loyalty solutions) and yayyy.shop (consumer-focused rewards and gifting marketplace. Capillary
            also provides cloud-based software platforms and solutions including loyalty program management, rewards management,
            amongst other tools (source: F&S Report) closely related to rewards and loyalty solutions provided by our Company.

          computing financial metrics, the figures presented above reflect the nearest comparable numbers based on available disclosures and may not be strictly
          comparable across the peer set.

            peers may not be directly comparable on a like-for-like basis.

Notes for our Company:
(1) Revenue from operations for the period/year as appearing in the Statement of Profit and Loss in the Restated Financial Information
(2) EBITDA is an acronym for earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation, which has been calculated by adding (i) finance costs, (ii) total tax
     expenses and (iii) depreciation and amortisation expense, and subtracting other income from profit after tax from continuing operations for the period/year
     (“EBITDA”).
(3) EBITDA Margin is EBITDA expressed as a percentage of revenue from operations (“EBITDA Margin”).
(4) Profit after tax for the period/year from continuing operations as appearing in the Statement of profit and Loss in the Restated Financial Information.
(5) PAT Margin is profit after tax for the period/year from continuing operations expressed as a percentage of revenue from operations (“PAT Margin”).
(6) Current Ratio is calculated as total current assets divided by total current liabilities.
(7) Net Capital Turnover Ratio is calculated as revenue from operations (from continuing operations) divided by Working Capital. Working Capital is calculated
     as current assets minus current liabilities (“Working Capital”).
(8) Return on equity (RoE) is calculated as Profit/(loss) for the period/year from continuing operations divided by Average Total Equity. Average Total Equity is
     calculated as total equity as at the beginning of the period/year plus total equity as at the end of the period/year, divided by two (“Average Total Equity”).
(9) Revenue from operations by type of income
•    Reward points business refers to revenue from our Rewards & loyalty business. This revenue is recognised on a gross basis.
•    Program Fees refers to revenue from our PPI Program Management and Distribution business. This revenue is recognised on a net basis.
•    Platform Fee/Service Fee refers to revenue from providing technical and platform development services to businesses, which we have branded as “DevStack”.
     This revenue is recognised on a gross basis.
(10) User Retention Rate refers to the percentage of transacting users in a given year who had also transacted in the immediately preceding year. This metric is
     only evaluated on an annual basis.
(11) Total transacting Users refers to the number of users who have completed at least one transaction within the period/year
(12) The average revenue per transacting user is calculated as revenue from operations divided by total transacting users. We consider total revenue from
     operations to be a more meaningful metric than average revenue per transacting user. Revenue from our Rewards and Loyalty Business and DevStack is
     recognised on a gross basis while Program Fee revenue is recognised on a net basis in accordance with Ind AS 115, and a single user journey may
     simultaneously generate both gross and net inflows across business verticals, making per-user metrics less meaningful in our view. Further, under the RBI
     regulatory framework governing Prepaid Payment Instruments, we receive only a consolidated share of interchange from PPI issuers and do not have access
     to card-level or user-level spend data.
(13) User acquisition and retention expenses for the period/year as appearing in the Statement of Profit and Loss in the Restated Financial Information. Includes
     certain amounts paid to certain related parties for referral and distribution services. For further details, see “Restated Financial Information – Notes to
     Restated Financial Information - Note 42: Related Party Disclosures” on page 309. All such payments were made on an arms’ length basis and no portion of
     the Net Proceeds are proposed to be paid to such related parties.
(14) User acquisition and retention expenses as a percentage of revenue from operations refers to user acquisition and retention expenses divided by revenue from
     operations.
(15) Average user acquisition and retention expenses per transacting user refers to total user acquisition and retention expenses divided by total transacting users.
     We consider user acquisition and retention expenses as a percentage of revenue from operations to be a more meaningful metric than average user acquisition
     and retention expenses per transacting user. User acquisition and retention expenses may be incurred at an offering/platform/distribution-channel level and
     may not be attributable to specific users, and expenditure incurred in a period may result to users acquired or retained in a different period.

                                                    Statement of Tax Benefits

STATEMENT OF POSSIBLE SPECIAL TAX BENEFITS AVAILABLE TO THE COMPANY AND THE
SHAREHOLDERS OF THE COMPANY UNDER THE APPLICABLE DIRECT AND INDIRECT TAX LAWS IN INDIA

This statement of possible special tax benefits is required as per Schedule VI (Part A)(9)(L) of the SEBI ICDR Regulations. While
the term ‘special tax benefits’ has not been defined under the SEBI ICDR Regulations, for the purpose of this Statement, it is
assumed that with respect to special tax benefits available to the Company, the same would include those benefits as enumerated
in this Annexure. Any benefits under the taxation laws other than those specified in this Annexure are considered to be general tax
benefits and therefore not covered within the ambit of this Statement. Further, any benefits available under any other laws within
or outside India, except for those mentioned in this Annexure have not been reviewed and covered by this Statement.

Outlined below are the special tax benefits available to the Company and its shareholders under the Income-tax Act, 2025
read with rules, circulars, and notifications thereunder (hereinafter referred to as ‘ITA Act, 2025’), as amended by the
Finance Act 2026, i.e. applicable for Tax Year 2026-27 (Financial Year 2026-27 relevant to Assessment Year 2027-28) and
presently in force in India.

Under the Income-tax Act, 2025 (“ITA, 2025”)

A. Special Direct tax benefits available to the Company

1. Corporate tax rate under section 200 of ITA, 2025 (erstwhile section 115BAA of the Income Tax Act, 1961 (“IT Act,
   1961)).

   The Company has opted for corporate tax rate of 25.168% (prescribed under section 200 of ITA, 2025 from FY 2021-22. The
   conditions for availing the same are specified in the notes mentioned below.

2. Deduction in respect of inter corporate dividends – section 148 of ITA, 2025 (erstwhile Section 80M of the IT Act, 1961)

   Up to 31st March 2020, any dividend paid to a shareholder by a company was liable to Dividend Distribution Tax (“DDT”),
   and the recipient shareholder was exempt from tax. Pursuant to the amendment made by the Finance Act, 2020, DDT stands
   abolished, and dividend received by a shareholder on or after 1st April, 2020 is liable to tax in the hands of the shareholder. The
   Company is required to deduct Tax Deducted at Source (“TDS”) at applicable rate specified under the Act read with applicable
   Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (“DTAA”) (if any).

   With respect to a resident corporate shareholder, section 148 of the ITA, 2025 (erstwhile section 80M of the IT Act, 1961) has
   been inserted in the Act to remove the cascading effect of taxes on inter-corporate dividends during FY 2020-21 and thereafter.
   The section provides that where the gross total income of a domestic company in any previous year includes any income by
   way of dividends from any other domestic company or a foreign company or a business trust, there shall, in accordance with
   and subject to the provisions of this section, be allowed in computing the total income of such domestic company, a deduction
   of an amount equal to so much of the amount of income by way of dividends received from such other domestic company or
   foreign company or business trust as does not exceed the amount of dividend distributed by it on or before the due date. The
   “due date” means the date one month prior to the date for furnishing the return of income under section 263 of ITA, 2025
   (erstwhile section 139 of the IT Act, 1961). The Company may avail the above-mentioned benefit subject to fulfilment of
   conditions specified under section 148 of the ITA, 2025.

3. Deduction in respect of additional employee cost incurred – Section 146 of ITA, 2025 (erstwhile Section 80JJAA of IT
   Act, 1961).

   The Company is entitled to claim a deduction of an amount equal to thirty percent of additional employee cost incurred in the
   course of the business in the previous year, for three assessment years including the assessment year relevant to the previous
   year in which the employment is provided under section 146 of ITA, 2025, subject to the fulfilment of the prescribed conditions.


B. Special tax benefits available to Shareholders


1. Dividend income earned by the shareholders would be taxable in their hands at the applicable rates. However, in case of domestic
   corporate shareholders, deduction under section 148 of ITA, 2025 would be available on fulfilling the conditions (as discussed
                                                                142
   above). Further, in case of shareholders who are individuals, Hindu Undivided Family, Association of Persons, Body of
   Individuals, whether incorporated or not, surcharge would be restricted to 15%, irrespective of the amount of dividend.

2. As per section 198 of ITA, 2025 (erstwhile section 112A of the IT Act, 1961), long term capital gains arising from transfer of
   an equity shares shall be taxed at 12.5% (without indexation), plus applicable surcharge and cess, subject to fulfillment of
   prescribed conditions. Tax shall be levied where such capital gains exceed INR 125,000.

3. As per section 196 of ITA, 2025 (erstwhile section 111A of the IT Act, 1961), short term capital gains arising from transfer of
   an equity share, or a unit of an equity-oriented fund or a unit of a business trust shall be taxed at 20% subject to fulfilment of
   prescribed conditions under the Act.

   Further, the surcharge on capital gains shall be restricted to 15%.

4. In respect of non-resident shareholders, the tax rates and the consequent taxation shall be further subject to any benefits available
   under the applicable DTAA, if any, between India and the relevant country subject to entitlement.

1        India Macroeconomic Outlook

         India is among the fastest-growing major economies in the world, with the IMF projecting real GDP growth of 6.4% in
         Fiscal Year 2026–27. India’s growth outlook is underpinned by sustained public capital expenditure (CAPEX), budgeted
         at ₹12.22 trillion (approximately USD 138 billion) for Fiscal Year 2026–27, resilient domestic consumption and services
         activity, and ongoing structural reforms.

         Moreover, compared with advanced economies, many of which face elevated public debt and ageing-related spending
         pressures, India benefits from relatively lower public debt levels (84.1% of GDP in Fiscal Year 2026 compared with
         108.2% of GDP in Calendar Year 2026 for advanced economies), alongside an expanding consumer base and competitive
         labour costs.

         While geopolitical tensions, elevated energy prices and global trade uncertainty pose near-term risks, India’s domestic
         demand led growth model, sustained investment and policy reforms provide a strong foundation for continued economic
         expansion. The IMF projects India’s growth at 6.4% in 2026, compared with 1.7% for advanced economies and 3.8% for
         emerging market and developing economies, underscoring India’s comparatively strong growth outlook.

1.1      India’s Leap in Nominal GDP by 2040

         India is expected to move from being the 6th largest economy in 2019 to the 4th largest by 2026, and further to the 3rd
         largest by 2030. By 2040, India’s nominal GDP is projected to reach USD11.5 trillion, more than double the 2026 GDP
         of Germany, Japan, and the United Kingdom (UK).

         Exhibit 1: Top 10 Countries Based on Nominal GDP, USD Trillion, Global, 2019, 2022, 2026, 2030, 2040

      India’s real GDP expanded by 7.1% in Fiscal Year 2025 and accelerated to 7.7% in Fiscal Year 2026, supported by robust
      private consumption, investment activity and strong growth across manufacturing and services. In Fiscal Year 2026,
      private final consumption expenditure grew by 7.7%, while gross fixed capital formation expanded by 7.1%;
      manufacturing, trade and financial, real estate and professional services recorded particularly strong growth. Growth is
      expected to moderate but remain strong in Fiscal Year 2027, with the IMF projecting real GDP growth of 6.4%, supported
      by resilient private consumption and services activity. Despite continued global trade uncertainty and geopolitical risks,
      India is expected to remain among the fastest-growing major economies globally.

      The September 2025 Goods and Services Tax (GST) reforms, effective from 22 September 2025, simplified the GST
      structure from the previous four principal slabs of 5%, 12%, 18% and 28% to two main rates of 5% and 18%, alongside a
                                                                                          146
      40% special rate for specified luxury and sin goods. Rate reductions across a broad range of goods and services were
      intended to lower consumer prices, support household demand and simplify compliance for businesses. In addition, the
      Union Budget 2025–26 introduced significant personal income-tax relief under the new tax regime. Resident individuals
      with normal income of up to ₹1.20 million have no income-tax liability after the applicable rebate, while salaried taxpayers
      can have income of up to ₹1.275 million with no tax liability after the ₹75,000 standard deduction. The revised tax slabs
      and rebates were designed to increase disposable income and support household consumption, savings and investment.

1.3   India’s Inflation Outlook

      India’s inflation fell sharply during Fiscal Year 2026, averaging just 1.7% during April–December 2025, primarily due to
      a correction in food prices, favourable agricultural conditions, supply-side interventions and favourable base effects.

      Inflationary pressures have, however, strengthened in Fiscal Year 2027. Under India’s revised Consumer Price Index (CPI)
      series (2024=100), headline inflation increased from 3.9% in May 2026 to 4.4% in June, 4.5% in July and 4.8% in August
      2026, with food inflation reaching 6.0% in August.

      Over the medium term, inflation is expected to remain broadly around the RBI’s 4.0% inflation target, although food and
      commodity price volatility remain important risks. The RBI’s inflation targeting framework currently specifies a 4.0%
      CPI inflation target with a tolerance band of 2.0–6.0%. The inflation outlook is supported by domestic supply conditions
      and policy measures, but remains sensitive to food prices, weather conditions, global energy and commodity prices, and
      geopolitical and supply-chain disruptions.

1.4   Fiscal Year India Per Capita Income and Demographic Outlook

      India’s per capita income, as measured by Gross National Income (GNI) per capita at current prices, increased from
      ₹186,184 in Fiscal Year 2023 to ₹204,746 in Fiscal Year 2024, ₹222,989 in Fiscal Year 2025 and ₹240,769 in Fiscal Year
      2026. This represents a CAGR of approximately 8.9% between Fiscal Years 2023 and 2026, reflecting continued
      expansion in economic activity and household earning potential. In Fiscal Year 2026 alone, per capita GNI increased by
      8.0% in nominal terms, while per capita GNI at constant Fiscal Year 2023 prices increased by 6.8% to ₹224,307, indicating
      a substantial increase in real income per person.

      The outlook for further income growth remains supported by India's relatively strong economic growth trajectory. Real
      GDP expanded by 7.7% in Fiscal Year 2026, with particularly strong growth across manufacturing and several services
      sectors, while private final consumption expenditure and gross fixed capital formation both grew by more than 7.5%. The
      IMF's latest July 2026 outlook projects India's real GDP growth at 6.4% in Fiscal Year 2027, suggesting continued
      expansion in economic activity and per-capita incomes despite a more challenging global environment. Continued
      economic growth, investment, employment creation and rising household incomes are expected to support higher
      discretionary spending and deeper consumption across income segments over the medium term.

1.5   Total Population, Proportion of Population By Age Groups

      In Calendar Year 2023, India became the world’s most populous nation, with a population of about 1,438.1 million, of
      which nearly 68.0% falls within the working-age group of 15-64 years. This favourable demographic profile, alongside
      improving education levels and expanding employment opportunities, positions India well for growth in high-skill and
      knowledge-intensive industries. By Calendar Year 2030, the share of the working-age population is expected to rise to
      around 68.9%, further reinforcing India’s economic potential. India is capitalising on this by prioritising skill development,
      job creation in emerging sectors like renewable energy, electronics manufacturing and electric vehicles, and sustained
      investment in public infrastructure. By aligning education and training with industry needs and expanding infrastructure
      capacity, the country is building a strong base for long-term growth and global competitiveness.

1.6   India’s Private Final Consumption Expenditure (“PFCE”) and Sector-wise Consumption Outlook

      India’s PFCE has been pivotal for maintaining economic stability and driving GDP growth. After a 1.0% decline in Fiscal
      Year 2021 due to the pandemic, PFCE rebounded strongly with an 18.5% increase in Fiscal Year 2022 and 15.0% in Fiscal
      Year 2023. Its growth remained strong at 9.7% in Fiscal Year 2025, supported by easing inflation in the final quarter
      (January-March 2025), strong domestic consumption in rural regions, and improving credit conditions. Looking ahead,
      PFCE growth is expected to come from household spending, particularly in sectors like food, health, education, and
      transportation, as well as the expansion of the digital economy and government initiatives focused on infrastructure and
      financial inclusion.

      Globally, Final Consumption Expenditure is projected to grow from USD 64.5 trillion in Calendar Year 2019 to USD
      107.0 trillion by Calendar Year 2030, reflecting steady annual growth in the approximate 4–5% range post-COVID
                                                              147
      normalization (from Calendar Year 2022 onwards). After rebounding from 4.2% in Calendar Year 2022 to 5.9% in
      Calendar Year 2023, growth is expected to stabilize within a narrow band of approximately 4–5%, settling at 5.0% by
      Calendar Year 2030 - indicating resilient and stable consumption demand in the medium term. In contrast, India’s PFCE
      demonstrates a strong structural uptrend, increasing from ₹ 112.1 trillion in Fiscal Year 2019 to ₹ 366.9 trillion by Fiscal
      Year 2031F. While growth moderates from a high of 18.7% in Fiscal Year 2022 to 15.0% in Fiscal Year 2023, and further
      to approximately 10–12% over the forecast period (reaching 10.9% by Fiscal Year 2030), it remains robust, highlighting
      sustained expansion in domestic consumption.er capita PFCE has also grown consistently, reaching ₹ 1,39,898.8 in Fiscal
      Year 2025, up from ₹ 81,513.3 in Fiscal Year 2019, at a CAGR of 9.4%. This points to stronger disposable incomes for
      people. Looking ahead, per capita PFCE will continue to rise. It is projected to reach ₹ 2,40,568.3 by Fiscal Year 2031,
      highlighting an expanding middle class and increasing consumer spending. The monthly per capita consumption
      expenditure (MPCE) further reinforces this trend. Rural MPCE grew from ₹ 1,430 in Fiscal Year 2011-2012 to ₹ 4,122 in
      Fiscal Year 2023-2024 (CAGR of 9.2%), while urban MPCE grew from ₹ 2,630 to ₹ 6,996 over the same period (CAGR
      of 8.5%). These trends show a wider and more even rise in consumption across India, with rural spending showcasing
      stronger growth.

      Fiscal Year 2030 underscores expanding discretionary incomes, increasing urbanization, and rising digital adoption,
      creating a fertile environment for consumer-focused fintech solutions. This expanding consumption landscape directly
      increases the addressable market for its D2C spend management and prepaid card offerings. As households spend more
      across multiple categories, the demand for tools that provide budgeting, spend visibility, and control through prepaid
      instruments is likely to rise, enhancing user engagement, adoption, and ultimately the scale and monetization potential of
      such platforms.

1.7   India’s Internet & Smartphone Penetration Outlook

      India’s digital ecosystem is expected to witness significant expansion, with the number of internet users projected to grow
      from 640 million in Calendar Year 2020 to 1,175 million by Calendar Year 2030, crossing the 1 billion mark by Calendar
      Year 2027. This growth is being driven by affordable mobile data, increasing smartphone affordability, expanding digital
      infrastructure, and deeper internet penetration across Tier-2, Tier-3, and rural markets. At the same time, smartphone users
      in India are projected to increase from 501.8 million in Calendar Year 2020 to 969.1 million by Calendar Year 2030, with
      penetration rising from 36.0% to 63.5% of the population. The rapid expansion of internet and smartphone adoption is
      significantly enlarging the country’s digital consumer base, enabling businesses to strengthen online distribution, digital
      engagement, mobile payments, and app-based service delivery. As smartphone penetration crosses the 50% threshold,
      mobile platforms are expected to become the primary channel for commerce, communication, and customer interaction,
      increasing the importance of mobile-first strategies, vernacular interfaces, and lightweight digital solutions for sustained
      growth and wider market reach.

1.9   Ecommerce transaction value and volume growth in India

      India’s e-commerce sector is undergoing a decade of transformational growth from Calendar Year 2020 to Calendar Year
      2030, with Gross Merchandise Value (GMV) projected to expand 6.3x from USD60 billion in Calendar Year 2020 to
      USD345 billion in Calendar Year 2030, reflecting a strong 19.1% CAGR and positioning India among the world’s fastest-
      growing digital commerce markets. The growth trajectory reflects two distinct phases: an accelerated expansion phase
      (Calendar Year 2020–2024), during which GMV grew at 24.1% CAGR, supported by pandemic-led digital adoption, rapid
      maturation of UPI infrastructure, rising smartphone penetration, and deeper internet access; followed by a consolidation
      phase (Calendar Year 2024–2030), with projected 15.9% CAGR as the market gradually shifts from scale-led expansion
      toward profitability and ecosystem efficiency. Over the same period, the online shopper base is expected to increase from
      155 million to 400 million users, implying 2.9x growth at 9.9% CAGR, with nearly 60% of incremental users coming
      from Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities, where digital payment adoption and logistics reach have improved materially. The Calendar
      Year 2026 represents peak growth velocity, with an estimated USD57 billion incremental GMV, driven by rapid adoption
      of quick commerce, social commerce, and higher purchase frequency across daily-use categories. Beyond 2027, growth is
      expected to moderate as market penetration rises and urban adoption matures, although structural enablers—including
      logistics cost optimization, expansion of digital payments, emergence of B2B e-commerce, and 5G-enabled digital
      shopping experiences—will continue to support long-term ecosystem expansion.

        smartphone penetration, which is accelerating digital adoption across payments, commerce, and financial services. At the

2       India Payments Landscape

2.1     Digital Payments Landscape in India

2.1.1   India’s Expanding Digital Payments Infrastructure

        India’s digital payments ecosystem has been fundamentally reshaped by the rapid rise of UPI, which has emerged as the
        backbone of real-time transactions in the country. UPI transaction value has surged from ₹ 21.9 trillion in Calendar Year
        2020 to ₹ 299.7 trillion in Calendar Year 2025, reflecting exponential growth in both adoption and usage intensity. This
        expansion has been driven by seamless interoperability, instant settlement, and strong participation from banks and fintech
        platforms. Increasing use cases including peer-to-peer transfers, merchant payments, bill payments, and emerging credit
        integrations have positioned UPI as a ubiquitous payment rail across urban and rural India alike.

        Exhibit 10: Growth in UPI Transaction Value, UPI QR Codes & POS Terminals, India, Calendar Year 2020-2025

        Point-of-sale (PoS) infrastructure has also expanded, at a more measured pace, reflecting its complementary role in the
        payment’s ecosystem. The number of PoS terminals increased from approximately 6 million in Calendar Year 2020 to
        approximately 11 million in Calendar Year 2025, driven primarily by organized retail, hospitality, and higher-value
        transaction segments where card-based payments remain relevant. While PoS devices continue to be critical for enabling
        debit and credit card acceptance, their growth has been constrained relative to QR codes due to higher deployment and
        maintenance costs. Nevertheless, innovations such as Android-based smart PoS devices and integrated payment solutions
        are expected to support steady expansion through Calendar Year 2030, particularly in Tier 1 and Tier 2 cities. In contrast,
        UPI QR codes have witnessed explosive growth, becoming the cornerstone of merchant acceptance in India’s digital
        payments landscape. The number of QR codes expanded dramatically from 25 million in Calendar Year 2020 to 731
        million in Calendar Year 2025, highlighting the rapid digitization of small and micro-merchants. QR-based payments offer
        a low-cost, easy-to-deploy solution that requires minimal infrastructure, making them ideal for widespread adoption across
        kirana stores, street vendors, and rural markets. This “QR-first” approach has significantly lowered entry barriers for
        merchants, accelerating financial inclusion and enabling real-time digital transactions at scale. Looking ahead, QR
        deployments are expected to continue driving the next wave of growth, further deepening the reach of digital payments
        across India.

        India’s large base of young, mobile-first digital consumers, a rapidly scaling entrepreneurial ecosystem, and a deeply
        penetrated digital payments infrastructure are collectively driving strong demand for spend management platforms and
        prepaid card programs. With nearly a billion smartphone users expected by 2030 and one of the highest per-user data
        consumption rates globally, consumers are increasingly accustomed to seamless, app-based financial interactions,
        accelerating adoption of digital-first financial tools. At the same time, the rise of over 200,000 startups and a fast-growing
        base of SMEs has created a parallel need for efficient expense tracking, employee benefits distribution, and cash flow
        management solutions. This demand is being further enabled by the ubiquity of Unified Payments Interface (UPI), along
        with widespread QR-based acceptance, which together provide the underlying rails for real-time, low-cost fund
        disbursement and usage. Fintech platforms and payment apps have normalized digital transactions across use cases, paving
        the way for prepaid instruments to evolve beyond traditional gifting into areas like employee incentives, corporate expense
        management, and targeted benefit distribution. As a result, India is witnessing a structural shift toward integrated,
        programmable, and scalable spend management solutions embedded within its broader digital financial ecosystem.

2.1.2   Total volume / value of digital transactions in India

        The Government of India has accelerated digital adoption to strengthen the financial system and improve ease of living,
        leading to a sharp rise in digital payments from 21 billion transactions in Fiscal Year 2018 to 187 billion in Fiscal Year
        2024 and 228 billion in Fiscal Year 2024–2025 (growing at a CAGR 40.6% from Fiscal Year 2018-2025), with total value
        reaching ₹3,509 trillion; this momentum continues in Fiscal Year 2025–2026, with 190 billion transactions worth ₹2,181
        trillion recorded by 14th December 2025. The surge is driven by user-friendly platforms such as BHIM-UPI, IMPS, and
        NETC, supported by backbone systems like NEFT and RTGS, which have seen strong growth over the past decade,
        alongside rising card usage—online card payments reached ₹14.4 trillion in Fiscal Year 2024, with credit card spending
        up 21% in first half of 2024 due to increased consumption.

        This growth has become a defining feature of the country’s economic landscape, driven by a confluence of factors.
        Government-led initiatives such as Digital India have built robust digital infrastructure, expanding access across urban and
        rural areas. Digital payments acceptance infrastructure in India has expanded significantly, with the number of point-of-
        sale (PoS) terminals standing at over 11 million as at December 31, 2025. The rollout of Aadhaar has streamlined
        authentication, improving both security and ease of transactions. Together with rapid smartphone penetration, affordable
        internet, and the widespread adoption of digital payment platforms, these developments have significantly accelerated the
        shift toward a less-cash economy.

        India’s digital payments ecosystem continued to expand strongly in first half of Calendar Year 2025, driven primarily by
        the growth of UPI transactions and rising merchant acceptance. UPI transaction volumes increased from 93.2 billion in
        second half of Calendar Year 2024 to 106.4 billion in first half of Calendar Year 2025, while UPI P2M transactions reached
        67.01 billion, reflecting deeper penetration across merchants and businesses. Credit card transactions also recorded healthy
        growth, supported by increasing consumer preference for credit-based spending, particularly in e-commerce and travel.
        Although debit card transaction volumes declined amid rising UPI adoption for low-value payments, higher average
        transaction sizes indicate their continued usage for higher-value transactions.

        Prepaid cards including both reloadable and non-reloadable prepaid cards, recorded 0.86 billion transactions in first half
        of Calendar Year 2025, registering a growth of 11%. The growth of prepaid cards has been driven by the increasing
        adoption of digital payment solutions across multiple consumer and business use cases, including retail purchases, e-
        commerce transactions, utility bill payments, transit payments, gift cards, employee benefits, and corporate expense
        management. Businesses and fintech players are increasingly leveraging prepaid instruments to offer convenient, secure,
        and controlled payment solutions for customers and employees, further supporting transaction growth.

        The continued expansion of merchant acceptance infrastructure, coupled with growing consumer familiarity and trust in
        digital payments, has accelerated the usage of prepaid cards across both online and offline channels. Reloadable prepaid
        cards, in particular, are witnessing increasing traction due to their flexibility, ease of reusability, and suitability for
        recurring digital transactions, while non-reloadable prepaid instruments continue to remain relevant for gifting,
        promotional campaigns, and limited-purpose payments. In addition, rising smartphone penetration, increasing internet
        accessibility, and the integration of prepaid payment solutions within digital wallets and fintech platforms have further
        strengthened the adoption of prepaid cards. The sustained growth in prepaid card transactions highlights their increasing
        importance as a flexible, secure, and convenient payment option within India’s rapidly evolving digital payments
        ecosystem.

2.1.3   Split Of Total Transactions Value

        UPI continued to dominate India’s digital payments landscape, with transaction values increasing from ₹ 172.2 trillion in
        Calendar Year 2024 to ₹299.74 trillion in Calendar Year 2025, driven by strong adoption across both low-value and high-
        value transactions. UPI P2M transaction value also grew significantly from ₹ 67.80 trillion to ₹ 85.23 trillion during the
        same period, reflecting expanding merchant acceptance. Credit card transaction value increased from ₹21.31 trillion in
        first half of Calendar Year 2024 to ₹ 23.65 trillion in Calendar Year 2025, supported by rising usage for high-value
        discretionary spending. In contrast, debit card transaction value witnessed decline , decreasing from ₹5.15 trillion to ₹4.48
        trillion, reflecting declining usage amid rapid UPI adoption, while continuing to remain relevant for direct bank-linked
        payments.

        Prepaid cards’ share is expected to remain relatively small compared to dominant payment modes such as UPI and credit
        cards, prepaid payment instruments (PPIs), including reloadable and non-reloadable prepaid cards, are projected to witness
        steady growth driven by expanding use cases in corporate expense management, employee benefits, transit payments,
        gifting, travel, and controlled-spend solutions. Increasing fintech participation, deeper integration with digital payment
        ecosystems, and rising adoption of prepaid solutions by enterprises are expected to support this growth. However, the
                                                                          154
        overall share of prepaid cards is likely to remain moderate due to the continued dominance of UPI in low-value retail
        transactions and the increasing preference for credit cards in higher-value spending categories.

2.1.6   Demographic dividend as a key driver for payment cards

        The demographic dividend, characterized by a growing working-age population, is poised to significantly drive the growth
        of payments card issuance. As more young adults enter the workforce, their financial independence and purchasing power
        increase, leading to a higher demand for banking services, including payment cards. This growth is fuelled by higher
        consumer spending, urbanization, digital adoption, financial inclusion efforts, access to credit, and financial innovation,
        collectively fostering a robust market for card-based transactions.

2.1.7   Key enablers for digital transactions in India

        1)         Structural enablers for growth in the digital payments:

                   •          Rapid Growth and Transformation: India's digital payments have seen significant growth, notably 48
                              billion transactions in 2020, transitioning from a cash-based to a cashless economy.

                   •          Government and Big Tech Initiatives: NPCI's various programs, government initiatives like the JAM
                              trinity (initiative to link JanDhan accounts, mobile numbers and Aadhaar cards), along with the entry of
                              big tech players, have enhanced the services and reach of digital payments.

        2)         Expansion of payment acceptance infrastructure:

                   •          Payment Infrastructure Development Fund (PIDF): Established by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
                              to subsidize the deployment of digital payment acceptance infrastructure in Tier-3 to Tier-6 centres and
                              Northeastern states. It includes creating 3 million new touchpoints annually for digital payments.

                   •          Subsidy and Support for Payment Devices: The RBI offers varying subsidies for the deployment of
                              various payment acceptance devices, including physical and digital PoS.

        3)         Credit cards and other digital payment services fuel the e-commerce:

                   •          Boost from Smartphone and Internet Penetration: The increase in smartphone users and internet
                              accessibility, aligned with the Digital India movement, has significantly contributed to the expansion of
                              e-commerce.

                   •          Diversity of Payment Methods: The availability of various payment methods such as credit cards, UPI,
                              e-wallets, have made online transactions more convenient, thereby boosting e-commerce.


                                                                         156
                     •         Security and Consumer Trust: Security measures, such as Payment Card Industry Data Security
                               Standard compliance, encryption, and OTPs, ensure safe transactions, encouraging repeat business and
                               higher spending.

           4)        Government initiatives:

                     •         Digital Payment Growth: Government efforts have led to a substantial increase in digital transactions.

                     •         Features and Benefits: Instant transfer features, enhanced financial inclusion, increased government
                               system transparency, and improved speed of transactions are some of the key benefits of these initiatives.

                     •         Specific Programs: NETC for highway toll payments, Bharat Bill Payment System (BBPS), now
                               branded Bharat Connect, for bill payments, and initiatives to enhance credit access and security have
                               further bolstered digital transactions in India.

           the world’s largest fintech ecosystems. Digital adoption fundamentals remain robust: internet subscribers reached 969
           million1 (March 2025), supporting mass-market digital distribution of payments, credit, insurance, and investments.

3.1        Prepaid Cards Market in India

           India’s prepaid cards market represents a dynamic pillar of the nation's burgeoning digital payments landscape, enabling
           financial inclusion for millions through versatile, reloadable and non-reloadable instruments tailored for retail, corporate,
           and gifting needs. Driven by government-led initiatives like Digital India and rising smartphone penetration, the sector

Prepaid Cards – Total Addressable Market (TAM)

The total addressable market in India remains considerably large, driven by strong acceptance and use of digital payment

2020 to 254.2 billion. (valued at ₹ 367.3 trillion) in Calendar Year 2025. It is estimated that by 2030, digital payment
transactions would touch 696.6 billion and ₹ 1,024.7 trillion in terms of volume and value, respectively, growing at a

transactions – UPI, credit & debit, and Bharat Connect – could be made by PPI cards and hence becomes the total
addressable market for prepaid cards in India.

Prepaid Cards – Serviceable Available Market (SAM)

India’s prepaid card market is rapidly growing, driven by their versatility for online shopping, contactless POS payments,
and ATM withdrawals. These cards offer secure, convenient, and pre-funded solutions, appealing to both urban consumers
and digitally transitioning users. Gifting is a key use of prepaid cards, enabling corporations and individuals to send digital,
multi-purpose cards for occasions like weddings, festivals, birthdays, and client appreciation, with instant delivery and tax
tracking.

India's Prepaid Cards market has been experiencing accelerated growth, primarily driven by the cards' multifaceted utility
of both reloadable and non-reloadable prepaid instruments that seamlessly fits into diverse aspects of daily financial life
and business operations. Reloadable prepaid cards are increasingly being adopted for recurring and higher-frequency
transactions such as travel, subscriptions, payroll, employee benefits, transit payments, and controlled-spend corporate
solutions due to their flexibility and reusability. Meanwhile, non-reloadable prepaid cards continue to witness strong
demand across gifting, promotional campaigns, incentives, and limited-purpose payment use cases. Consumers
increasingly turn to Prepaid Cards for hassle-free transactions on popular e-commerce platforms, where they provide a
secure, pre-funded alternative to linking bank accounts, minimizing fraud risks during online shopping sprees for
everything from groceries to electronics. In merchant stores, ranging from neighbourhood Kirana shops to large retail
chains, these cards facilitate quick contactless payments at point of sales ("POS") terminals, appealing to urban shoppers
seeking speed and convenience over cash handling.

Prepaid cards, including reloadable and non-reloadable variants, have become integral to modern consumer behaviour,
with total prepaid transactions in India estimated to reach 2.0 billion in Calendar Year 2025 and ₹700.9 billion in terms of
transaction value reflecting broad adoption across categories such as retail, travel, and everyday purchases. Growth is
expected to remain consistent over the next five years, with total prepaid transactions in India projected to reach 4.5 billion
and ₹1,028.9 billion in value by Calendar Year 2030, reflecting strong acceptance of the prepaid card model.

Average Ticket Size

The average ticket size (ATS) for prepaid cards has seen fluctuations over the years. During the prime COVID-19 period
(when digital payments system was still evolving), people preferred minimum cash handling and relied heavily on digital
transaction even for large value payments. ATS in Calendar Year 2020 was ₹. 460.5 and increased till Calendar Year 2022
(₹. 494.9) following which ATS started declining consistently till Calendar Year 2025 (₹. 350.9). The declining trend
implies more frequent low-value transactions amid digital payment adoption. Competitive pressures from UPI's dominance
in small-ticket peer-to-merchant flows have kept ATS restrained, even as virtual cards gain traction for e-commerce and
one-off digital payouts, stabilizing the segment's role in financial inclusion without aggressive escalation.

(a)        Point of Sale (PoS)

           Prepaid card transaction at Point of Sale (PoS) hold a resilient foothold within the dynamic digital payments
           ecosystem, particularly excelling in fast-paced scenarios like quick-service retail, public transit ticketing, and
           informal merchant dealings. Near field communication (NFC) taps deliver unmatched convenience and hygiene
           benefits over cash or competing methods through rewards and cashbacks. The segment’s growth trajectory is
           propelled by the proliferation of EMV chip-enabled physical cards across burgeoning merchant infrastructures in
           metros, urban pockets, and fast emerging towns, enabling seamless adoption among small vendors previously
           cash-bound, even as UPI's pervasive low-value peer-to-merchant dominance exerts downward pressure on overall
           transaction shares. Reloadable prepaid models are gaining further momentum through strategic tie-ups with
           mobile wallets and enterprise platforms. It was estimated that in Calendar Year 2025, India had prepaid card
           transactions at 0.9 billion. in terms of volume and ₹ 123.5 billion. in terms of value. Prepaid card transaction
           volume is likely to nearly double to touch 1.7 billion by the end of Calendar Year 2030.

3.2   Issuing, Acquiring, and Processing Market in India

      India’s digital payments infrastructure hinges on four interconnected layers: card issuing, transaction processing, merchant
      acquiring and program managers. Issuing banks (and fintech issuers) provide payment instruments (credit, debit, prepaid
      cards) to consumers, while payment processors and card networks (such as Visa, Mastercard, RuPay) handle authorization,
      clearing and settlement. Acquirers (banks and payment service providers) enable merchants to accept card payments across
      POS terminals, gateways and QR systems. This entire stack from issuance through acceptance has grown explosively in
      recent years, driven by booming e-commerce and fintech adoption.

      The total number of payment cards in circulation in India, encompassing credit cards, debit cards, and PPIs, stood at 1,083
      million units in Fiscal Year 2020. By Fiscal Year 2025, this figure had increased to 1,573 million units and is anticipated
      to grow to 2,392 million units by Fiscal Year 2030, with an expected CAGR of 8.7% from Fiscal Year 2025 to Fiscal Year
      2030.

•         Issuers (Banks & Fintechs): Issue payment cards (plastic or virtual) to customers and corporate clients. They
          manage the full card life cycle (such as onboarding, KYC, issuance, credit limits) and perform transaction
          authorization and fraud checks. Leading issuers include public & private sector banks as well as new fintech
          platforms. Private banks now hold 70% of India’s credit cards, reflecting aggressive co-branding and digital
          strategies.

•         Card Networks & Processors: Companies like Visa, Mastercard, RuPay and Amex operate the transaction
          network that connects issuers and acquirers. Modern issuers also rely on issuing processors (technology service
          providers ) that provide the back-end technology for card management and transaction routing. These platforms
          are the backbone of India’s payments ecosystem, enabling real-time authorization and global settlement.

•         Acquirers/Payment Service Providers: Acquirer banks and aggregators (e.g., PayU, Razorpay) on-board
          merchants, provide POS terminals or gateways, and handle settlement to merchant accounts. They bundle
          connectivity to multiple banks and networks, simplifying acceptance for retailers. Thanks to widespread POS
          proliferation (hundreds of thousands of terminals) and QR/e-commerce acceptance, even small merchants can
          accept card and QR payments.

                                                      162
•        Merchants & Consumers: All types of merchants (retail stores, restaurants, online marketplaces, service
         providers) form the acceptance base. Consumers link their issued cards to these channels via swipe machines,
         contactless taps, or online checkouts. Together, these layers enable seamless tap-to-transact payments across
         India.

•        Program Managers (PMs): PMs design, launch and manage prepaid card programs in coordination with issuers.
         PMs manage relationships with cardholders and drive prepaid card adoption. Issuers tie up with PMs to scale user
         acquisition, engagement, and retention. They are primarily responsible for growing the volume and value of
         prepaid card transactions, coordinating marketing, onboarding, and loyalty programs to expand the card’s user
         base.

Use Cases & Growth Drivers

Issuing and prepaid solutions now power a wide range of use cases beyond traditional cards.

•        Gift cards and loyalty programs have become mainstream payment instruments, with major platforms like
         Amazon Pay, PhonePe, and Flipkart distributing wallet-native gift and prepaid cards directly to consumers.
         Corporate and channel incentives such as sales rewards, employee benefits, and expense cards are increasingly
         issued via prepaid solutions.

•        Other use cases include incentives and promotions, meal/expense cards, digital wallets, travel/forex cards, mobile
         wallets with stored value, cross-border remittance cards, prepaid instruments linked to the Automated Permanent
         Academic Account Registry (APAAR) which is "One Nation, One Student ID”, a unique 12-digit digital identifier
         for students in India and the National Common Mobility Card (NCMC), which enables seamless contactless
         payments across metro systems, buses, tolls, and retail merchants, integrating transport and retail payments on a
         single platform. Giftcards (gift/fuel/retail/multi-brand prepaid) cards account for a significant share of issuance,
         while Prepaid cards (bank-issued Visa, Mastercard, RuPay) dominate high-value spends. Each use case reflects
         innovative ways to engage customers and control spend: gift cards acquire new shoppers and capture loyalty data,
         corporate cards streamline employee spending, digital wallets embed payments into super apps, APAAR cards
         facilitate payroll and subsidy disbursements, and NCMC simplifies daily commuting while promoting cashless
         transactions. RBI-driven expansion of acceptance, including UPI integration and IoT payments, has further
         broadened the total digital payment volume opportunity.

Meal Card / Prepaid Benefits – Regulatory Tailwind: Recent changes under India’s income tax rules (2026) have
increased the tax-exempt limit on meal cards and prepaid instruments, enhancing their attractiveness for salaried
consumers and expanding their usage in everyday spend categories. This structurally strengthens the prepaid ecosystem
by driving higher adoption, transaction volumes, and consumer familiarity with stored-value instruments. For platforms
operating in prepaid cards, spend management, and digital engagement, this creates a larger addressable base and
accelerates mainstream adoption of prepaid-led use cases across retail consumption. Digital payment transactions in India
have risen from 21 billion transactions in Fiscal Year 2017-2018 to a substantial 187 billion transactions in Fiscal Year
2023-2024 and 228 billion in Fiscal Year 2024-2025, growing at a CAGR of 40.6 per cent from Fiscal Year 2018 to Fiscal
Year 2025. During the same period, the value of transactions has grown to ₹ 3,509 trillion. Momentum has continued into
the current Fiscal year (Fiscal Year 2025–2026), where, as of 31 December 2025, digital transaction volumes have already
reached 203.43 billion with a total value of ₹2,357 trillion.

Prepaid, Gifting, and Spend Management Solutions - Regulatory Tailwinds Supporting Expansion: The draft Master
Direction on Prepaid Payment Instruments (PPIs), 2026 issued by the Reserve Bank of India is expected to significantly
strengthen and formalize the prepaid payments ecosystem through enhanced capital requirements, stricter customer due
diligence norms, and clearly defined categories of PPIs. These regulatory developments are likely to increase entry barriers,
drive consolidation, and favour compliant and well-capitalized platforms. For companies such as Paramotor, this creates
substantial growth opportunities across prepaid cards, digital gifting, and spend management solutions. The enhanced
capabilities of Full-KYC PPIs, including higher permissible limits and interoperability with UPI and card networks, are
expected to drive increased transaction volumes and enterprise adoption, particularly in corporate expense management
and incentive programs. Additionally, the formalization of gift PPIs and the introduction of co-branding arrangements
enable scalable distribution and expansion of digital gifting solutions. Overall, these regulatory changes are anticipated to
accelerate adoption of prepaid instruments, enhance trust in digital payment platforms, and support the development of
integrated, scalable fintech ecosystems.

SEBI Proposal – Expansion of Digital Gifting & PPI Use Cases: Securities and Exchange Board of India consultation


                                                        163
         paper 2 dated 24th March 2026, proposes to enable mutual fund gifting through prepaid payment instruments (PPIs),
         marking a significant expansion of digital gifting use cases into financial products. By allowing PPIs to be used for
         investment gifting, the regulation broadens the utility of prepaid instruments beyond consumption into wealth creation.
         This is expected to deepen consumer engagement with digital gifting platforms and reinforce prepaid infrastructure as a
         scalable distribution layer, benefiting companies operating in rewards, gifting, and prepaid ecosystems.

         This rapid growth has made India one of the world’s largest issuing markets: over 1.5 billion cards in force by Fiscal Year
         2025 and counting, powering a multi-hundred-billion-dollar payments economy.

3.3      Direct to Consumer (D2C) Spend Management Market in India

         The Direct to Consumer (D2C) prepaid spend-management market in India sits at the intersection of:

         1.        Prepaid payment instruments (PPIs) issued by banks and authorized non-banks; and

         2.        Personal finance management-style features (spend tracking, budgets, alerts, controls) delivered via
                   apps/dashboards/ platforms.

         Unlike pure budgeting apps that only track spend, prepaid-card-linked platforms (such as SpendPro offered by Paramotor)
         can embed hard controls (e.g., spending restrictions, limits, and real-time authorizations) because the user’s spending
         happens through the instrument governed by the program rules. This converts budgeting from advice/insight into insight
         + enforceable controls, which is a meaningful functional upgrade in a digital first spending environment.

         India’s D2C spend management and prepaid cards landscape is evolving rapidly, driven by rising digital adoption among
         retail consumers, expanding acceptance infrastructure, and regulatory support for seamless, secure payments. Prepaid
         cards, both physical and virtual, are increasingly being used by individuals for everyday purchases, online shopping, travel,
         gifting, and personal budgeting. Market directionally, prepaid instruments continue to carve out a specialized role even as
         UPI dominates everyday payments. In 2024, outstanding prepaid cards witnessed a 34% growth YOY, expanding the
         addressable base for platforms like SpendPro powered by Paramotor to onboard users into spend management ecosystems.,
         While such platforms enable consumers to access, activate, and manage these cards through intuitive digital experiences,
         consumers on the other hand value the control, safety, and flexibility that prepaid cards offer as spend can be capped, usage
         tracked in real time, and risk of overspending or fraud minimized. In parallel, India’s policy environment has helped unlock
         demand: RBI has mandated interoperability for full-KYC PPIs, enabled UPI integration for wallets, and improved trust
         through tokenization and data protection norms. With card acceptance growing across small merchants, e-commerce, and
         services, prepaid instruments now offer near-universal usability without requiring a full banking relationship. As digital
         financial inclusion deepens and consumers look for smarter, controlled ways to transact, the prepaid and Direct to
         Consumer spend management ecosystem is becoming a key pillar in India’s everyday retail economy combining
         convenience with financial discipline.

         Macro trends and demand drivers in India

         Several macro forces support consumer-focused prepaid spend-management platforms:

         Rapid growth in digital payment transactions Digital payment transactions in India have grown significantly from 21
         billion transactions in Fiscal Year 2018 to 187 billion in Fiscal Year 2024 and 228 billion in Fiscal Year 2025, reflecting
         a CAGR of 40.6% between Fiscal Year 2018 and Fiscal Year 2025. Over the same period, the value of transactions reached
         ₹ 3,509 trillion, indicating a broad structural shift toward digital payment modes including cards and prepaid instruments.
         During Fiscal Year 2026 (up to 14 December 2025), India recorded 190.4 billion digital payment transactions, with a
         cumulative transaction value of INR 2,181 trillion., reinforcing the importance of spend visibility and budgeting tools
         linked to digital payment instruments.

         Expansion of digital payment acceptance infrastructure Government initiatives such as the Payments Infrastructure
         Development Fund (PIDF) have significantly expanded digital payment acceptance infrastructure across India. Through
         financial incentives for deployment of payment acceptance touchpoints such as POS terminals and QR codes, the scheme
         has supported the onboarding of small and underserved merchants, reduced dependence on cash and advanced financial
         inclusion. As of October 2025, 54.5 million digital touchpoints had been deployed across Tier-3 to Tier-6 cities, while
         568.6 million QR codes were deployed across 65 million merchants by Fiscal Year 2025. India’s UPI QR network more
         than doubled from 321 million to 678 million between early 2024 and mid‑2025, and PoS terminals rose above 11 million
         by December 2025, reflecting strong growth in both scan-based and traditional acceptance channels. As merchant

acceptance increases, prepaid cards become more usable for everyday spending, enhancing the value proposition of
platforms that provide spend tracking and budgeting insights.

Rising consumer adoption of prepaid instruments for controlled spending Prepaid cards are increasingly used as
specialized financial tools for managing spending. They appeal particularly to consumer segments seeking controlled
financial behaviour such as students, gig economy workers, households managing budgets, deal-seekers using event-based
purchase cards, and consumers allocating discretionary spending into dedicated balances for categories like shopping,
travel, or subscriptions. These consumer segments prefer prepaid cards given the expectation of faster issuance and greater
control over spends. Paramotor’s strong market position is supported by its rapid prepaid card issuance capabilities,
enabling efficient and scalable deployment.

Growth of digital gifting and reward ecosystems Gift cards and reward cards have become an important component of
digital consumer spending. From Calendar Year 2025 to Calendar Year 2030, India’s digital gift card market is projected
to grow at a robust CAGR of 17.4%, reaching USD 33.65 billion by Calendar Year 2030. This rapid expansion is supported
by the convenience and flexibility of digital gift cards, wider corporate adoption for employee rewards and client
engagement, increasing personalization, e-commerce penetration, and sustained festive demand. Spend management
platforms can integrate these incentives into payment flows, allowing consumers to combine budgeting with promotional
benefits such as cashback or merchant discounts.

Structural growth of virtual card issuance Virtual card issuance and digitized card credentials are gaining momentum
as financial institutions move toward digital-first card issuance models. This trend supports platforms that deliver prepaid
cards digitally and provide real-time access to spending insights, making digital card infrastructure a natural foundation
for consumer spend management platforms.

Gap in retail-focused spend management solutions While corporate prepaid and expense management solutions are
widely available, consumer-focused spend management tools remain relatively limited. Direct-to-consumer prepaid
platforms address this gap by combining instant card issuance, budgeting tools, transaction analytics, and spending
controls, offering retail users functionality that mirrors corporate expense management capabilities.

Improved security frameworks supporting card usage Enhancements in payment security, including RBI-mandated
tokenisation frameworks, have strengthened the safety of digital card transactions. Tokenised card payments ensure that
actual card details are not shared with merchants during processing, which improves trust and supports greater usage of
prepaid and virtual cards for e-commerce transactions and recurring digital payments.

The Direct-to-Consumer (D2C) Spend Management market in India, measured through interchange revenue generated on
prepaid card transactions, is estimated to grow from ₹ 12.2 billion in Calendar Year 2020 to approximately ₹ 22.6 billion
by Calendar Year 2030. The market experienced strong expansion during the early years of digital payment adoption,
reaching ₹ 18.1 billion in Calendar Year 2022, followed by a temporary normalization in Calendar Year 2023–Calendar
Year 2025 as the ecosystem adjusted to evolving prepaid regulations and changing consumer payment preferences. Growth
                                                               165
is expected to resume from Calendar Year 2026, driven by rising prepaid usage, digital transactions, virtual card adoption,
and increasing demand for spend management tools, supporting steady market expansion alongside wider merchant
acceptance.

Interchange fees are not levied directly on the consumer but are paid by the merchant’s bank (acquiring bank) to the card-
issuing bank to process transactions every time any customer uses a card to make purchases from a merchant’s store.
Interchange fees are decided by the payment networks of Rupay, Mastercard, and Visa (collectively, the “Payment
Networks”) in accordance with contractual arrangements between the Payment Networks and the PPI Issuers and is
broadly influenced by the industry of the merchant where the card is used, the merchant category and transaction value.

Regulatory and policy environment

A D2C prepaid card program with spend-management dashboards is tightly shaped by Indian regulation, particularly PPI
rules and card security policy.

PPI issuance and licensing. RBI clarifies that PPIs can be issued by banks (after RBI approval) and by non-banks (Indian
companies) after RBI authorization to operate a payment system for issuing PPIs. This makes the issuing layer inherently
regulated; distribution and program management must be aligned to the issuer’s compliance regime.

KYC tiers, loading, and product design. RBI describes small PPIs (minimum detail) vs full-KYC PPIs, with differing
permissions; for example, certain small PPIs must be converted to full-KYC within prescribed timelines, and PPIs can be
loaded through channels such as cash (with limits), bank account debit, cards. For D2C platforms, KYC flows, limits, and
permissible features directly determine onboarding friction, unit economics, and which segments can be served.

Gift PPI constraints (relevant if prepaid cards are sold as gift instruments). RBI specifies that Gift PPIs have a
maximum value of ₹10,000, are not reloadable, and do not permit cash-out or fund transfer (with limited ‘back to source’
transfer allowed with consent). This matters if the D2C distribution is driven by gifting or deal/event issuance.

Authentication and customer protection. RBI states that wallet transactions involving debit require 2FA, and AFA (a
security process that requires users to provide at least two distinct authentication factors to verify a digital payment
transaction) requirements for PPI cards (physical or virtual) are the same as debit cards (with exceptions for gift PPIs and
certain transit PPIs). RBI also requires a formal, publicly disclosed grievance redressal framework, including a designated
nodal officer and defined escalation / turnaround. For a consumer spend management product, trust plumbing (dispute
handling, alerts, service SLAs) is a non-negotiable adoption driver.

Interoperability and UPI linkage. RBI’s Master Directions require that if PPIs are issued as wallets, interoperability
should be enabled via UPI; if issued as cards (physical or virtual), they must be affiliated to authorized card networks and
interoperability is mandatory for KYC compliant PPIs. Further, RBI’s Dec 27, 2024 circular specifies that only full KYC
PPIs may be enabled for UPI payments by linking to the issuer’s UPI handle; discovery / linking via third-party UPI apps
is also contemplated under defined constraints.

Overall, the regulatory environment is enabling but rigorous. RBI support (for digital payments expansion) creates
opportunity, but high KYC and compliance standards mean that only accredited players (banks and authorized program
managers) can operate. This raises the bar for market entry but also builds user trust.
