In a D2C prepaid virtual card model, the stakeholder ecosystem typically includes:

•         Consumer / cardholder: Purchases/loads prepaid value and uses it for merchant payments; consumes spend
          analytics dashboards.

•         Merchant and acquirer: Accepts card payments and routes authorization through the network.

•         PPI issuer / sponsor bank (issuer): Holds the regulated issuance permission and compliance obligations;
          manages PPI rules and customer protection duties.

•         Program manager: Orchestrates program design, compliance operations, distribution, customer ops, and the
          spend-management software layer. Earns its service fee from interchange (often the largest revenue piece).

•         Card network: Provides the global payment infrastructure that connects issuing banks, acquiring banks,
          merchants, and payment processors.

•         Switch provider: Operates the technical infrastructure that processes payment transactions by routing
                                                      167
         authorization messages between issuing banks, acquiring banks, payment processors, and card networks.

•        Issuer processor / processing stack: Maintains cardholder account records and supports authorization and
         settlement.

•        KYC/verification and fraud vendors: Supports onboarding and transaction monitoring consistent with
         regulatory expectations.

Program manager as the most critical stakeholder in the Value Chain

Program managers, such as Paramotor, are the most critical in the value chain, hence pocket the largest revenue piece. In
a consumer prepaid and spend-management model, the program manager is the operating brain coordinating issuance,
compliance, technology, and distribution at scale. Several critical functions undertaken by them involve:

•        Issuer partnership orchestration: Working with RBI authorized PPI issuers to structure the product (KYC tiers,
         limits, card type, T&Cs).

•        Network and interoperability readiness: Ensuring card-based PPIs are network affiliated and interoperable as
         required, with certifications and governance controls.

•        Customer Acquisition & Service: Market the card to consumers (e.g. via partnerships or online campaigns) and
         provide customer support. This direct relationship with end users is unique to PMs.

•        Risk, fraud, and customer protection: Two factor authentication, real time alerts / controls, velocity checks,
         transaction monitoring and grievance redressal processes appropriate for retail consumers.

•        Product and analytics layer: Converting raw transaction feeds into consumer facing spend dashboards
         (categories, budgets, alerts), which is the core differentiator of retail spend management.

The program manager’s value proposition lies in bundling all these functions. It enables banks (which hold regulatory
liability) to offer a consumer prepaid product without building the end-to-end system themselves. It also enables a leaner
go-to-market as it can rapidly issue cards to end users (often instantly), whereas a bank alone might take much longer to
launch a new retail prepaid product.

Why Retail-Focused Program Managers Are in a Sweet Spot

Program Managers focussed on retail consumers are in a sweet spot as they positioned for:

•        Large Addressable Market: India has a huge retail population with growing digital aspirations. While many
         fintechs target corporate spends, focusing on retail taps into a far larger segment of card users and digital-first
         consumers.

•        Rapid Go-to-Market: Issuing retail prepaid cards is faster than corporate contracts. A consumer can sign up
         digitally in minutes, whereas enterprise onboarding can take months. This agility allows program managers
         focused on retail consumers to scale quickly.

•        Event-Driven Volume Spikes: Major shopping festivals (e.g. Amazon Prime Day, Flipkart Big Billion Day)
         drive bursts of consumer spend. Retail prepaid model lets users capitalize immediately (e.g. using cards with
         special discounts). Corporate programs have no analogous feature, giving retail focused model a competitive edge
         during sales events.

•        Brand Engagement: Consumers often seek convenient budgeting tools. Offering a slick prepaid app builds brand
         loyalty. Word of mouth among tech savvy users (e.g. bloggers, young professionals) can accelerate adoption.

•        Financial Inclusion Angle: Serving consumers directly aligns with government pushes for financial inclusion
         and digital payments proliferation. This can open collaborative opportunities (e.g. partnering on social benefit
         disbursements) in the future.

In essence, a retail focused prepaid spend management program addresses unmet needs with quick rollout and strong user
appeal. The critical factors for success in this space include instant card delivery, digital KYC, and an intuitive app
interface. Retail prepaid programs can have structurally faster activation loops than corporate programs that require
enterprise sales cycles and employee onboarding. This can make retail programs advantageous in event-driven spikes (e.g.,
                                                       168
sale seasons) and consumer deal-led acquisition. The virtual-first model (cards delivered via email/WhatsApp) means
immediate visibility of the new card in the app. Fast funding and real-time alerts ensure consumers feel in control,
reinforcing the product’s attractiveness.

Entry barriers and critical success factors for program managers

There are significant barriers to entry to distribute Prepaid Cards, as onboarding of distributors by PPI Partners typically
involves rigorous empanelment and due diligence processes encompassing compliance, technology, and operational
assessments. Becoming a scaled program manager in India is difficult because it combines regulated ecosystem access
with operational excellence.

•        Bank Partnerships: PMs must partner with banks (to hold customer funds and obtain PPI license backing). Such
         partnerships demand rigorous due diligence by banks on the PM’s technology, security architecture, compliance
         frameworks, governance standards, financial stability, and operational capabilities. This is a time-intensive
         process, typically spanning 6–12 months, and only credible, established fintech players are able to successfully
         secure and maintain such relationships.

•        Technology & Security: A world-class payments platform requires secure, scalable tech (fraud prevention,
         encryption, uptime SLAs). Developing or acquiring this capability is costly.

•        Payment Network Integrations: PMs must integrate with card networks (Visa/Mastercard/RuPay) and payment
         gateways. Each network certification and switch connection is time-consuming and complex.

•        Brand & Trust: Attracting retail customers requires building trust. New PMs struggle to achieve consumer
         confidence compared to established banks or fintech brands.

•        Customer Support & Scale: Supporting potentially millions of consumers necessitates robust customer service
         operations. High volume (especially during sales events) demands a scalable infrastructure.

Together, these factors make the PM role highly specialized. The critical success factors include proven fintech pedigree,
strong compliance culture, and deep partnerships (banks, networks, and distribution channels).

Business Model / Revenue Model in the Market

The revenue model typically blends:

•        Interchange / transaction-linked revenue share (varies by card type, merchant category, and scheme rules);
         and

•        Platform economics (software fees, premium features, service/support fees).

Interchange fees earned are usually charged as a percentage of the transaction amount and can be as high as 2.20% of the
value of spend incurred by users on prepaid cards at offline and/or online merchant outlets. Interchange fees vary across
types of merchants, the percentages of which are set by the third-party payment networks (the “Payment Networks”), such
as Mastercard, Visa, and RuPay and are generally driven by: (i) the merchant’s business segment; (ii) applicable merchant
category codes; (iii) transaction size.

The specifics are as follows:

•        Interchange Income: Each transaction on a card generates an interchange fee (typically up to approximately
         2.2% of transaction value) paid by the merchant’s acquiring bank. A program manager negotiates a share of this
         interchange with the Issuer. There are also arrangements where there is an incentive (share of interchange) paid
         to the Program manager by the Card network and the Switch service provider. The exact rate depends on the
         Merchant Category Code (MCC) (a four-digit number used by card networks to classify and identify the type of
         business in which a merchant is engaged) and card variant but can be as high as 2.2% per transaction (plus
         applicable GST). Higher-fee categories (like luxury goods) or premium cards yield more interchange.

•        Subscription / SaaS Fees: The program managers may charge a periodic platform fee or per-card issuance fee
         to cover the service. While corporate clients usually pay per- user or monthly SaaS fees, the retail model may
         instead be covered through nominal card fees or by embedding fees in cashback offers.

•        Implementation & Service: There may be one-time setup charges for integrating banks or custom support
                                                       169
                contracts, although for a ready consumer app this is likely minimal compared to corporate products.

      •         Float Income: Because prepaid cards hold user funds, there is a small float between loading and spending. The
                program manager (via its bank partner) can earn interest on these funds, although regulations require quick
                settlement so float is limited.

      Revenues scale with transaction volume and value. If users collectively spend ₹1 billion per month and PM’s effective
      take is 1.6%, that’s ₹16 million monthly revenue. Growth in users and spend volume directly drives PM earnings.
      Therefore, high-frequency usage (daily expenses) and widespread adoption are key to profitability.

      Key risks and challenges

      •         Regulatory tightening and compliance burden across KYC, disclosures, 2FA/AFA, grievances, and
                interoperability can materially increase operating costs.

      •         Dependence on issuer partners and card scheme rules (including network memberships, certifications, and
                audits) creates strategic risk, which, combined with potential pressure on unit economics from interchange
                compression and rising customer acquisition costs, can impact overall profitability.

      •         Concentration and competition: Wallets, neo-banks, and big fintech apps can replicate budgeting / alerts
                features on top of bank accounts, raising competition for attention and reducing differentiation unless the prepaid-
                linked control layer is compelling.

3.4   India Outsourced Spend Management (SaaS) Market

      The outsourced spend SaaS in India is rapidly expanding, driven by digital transformation and increased focus on cost
      optimization. As businesses face mounting pressure to streamline their operations and optimize expenditure, the demand
      for SaaS solutions catering to outsourced spend management has gained significant traction. This factor makes outsourced
      spend SaaS particularly appealing to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which constitute a substantial portion
      of India’s business ecosystem. By leveraging these solutions, SMEs can effectively control spending without investing
      heavily in IT infrastructure. One of the core drivers behind the adoption of outsourced spend SaaS in India is the value it
      brings to procurement and vendor management processes. Companies are now outsourcing procurement functions to
      specialized providers, seeking operational efficiencies and cost savings. The need for transparency and accountability in
      managing these outsourced activities is met by SaaS platforms that offer real-time visibility into procurement operations,
      track compliance, and manage spending against predefined budgets. Features such as e-procurement, contract lifecycle
      management, and spend analytics make SaaS a compelling choice, allowing businesses to make data-driven decisions and
      achieve greater control over their outsourced spending.

        Procurement Priorities and Barriers

        Across industries, procurement organizations have shifted priorities and recognize several barriers:

        •         Top Priorities: Cost control and risk mitigation dominate. Procurement leaders witnessed increased supply-chain
                  risk in 2023, with inflation and shortages as the leading concerns. Consequently, they look to double down on
                  spend visibility and diversification of suppliers. Sustainability is also rising rapidly: ESG has become an
                  important enterprise priority, and many companies now rate suppliers on some sustainability criteria. Digital
                  transformation of procurement is itself a priority.

        •         Behavioural Shifts: High-performing procurement teams are moving from transactional tasks to strategic
                  collaboration. They engage business stakeholders and suppliers, leveraging analytics to demonstrate
                  procurement’s impact on business goals. Cloud spend tools free buyers from routine work. With AI automating
                  reviews and approvals, procurement professionals can focus on negotiations and category strategy.

        •         Barriers: Common obstacles include talent gaps and change management. Many companies struggle to find
                  skilled procurement technologists. Moreover, moving to a unified spend platform often requires a cultural shift
                  which is employees must trust the new system and learn new processes. Without training and change
                  management, organizations may resist adoption. Other barriers include legacy system integration (ERP, finance,
                  HR), data silos, and concerns over security/compliance when migrating sensitive spend data to the cloud.

        The outsourced spend management SaaS market is being transformed by AI-driven capabilities and ESG considerations,
        even as enterprises grapple with skills and integration challenges. Vendors that combine advanced analytics, user-friendly
        automation and sustainability features while addressing organizational change are poised to capture the growth ahead’

        •        Cloud Adoption & Enhanced Visibility: The shift to cloud-based SaaS procurement solutions is enabling real-

4       Indian Rewards & Loyalty Market

4.1     Market Overviews

        The Indian Rewards & Loyalty Market comprises of systems and programs designed by brands to engage customers,
        encourage repeat purchases, and foster long-term loyalty. These initiatives include points-based rewards, cashback offers,
        tiered memberships, coalition programs, gamified incentives, subscription benefits, and other value-driven mechanisms
        that enhance the customer experience. At a broader level, the market also includes the entire ecosystem of products,
        services, platforms, channels, and vendors that create, distribute, and enable customer- and partner-focused reward, loyalty,
        and incentive activities. This macro market spans hardware, cards, gifting solutions, program operators, analytics
        providers, system integrators, and other supporting stakeholders.

        The Indian Rewards & Loyalty Market is broadly divided into three primary segments: Rewards and Loyalty Program
        Market, Rewards and Loyalty Management Market and Channel Rewards & Recognition Market. India’s rewards and
        loyalty ecosystem is witnessing rapid growth, with the market estimated to reach USD 5.09 billion by Calendar Year 2025
        and expected to expand significantly through the latter half of the decade to reach USD 10.57 billion at a CAGR of 15.8%
        from Calendar Year 2025-2030, in terms of revenue. In Calendar Year 2025, the Rewards & Loyalty Program segment
        was estimated to account for nearly 80.23% of the total market revenue, the Rewards & Loyalty Management segment
        contributes around 14.26% of the market, while the remaining share is contributed by the Channel Rewards & Recognition
        segment. The growth of the Indian rewards and loyalty ecosystem is fuelled by digital transformation, increasing
        smartphone and internet penetration, changing consumer preferences, and the widespread integration of rewards into
        everyday spending categories such as retail, banking, travel, food delivery, and e-commerce. The acceleration of digital
        transformation across online shopping and payment ecosystems—driven by UPI, digital wallets, in-app commerce, and
        seamless checkout experiences—has further embedded rewards and loyalty programs into routine consumer transactions.

        The market is evolving into a highly digital, mobile-first, and data-driven ecosystem, with a strong focus on
        personalization, real-time engagement, and cross-industry partnerships. Brands are increasingly leveraging loyalty
        platforms and marketplaces such as Paramotor’s RewardOn (enterprise and channel loyalty solutions) and yayyy.shop
        (consumer-focused rewards and gifting marketplace), alongside established players like Capillary Technologies, Payback
        India, Tata Neu, Edenred, Zaggle Propel and emerging loyalty SaaS providers, to deliver meaningful value and
        differentiated customer experiences.

        Overall, the Indian Rewards & Loyalty Market is positioned for sustained long-term growth, driven by innovation,
        consumer demand for tangible benefits, the increasing adoption of customer engagement and loyalty programs by
        consumer brands and the growing importance of loyalty as a competitive advantage.

        Prominent players in the Rewards & Loyalty market include Capillary Technologies India Limited, Paramotor
        (RewardOn), Zaggle Prepaid Ocean Services Limited, Easyrewardz Software Services Private Limited, Edenred (India)
        Private Limited, Nreach Online Services Private Limited (operates Xoxoday / Plum / Empuls), Thriwe Consulting Private
        Limited (erstwhile GolfLan Technology Solutions Private Limited).

4.2     Key Market Segments

        The Indian Rewards & Loyalty Market is broadly divided into three primary segments: Rewards and Loyalty Program
        Market, Rewards and Loyalty Management Market and Channel Rewards & Recognition Market.

        1.       Rewards and Loyalty Program Market (Customer-Facing Rewards & Loyalty Programs)

                 Refers to the actual reward schemes operated by brands to incentivize customers and influence purchasing
                 behaviour. These programs include points-based reward systems, cashback and instant rewards, tiered

              models. Their core objective is to drive customer engagement, encourage repeat purchases, improve retention,
              and enhance overall customer lifetime value by creating meaningful and value-driven interactions between brands
              and consumers.

              This market is predominantly digital and mobile-first, with loyalty programs delivered through mobile
              applications, websites, and integrated e-commerce or payment platforms. The widespread adoption of
              smartphones and digital wallets in India has accelerated the shift away from traditional physical loyalty cards
              toward seamless, web and app-based reward experiences. Brands are increasingly leveraging AI, advanced
              analytics, predictive modelling, and personalization, and in some cases blockchain, to make rewards more
              relevant, timely, and engaging while improving program efficiency and transparency.

                                                            173
      based loyalty technology players offering cloud-native, modular, and API-driven platforms, enabling rapid deployment,
      scalability, and real-time personalization. This segment is primarily adopted by retailers, banks, fintech companies, travel
      and hospitality brands, and large enterprises that require robust, scalable, and data-driven loyalty infrastructure.

      At its core, the market is built around two key components: technology solutions and services. Technology Solutions
      represent the core software platforms that manage loyalty rules, customer data, reward issuance, and redemption
      workflows, and they accounted for the largest share of revenue, (more than 60%) in Calendar Year 2025. Services—
      covering system integration, consulting, customization, analytics support, and ongoing managed services—form the
      fastest-growing component, reflecting increasing demand for tailored implementations and advanced optimization
      capabilities. Together, these components enable seamless program execution across multiple channels and customer
      touchpoints.

      The Loyalty Management Market is supported by a mix of global technology providers and specialized vendors.
      Specialized consultancies and SaaS vendors focused on the Indian market play an important role in addressing local
      integration and customization needs, with emerging platforms such as Paramotor’s RewardOn gaining traction for
      enterprise and channel loyalty management through flexible, modular, and data-driven loyalty solutions.

      In India, the Loyalty Management Market generated revenues of USD 0.38 billion in Calendar Year 2020. Having grown
      at a CAGR of 13.8% from Calendar Year 2020-2025, the market was estimated to reach USD 0.73 billion in Calendar
      Year 2025 and is expected to expand further to around USD 1.48 billion by Calendar Year 2030, reflecting a CAGR of
      15.3% from Calendar Year 2025 to Calendar Year 2030, in terms of revenue. This growth is driven by the increasing
      sophistication of loyalty programs, rising demand for personalization, and the need for real-time analytics and omnichannel
      integration.

      Functionally, this segment serves as the backbone technology layer supporting the broader Rewards and Loyalty Program
      Market. The effectiveness of customer-facing loyalty initiatives is directly influenced by the quality, flexibility, and
      intelligence of these platforms. Core capabilities include data analytics and customer segmentation, configurable reward
      engines and rules management, API-based integration with POS systems, wallets, and mobile apps, and real-time
      personalization across digital channels. In essence, the Loyalty Management Market represents the technology and
      operational infrastructure that powers, tracks, and scales loyalty programs, enabling brands to deliver consistent, engaging,
      and measurable reward experiences.

3.    Channel Rewards & Recognition market

      India’s Channel Rewards & Recognition market includes the ecosystem of programs, platforms, and services designed for
      corporates to motivate, engage, and incentivize employees as well as indirect sales partners including distributors, dealers,
      resellers, retailers, agents, & other channel intermediaries. These initiatives use structured reward, incentive, and
      recognition frameworks tied to performance metrics, sales achievements, brand advocacy, and broader business objectives.
      Channel rewards programs typically combine financial and non-financial incentives—such as cash bonuses, rebates,
      discounts, gift vouchers, travel experiences, digital points, and formal recognition—to influence partner behaviour and
      align it with the company’s strategic priorities. This is a B2B/B2B2C sub-market focused on rewarding channel partners
      (and sometimes channel employees) rather than end customers. Programs in this segment commonly use different
      mechanics such as sales credits, rebates, certification rewards, travel or gift incentives, and partner dashboards for tracking
      performance and engagement.

      The market is gaining significant traction as organizations increasingly focus on strengthening relationships with their
      distribution and retail networks. Through tailored incentive and recognition programs, businesses aim to enhance partner
      motivation, accelerate sales growth, and build long-term brand loyalty. The approach is evolving beyond traditional reward
      mechanisms toward more personalized and engaging models, incorporating digital vouchers, experiential rewards, and
      gamified platforms to improve participation and effectiveness.

      Data analytics plays a growing role in enabling performance-based customization of incentives, fostering healthy
      competition among partners and improving overall satisfaction. As the market matures, technology-driven solutions are
      helping organizations optimize channel engagement and ensure rewards are more impactful and closely aligned with
      business objectives. The Channel Rewards & Recognition market in India is projected to grow from USD 0.23 billion in
      Calendar Year 2024 to USD 0.28 billion in Calendar Year 2025, reaching USD 0.50 billion by Calendar Year 2030,
      registering a CAGR of 12.4% during Calendar Year 2025–2030, in terms of revenue.

4.3   Key Trends

      Key Trends Shaping the India Rewards & Loyalty Market:

                                                               174
1.   AI & Data-Driven Personalization: Indian brands are increasingly leveraging Artificial Intelligence (AI) and
     data analytics to deliver personalized loyalty experiences. By analysing customer behaviour, shopping history,
     and preferences, companies can offer highly targeted rewards and communications, enhancing satisfaction and
     long-term retention. For example, Myntra’s Myntra Insider program tailors’ discounts and promotions based on
     individual shopping patterns, while BigBasket customizes loyalty rewards to reflect preferences for groceries or
     household items.

     Looking ahead, AI-driven personalization is expected to become central to loyalty strategies. By 2027, most
     major brands in India are likely to use AI extensively to offer tailored rewards, boosting customer engagement
     and loyalty. However, businesses will need to carefully navigate data privacy regulations to ensure responsible
     collection and use of consumer information.

2.   Mobile Integration & Seamless Access: With smartphones becoming the primary channel for consumer
     interaction, loyalty programs are increasingly mobile-first. Mobile apps allow users to track points, receive
     personalized offers, and redeem rewards conveniently, driving sustained engagement.

     Exhibit 28: Key Trends Shaping the India Rewards & Loyalty Market




3.   Cross-Industry & Cross-Brand Partnerships: To enhance the value of loyalty programs, Indian companies are
     forging partnerships across industries, enabling customers to earn and redeem rewards across multiple sectors.
     For instance, HDFC Bank’s SmartBuy program allows users to collect points through transactions with partners
     like Amazon, BookMyShow, and Myntra, offering flexibility and a richer rewards ecosystem.

     This trend is fuelled by the desire to differentiate loyalty offerings in a competitive market while sharing
     fulfilment costs. Over the next few years, we can expect an expansion of integrated loyalty ecosystems, where
     rewards span categories such as retail, travel, entertainment, and lifestyle. Effective management of these
     partnerships will require clear agreements on data sharing, customer privacy, and operational coordination.

4.   Sustainability & Social Responsibility: Sustainability is emerging as a key factor in consumer decision-making,
     especially among Millennials and Gen Z. Indian brands are increasingly integrating eco-friendly initiatives into
     loyalty programs to appeal to environmentally conscious customers. For example, IKEA India’s IKEA Family
     program awards points for purchases of sustainable products, while Tata CLiQ rewards eco-conscious behaviour.

     As environmental awareness grows, sustainable loyalty programs are expected to become more prominent. By
     2027, many programs may reward consumers for eco-friendly actions such as buying sustainable products or
     participating in recycling efforts. While this approach strengthens brand differentiation and loyalty, companies
     will need to balance sustainability goals with profitability, as implementing green initiatives may involve higher
     costs.

5.   Gamification to Boost Engagement: Brands are increasingly using gamified elements such as challenges, spin-
     the-wheel rewards, leaderboards, and tier progression to make loyalty programs interactive and fun. Gamification
     encourages repeat participation beyond simple transactions and keeps customers engaged with the brand over the
     long term. For example, Flipkart SuperCoins and Amazon Prime incorporate elements of gamification to drive
     engagement.

                                                   175
      6.      Tiered & Subscription-Based Loyalty Models: Tiered loyalty programs and paid memberships are gaining
              traction as a way to offer exclusive benefits and experiences. Programs like Amazon Prime, Flipkart Plus, and
              Tata Neu provide different membership levels or subscription perks, incentivizing higher spending and enhancing
              customer retention. Tiered structures reward loyal customers more heavily, fostering lifetime value growth.

      7.      Instant Rewards and Cashbacks: Consumers increasingly prefer instant gratification over delayed benefits.
              Real-time cashback, instant reward redemption, and digital gift cards are becoming standard features in Indian
              loyalty programs. Integration with UPI and digital wallets allows seamless earning and redemption, making
              loyalty programs more convenient and appealing.

      8.      Focus on Data Privacy and Trust: As loyalty programs become more personalized, data privacy and security
              are critical. Consumers are increasingly aware of how their data is used, and brands that maintain transparency
              and trust will have a competitive edge. Compliance with regulations like India’s Digital Personal Data Protection
              Act is essential for building long-term consumer confidence.

              The Indian rewards and loyalty market is moving toward innovative, customer-centric solutions, driven by rising
              corporate spends on engagement, AI-powered personalization, and digital payment-linked rewards such as gift
              cards and e-vouchers. Mobile-first experiences, gamification, subscription-based models, cross-industry
              partnerships, and sustainability-focused incentives are deepening engagement, reflecting evolving consumer
              preferences for greater relevance, convenience, and value, while fostering stronger long-term loyalty.

4.4   Use cases / workflows

      The Indian rewards and loyalty market is poised for strong growth, driven by rapid digital adoption, widespread
      smartphone usage, and the dominance of UPI-led payments. The ecosystem is distinctly mobile-first, technology-enabled,
      and data-driven, with a clear shift toward personalized, real-time, and experiential rewards. High price sensitivity
      combined with a strong preference for instant gratification has transformed loyalty programs from traditional “earn-and-
      burn” models into always-on engagement engines. Today, loyalty in India functions as an integrated framework for
      customer acquisition, retention, and lifetime value enhancement, embedded across consumer, enterprise, and employee
      ecosystems.

      Key Use Cases in the Indian Market

      The core use cases span both Business-to-Consumer (B2C) and Business-to-Business (B2B) contexts, with a strong
      emphasis on digital payments integration, instant rewards fulfilment, and analytics-led personalization.

      1.      In the retail and e-commerce segment, loyalty programs are primarily designed to increase purchase frequency,
              improve retention, and drive higher basket sizes across online and offline channels. Platforms such as Amazon
              Prime and Flipkart Plus blend subscription-based and tiered loyalty structures to deliver consistent, high-visibility
              value. Benefits including free and faster shipping, early access to sale events, exclusive discounts, and bundled
              digital services like OTT subscriptions help strengthen brand affinity and justify sustained engagement beyond
              transactional incentives.

              Operationally, customers are onboarded using mobile numbers at checkout or via brand apps, reflecting India’s
              mobile-centric behaviour. Each transaction converts rupee spend into points, coins, or cashback, which is credited
              instantly to meet expectations of immediacy. Rewards can be redeemed seamlessly for discounts, free products,
              vouchers, or priority access to promotions. Over time, customer data is analysed across spend patterns, frequency,
              and category preferences to build segmented cohorts. Personalized offers are then delivered through high-
              engagement channels such as app notifications, SMS, and WhatsApp. Simplicity, transparency, and real-time
              reward visibility are critical, as complex mechanics or delayed redemption significantly reduce program
              effectiveness in the Indian market.

      2.      Employee rewards and recognition (R&R) programs have emerged as strategic levers for improving
              engagement, morale, and retention. Managers and HR teams allocate points for performance, milestones, and
              peer recognition, with employees receiving instant notifications. Rewards are redeemed from curated catalogues
              that include vouchers, merchandise, experiences, or prepaid cards. Indian R&R programs emphasize compliance,
              tax efficiency, and festive gifting, with usage peaking during Diwali and annual appraisal cycles. These rewards
              are typically delivered through digital gift cards, prepaid instruments, or loyalty points that can be redeemed
              across a wide network of merchants, including e-commerce platforms, retail stores, restaurants, travel portals,
              supermarkets, and lifestyle brands, enabling employees to use benefits conveniently across online and offline
              retail ecosystems.

                                                             176
3.   In financial services and fintech, loyalty programs are deeply embedded within everyday financial interactions
     such as credit card usage, UPI transactions, and bill payments. Banks like HDFC and Axis, along with fintech
     platforms such as Paytm and Cred, leverage the ubiquity of digital payments to deliver instant cashback, reward
     points, and e-vouchers. Unlike traditional models focused on long-term accumulation, fintech-led loyalty
     emphasizes daily habit formation and sustained engagement. Each transaction can trigger gamified rewards such
     as scratch cards, coins, or cashback, reinforcing repeat behaviour. Rewards are credited in real time to wallets or
     loyalty balances and redeemed for utilities, mobile recharges, shopping vouchers, digital gold, or investment
     products. Tier-based structures further incentivize high-frequency or high-value users by unlocking enhanced
     benefits and exclusive privileges, aligning closely with Indian consumers’ preference for speed, ease, and tangible
     value.

4.   Banking and credit card loyalty programs follow a more structured and tier-driven approach, targeting affluent
     and high-spending customer segments. Cardholders earn reward points on everyday spends, with accelerated
     accrual for premium categories such as travel, dining, and partner merchants. These points are consolidated into
     centralized rewards platforms, enabling redemption for flights, hotel stays, vouchers, or airline miles. Status tiers
     like Silver, Gold, and Platinum enhance the proposition through differentiated privileges, including lounge access,
     priority service, and concierge support. In India, these programs also act as monetization ecosystems, allowing
     banks to generate incremental revenue through merchant partnerships and commission-based integrations within
     the loyalty journey.

5.   In the travel and hospitality sector, loyalty programs are built around frequency-based, points-driven models
     that reward brand preference in a highly competitive environment. Airlines such as IndiGo, through initiatives
     like 6E Rewards, and hotel chains like Marriott Bonvoy encourage repeat usage by offering upgrades,
     complimentary stays, priority services, and lounge access. These programs focus on experiential and status-
     oriented benefits, helping brands build emotional loyalty and influence long-term travel choices beyond price
     considerations.

6.   In restaurants & Quick Service Restaurants (QSR) segment, loyalty programs are designed to drive frequent
     visits, increase average order value, and strengthen brand recall in a highly competitive market. Common use
     cases include birthday and anniversary perks, where customers receive special vouchers, complimentary desserts,
     or exclusive offers as part of their membership benefits. Mobile app order rewards are widely adopted, offering
     points, cashback, or instant discounts for orders placed through brand apps or digital channels, reinforcing app-
     based ordering behaviour. Many brands also integrate gamified challenges such as streak rewards, milestone
     incentives, and referral bonuses to further boost engagement. Rewards are typically redeemed for free items,
     discounts, meal upgrades, or priority access to new menu launches, with real-time tracking and redemption
     visibility through mobile apps. This segment increasingly leverages data-driven personalization, enabling
     targeted offers based on ordering frequency, preferred cuisine, and time-of-day patterns, thereby converting
     casual customers into loyal repeat diners.

7.   The wellness and lifestyle segment reflects a growing shift toward experience-led loyalty. Programs increasingly
     offer rewards such as fitness memberships, wellness subscriptions, preventive health checkups, and access to
     exclusive events or workshops. This evolution mirrors the preferences of urban, digitally savvy consumers who
     value holistic lifestyle enhancement over simple discounts. By integrating wellness-oriented rewards, brands
     position themselves as long-term partners in customers’ personal and professional well-being.

8.   On the B2B side, channel partner loyalty programs are critical tools for driving sales and influencing behaviour
     across FMCG, automotive, consumer electronics, and building materials industries. Distributors, retailers, and
     dealers are incentivized through structured rewards such as points, gift cards, merchandise, or aspirational
     experiences like travel packages. Channel partners are onboarded onto dedicated digital platforms where targets
     are assigned, performance is tracked through invoice uploads or system integrations, and rewards are credited
     after validation. These programs are designed to drive sell-in, sell-out, and focus on priority products, with
     transparency, trust, and aspirational rewards serving as key success factors in India’s fragmented channel
     landscape.

9.   Sales force incentive programs aim to motivate internal teams by aligning performance outcomes with clearly
     defined KPIs. Real-time dashboards offer continuous visibility into progress, while gamification elements such
     as leaderboards, badges, and milestone challenges foster competition and engagement. Incentives are typically
     distributed monthly or quarterly and combine tangible rewards with public recognition. In India, these programs
     are particularly effective when aligned with social recognition and festival-linked incentives, reinforcing cultural
     relevance.

                                                    177
      10.      Finally, short-term promotional loyalty campaigns are extensively deployed for festive sales, new product
               launches, and user reactivation. These campaigns operate on time-bound rules, offer instant gratification through
               cashback or vouchers, and are governed by strict budget controls. Integrated fraud checks and analytics ensure
               ROI tracking, while clear communication and immediate rewards drive effectiveness during peak demand
               periods.

               Across all these use cases, data and analytics form the backbone of the Indian rewards and loyalty ecosystem.
               Continuous ingestion of transactional and behavioural data enables segmentation by value, frequency, and
               preferences. Personalized offers are delivered through high-reach channels such as WhatsApp, SMS, and app
               notifications. This system—connecting data, rewards, and behaviour—allows continuous optimization and
               positions loyalty programs in India as strategic growth enablers rather than standalone cost centres.

4.5   Role of Technology in Powering Modern Rewards & Loyalty Programs

      Technology is transforming how loyalty programs are designed, delivered, and experienced. Modern programs leverage
      AI, data analytics, automation, and digital platforms to create highly personalized, efficient, and engaging experiences for
      customers.

      1.       AI, ML and Data-Driven Personalization: Indian companies are increasingly using AI, Machine Learning
               (ML) and data analytics to make loyalty programs more relevant and tailored to individual customers. For
               example, Myntra’s Myntra Insider program analyses shopping history to deliver personalized discounts and
               promotions, while BigBasket customizes rewards for specific grocery and household preferences.

               The growing availability of data, combined with advanced AI & ML technologies, allows businesses to gain
               deeper insights into customer behaviour. Retailers, especially e-commerce platforms, are leading this trend, using
               analytics to optimize loyalty offerings and maximize engagement. India’s expanding digital infrastructure also
               makes these technologies more accessible to businesses of all sizes.

               Over the next few years, AI-driven personalization is expected to be central to loyalty strategies. By 2027, most
               large Indian brands are likely to rely heavily on AI to deliver targeted rewards, improving customer satisfaction
               and retention. However, companies must also navigate data privacy regulations and ensure responsible use of
               consumer data.

      2.       AI-Powered Chatbots and Customer Support: AI-driven chatbots, using Natural Language Processing (NLP),
               provide fast, personalized assistance for queries related to points, rewards, or program participation. This
               enhances customer experience while reducing operational costs.

      3.       Fraud Detection and Security: AI also helps monitor loyalty accounts for fraudulent activity, protecting both
               customers and business interests. For instance, Amazon leverages AI to detect and prevent fraud within its loyalty
               ecosystem.

      4.       Data Analytics for Customer Insights: Advanced analytics tools enable brands to monitor metrics such as
               Customer Satisfaction Score (CSAT), Net Promoter Score (NPS), Customer Effort Score (CES), and RFM
               (Recency, Frequency, Monetary) analysis. These insights help identify churn risks, predict purchase intent, and
               design targeted retention campaigns. Loyalty management platforms generate detailed customer profiles,
               allowing businesses to optimize engagement, repeat purchases, and lifetime value.

      5.       Real-Time Rewards and Automation: Modern loyalty platforms support instant reward issuance, redemption,
               and notifications, improving customer convenience and satisfaction. Automation reduces operational
               inefficiencies, minimizes errors, and allows brands to scale programs effectively. Digital gift cards and instant
               cashback offers are now standard features in India’s loyalty ecosystem.

      6.       Integration with Digital Payments and UPI: Seamless integration with digital wallets and UPI platforms like
               Paytm and PhonePe enables real-time earning and redemption of loyalty points, encouraging frequent
               participation and engagement.

      7.       Repeat Purchases & Optimizing Costs: Loyalty programs allow organizations to focus on retaining existing
               customers rather than spending heavily on acquiring new ones. By encouraging repeat purchases, businesses can
               reduce marketing costs while maximizing customer lifetime value. As a result, strengthening repeat purchase
               rates has emerged as a central driver for loyalty program adoption, since retention strategies are more cost-
               effective and revenue-generating than acquiring new customers.

                                                             178
      8.     Advanced Customer Monitoring & Engagement Tools: Modern loyalty solutions offer businesses real-time
             insights into customer behaviour and engagement through metrics such as Customer Satisfaction Score (CSAT),
             Net Promoter Score (NPS), Customer Effort Score (CES), and RFM (Recency, Frequency, Monetary) analysis.
             These tools help brands monitor loyalty trends, predict churn, and design targeted campaigns for specific
             customer segments. By leveraging behavioural insights, companies can enhance engagement, improve retention,
             and increase overall revenue.

      9.     Predicting Customer Intent & Driving Retention: Loyalty management solutions help organizations identify
             customer interests and forecast purchase intent. Analytics allow marketers to predict which customers are at risk
             of churn and implement targeted retention strategies, such as personalized discounts or product upgrades. By
             mapping all customer touchpoints and delivering tailored interactions along the journey, companies can ensure
             higher product adoption, stronger engagement, and an expanded market share.

      10.    Rising Demand for Personalized Loyalty Experiences: Indian consumers increasingly expect personalized and
             relevant loyalty experiences. Brands are responding by offering individualized discounts, offers, and promotions
             based on multichannel data. Personalized programs enhance customer trust, improve satisfaction, and drive
             adoption across industries, making tailored experiences a key growth driver in the loyalty market.

             Technology has become the backbone of modern loyalty programs in India. From AI-powered personalization
             and predictive analytics to mobile-first platforms, real-time rewards, and fraud prevention, technology empowers
             brands to deliver relevant, convenient, and engaging loyalty experiences. These innovations not only enhance
             customer satisfaction but also drive repeat purchases, retention, and long-term business growth.

4.7   Value Chain and stakeholder ecosystem

      The Indian rewards and loyalty market operates through a complex ecosystem of interconnected stakeholders, each playing
      a distinct role in ensuring seamless program design, delivery, engagement, and redemption. The ecosystem can be broadly
      categorized into three major layers:

      Exhibit 33: Value Chain & stakeholder ecosystem for Indian Rewards & Loyalty Market




      1.      Program Designers / Agencies:

              These are consulting firms, marketing agencies, or specialized loyalty solution providers that conceptualize and
              design loyalty programs. They define program objectives, tier structures, reward policies, and engagement
              strategies while designing customer journeys, gamification elements, and personalized campaigns. They also
              ensure compliance with regulatory and tax requirements in India, making them critical for creating strategic,
              legally sound, and customer-centric loyalty frameworks.

      2.      Loyalty Platforms and Technology Providers:

              These digital platforms and SaaS providers form the operational backbone of loyalty programs. They handle
              enrolment, reward tracking, and management, and integrate seamlessly with POS systems, e-commerce
              platforms, wallets, and UPI infrastructure. Advanced analytics, AI/ML engines, and predictive personalization
              tools enable customer segmentation, targeted campaigns, and behaviour-driven rewards. Security and fraud
              prevention mechanisms ensure safe reward issuance and redemption. Prominent players in India include
              RewardOn powered by Paramotor, Paytm Loyalty, Vouchagram India Private Limited (operating under the brand
              name Gyftr), Pine Labs Ltd., Points (formerly Points International Ltd.), Amazon Internet Services Private
              Limited, and other tech-driven platforms.


                                                                    181
      3.      Catalogue Aggregators and Brand Partners:

              These stakeholders deliver the actual value that customers redeem. Catalogue aggregators curate diverse reward
              catalogues encompassing products, vouchers, and experiences, while brand partners—including retailers, e-
              commerce platforms, airlines, hotels, F&B chains, and wellness providers—expand redemption options, co-brand
              campaigns, and drive customer engagement. Their collaboration ensures a rich, aspirational, and flexible reward
              ecosystem.

      4.      Cross-Functional Stakeholders:

              Beyond the core layers, additional entities enable seamless operations. Payment networks (UPI providers, card
              networks, wallets) facilitate real-time earning and redemption. Analytics and data providers supply insights for
              personalization, campaign optimization, and behavioural prediction. Marketing channels such as app
              notifications, SMS, WhatsApp, and email ensure targeted, high-impact communication to end-users.

      5.      Technology & Platform Layer:

              This layer underpins modern programs with tools like digital platforms and apps (Paramotor, Amazon, Paytm,
              Tata Neu), blockchain solutions for security and transparency, and specialized rewards providers offering
              experiential incentives such as wellness, travel, or exclusive access. Loyalty-as-a-Service (LaaS) firms like
              Zillion, Thriwe help brands build, manage, and optimize programs efficiently, while payment gateways and
              fintechs integrate loyalty into daily transactions.

      6.      Brands and Merchants (Issuers):

              Brands across sectors act as issuers of loyalty rewards. These include retail and e-commerce (Amazon, Flipkart,
              Shoppers Stop), hospitality and travel (airlines, hotels), BFSI (banks and non-banking financial companies
              (NBFCs)), and FMCG, telecom, and utilities. They define the rewards ecosystem, sponsor points, and provide
              redemption opportunities that align with customer preferences.

      7.      Consumers (End Users):

              The ultimate beneficiaries of loyalty programs are digitally savvy, value-conscious consumers who seek instant
              gratification, seamless redemption, and experiential rewards. Their behaviour and engagement provide data that
              fuels personalization and program optimization.

      8.      Regulators and Policymakers:

              Regulatory bodies and advisory firms (e.g., PwC India) oversee compliance, taxation, and legal frameworks,
              ensuring loyalty programs operate transparently and within the law, which is especially critical in financial
              services and fintech-led programs.

4.8   Business Model / Revenue model Monetization / economics

      The Indian rewards and loyalty market operates on a multi-layered revenue model that combines direct fees, financial
      mechanisms, and strategic partnerships. These models are designed to ensure profitability for platforms, brands, and
      service providers while delivering tangible value to consumers. Key monetization strategies include:

      1.      Platform Licensing and Per-Programme Fees:

              Loyalty program providers generate revenue by licensing their software and platforms to businesses, including
              brands, retailers, and financial institutions. Revenue streams in this category include:

              a.       Software & Platform Licensing: Charging for access to technology infrastructure that manages points,
                       tracks customer activity, and runs campaigns.

              b.       Setup and Integration Fees: One-time charges for integrating the loyalty platform with POS systems,
                       e-commerce portals, CRM tools, or payment gateways.

              c.       Subscription or Per-Programme Fees: Ongoing fees based on the size of the customer base,
                       transaction volumes, or the scale and features of the program.

              d.       Consulting and Managed Services: Fees for expertise in program design, campaign management, data
                                                           182
                       analytics, and ongoing loyalty program operations.

      2.      Breakage, Float, and Commercial Margins:

              Financial mechanisms also drive revenue in loyalty programs:

              a.       Breakage: Income derived from unredeemed points, vouchers, or rewards, which reduces the liability
                       on company books.

              b.       Float: Funds collected when points are issued but not immediately redeemed can earn interest, providing
                       additional financial leverage.

              c.       Commercial Margins: Loyalty companies often buy rewards (flights, merchandise, vouchers) at
                       wholesale prices and offer them at higher perceived value in points, capturing the margin between cost
                       and redemption value.

      3.      Co-Branded and Partnership Propositions:

              Strategic partnerships form another critical revenue pillar:

              a.       Partner Commissions: Brands and retailers pay commissions when loyalty members transact with
                       them, especially in coalition loyalty programs spanning multiple businesses.

              b.       Marketing and Promotion Fees: Platforms charge brands for in-program advertising, sponsored offers,
                       or premium placement within the loyalty ecosystem.

              c.       Super App Integrations: In India, platforms like Paytm, Tata Neu, and PhonePe integrate loyalty
                       features across multiple services and retail partners, creating large, interconnected ecosystems that drive
                       transactional volume and recurring revenue.

              Overall, the Indian loyalty market leverages a blend of licensing fees, transaction-based charges, breakage, float,
              co-branded partnerships, and data monetization, forming a robust and scalable business model. This multi-
              channel revenue approach ensures sustainability for providers while enhancing engagement, retention, and value
              for both brands and consumers.

4.9   Key Risks & Challenges

      The Indian rewards and loyalty market is growing rapidly, but several regulatory, operational, and market-related
      challenges need careful management to ensure program effectiveness and long-term sustainability.

      1.      Data Protection & Privacy:

              The upcoming Personal Data Protection Bill will require companies to enhance data privacy measures, ensuring
              transparency in customer data collection, storage, and usage. Programs like Amazon Prime and Flipkart Plus will
              need to invest in secure systems to remain compliant and maintain customer trust.

      2.      Fraud and Misuse of Loyalty Points:

              Fraudulent activities, such as account hacking or unauthorized redemptions, pose risks to program integrity.
              While AI-based monitoring and security protocols help, smaller companies may struggle to implement these
              systems effectively.

      3.      High Operational & Technology Costs:

              Developing, maintaining, and upgrading loyalty platforms—including AI, analytics, and mobile integrations—
              can be expensive, particularly for SMEs. Scaling programs while maintaining efficiency and user experience
              remains a challenge.

      4.      Dependence on Digital Infrastructure:

              Mobile-first loyalty programs rely heavily on internet connectivity, digital wallets, and smartphones. Limited
              access in rural or underserved areas may restrict program reach.

                                                             183
               The Indian rewards and loyalty market offers substantial growth opportunities, but brands must proactively
               manage data privacy, operational complexity, fraud risks, regulatory compliance, customer engagement, and
               program differentiation. Successfully navigating these challenges is crucial to sustaining competitive advantage,
               maximizing ROI, and building long-term customer loyalty.

5     Indian Digital Gift Card Market

5.1   Market Overview / key trends

      India’s digital gift card market encompasses the end-to-end ecosystem for purchasing, distributing, and redeeming
      electronic gifts such as e-gift cards, vouchers, prepaid credits, digital subscriptions, and virtual or experiential rewards
      through online platforms, mobile apps, and social channels. Valued at approximately USD 15.1 billion in Calendar Year
      2025 in terms of GTV, this market is expected to grow at a CAGR of 17.4% from Calendar Year 2025-2030. This market
      is significantly larger than the narrower online gifting segment, which focuses on the e-commerce sale of physical gifts
      and operates at a much smaller scale.

      The market is witnessing rapid and sustained growth, driven by widespread digital adoption, a base of over 900 million
      internet users, and a robust cashless payments infrastructure led by UPI, which processes billions of transactions each
      month. Digital gifting enables instant delivery via e-commerce platforms, wallets, and social media—eliminating the
      logistics, delays, and costs associated with physical gifts. At the same time, it supports high levels of personalization
      through AI-driven recommendations, flexible denominations, and gamified formats, making it especially attractive for
      festive, corporate, and everyday gifting use cases. Together, these factors position digital gifting as a fast-growing,
      convenience-led, and experience-oriented segment within India’s broader digital commerce and rewards ecosystem.

      Prominent players in the Digital gift card market include Paramotor (operates yayyy.shop), Pine Labs Limited (operates
      Woohoo), Vouchagram India Private Limited (operates GyFTR) and Parity Cube Private Limited (operates Zingoy).

      Key Trends

      India's digital gift card market is surging, propelled by e-gift cards' instant delivery and flexibility, replacing physical gifts
      for consumers and corporates alike. Key trends shaping the India digital gifting market:

      1.       Rapid Growth of Digital & E-Gift Cards

               Digital and e-gift cards continue to gain traction as the preferred gifting instrument due to their convenience,
               instant delivery, and flexibility. They are increasingly replacing physical gift options, appealing to both
               consumers and corporates looking for hassle-free gifting solutions. Globally, digital and e-gift card market is
               projected to exceed USD 1.4 trillion by Calendar Year 2030, up from USD 0.4 trillion in Calendar Year 2025,
               reflecting strong adoption in India as part of the broader loyalty ecosystem.

      2.       Integration with Digital Payments & Wallets

               Seamless integration of digital gifting with mobile wallets, UPI, and fintech apps has made purchasing, sending,
               and redeeming digital gifts faster, secure, and frictionless. This creates a unified digital gifting experience that
               resonates with India’s cashless ecosystem.

      3.       Personalization & Customization

               Consumers increasingly demand tailored gifting experiences—from customized messages and value
               denominations to themed designs and multimedia elements. AI-driven personalization enhances emotional
               connection and recipient satisfaction, driving higher adoption.

      4.       Expansion of Experiential & Subscription-Based Gifting

               Beyond standard gift cards, experiential gifts (e.g., travel vouchers, wellness memberships, event passes) and
               digital subscriptions are rising in popularity. This shift reflects the preference for meaningful and memorable
               gifting over traditional material items.

      5.       Corporate Spend & Strategic Adoption

               Businesses are increasingly incorporating digital gifting into employee rewards, channel incentives, and customer
               engagement programs. Digital gift cards offer scalability, minimal logistics, and measurable impact—making

                                                                184
              them especially effective in hybrid work environments. In India, the B2B segment represents a major share of
              gift card usage, with corporate entities increasingly adopting digital gift cards for rewards, incentives, and
              promotional campaigns. Adoption continues to grow across sectors such as IT, retail, financial services, and
              consumer goods, as companies rely on digital gift cards as a preferred tool for engagement, motivation, and
              retention.

      6.      Discount-Driven Engagement & Value Incentives

              A key trend in India’s digital gift card market is the increasing use of attractive discounts, cashbacks, user rewards,
              and bonus value to drive customer engagement and adoption. Digital gift cards are often offered at discounted
              prices or bundled with platform rewards, making them a value-driven purchase rather than just a gifting
              instrument. This strategy strongly appeals to India’s price-sensitive consumers, encouraging impulse purchases,
              higher redemption rates, and repeat usage. For platforms and brands, discount-led gifting helps boost transaction
              volumes, acquire new users, and stimulate incremental spending when gift card values are redeemed—creating a
              win-win ecosystem for consumers, merchants, and intermediaries alike.

      7.      Rising Sales Volumes & Seasonal Peaks

              Festive occasions such as Diwali, Raksha Bandhan, Christmas, and weddings significantly boost digital gifting
              activity. During these peak periods, platforms and brands often run high visibility offers and thematic campaigns,
              which further amplify demand. Digital gift card volumes typically spike during major festive and sales events,
              with platforms reporting millions of transactions in these seasons. For example, network gift cards launched on
              India’s ONDC platform recorded around 1.2 million transactions during a recent festive period, indicating
              growing penetration across cities and categories.

              In summary, India’s digital gift card market is evolving rapidly from simple e-gift card purchases to a broader,
              technology-empowered ecosystem that emphasizes personalization, convenience, and experiential value,
              supported by seamless digital payments and expanding corporate use cases.

5.2   Gift Card Segmentation in the Indian Digital Gifting Market

      The Indian digital gift card market can be broadly segmented based on the issuer and redemption ecosystem, with each
      segment serving distinct consumer needs, use cases, and distribution models. Together, these segments form the backbone
      of India’s rapidly expanding digital gifting and rewards landscape.

      1.      Brand-Specific Gift Cards:

              Brand-specific gift cards are issued directly by individual brands and are redeemable only within that brand’s
              ecosystem. These are most common among retailers, fashion brands, food & beverage chains, electronics stores,
              and hospitality players. Such gift cards are typically used for targeted gifting, promotions, and loyalty rewards,
              as they help brands lock in future spend, increase repeat purchases, and strengthen brand affinity. For consumers,
              they offer clarity and simplicity, while for brands, they ensure guaranteed redemption within their own outlets,
              making them an effective retention and revenue assurance tool.

      2.      E-commerce Issued Gift Cards:

              E-commerce platforms issue gift cards that can be redeemed across a wide range of categories available on their
              marketplaces, including retail products, digital services, and partner offerings. These cards are highly popular for
              both personal and corporate gifting due to their flexibility, wide acceptance, and ease of redemption. They appeal
              strongly to urban and digital-first consumers, as recipients can choose from thousands of products and services,
              making them one of the most versatile gifting instruments in India’s digital economy.

      3.      Bank-Issued Gift Cards/ RBI licensed PPI Issued Gift Cards:

              Bank-issued gift cards/ RBI licensed PPI issued gift cards are typically prepaid instruments offered by banks and
              financial institutions, either as standalone products or linked to credit cards, debit cards, or corporate payout
              programs. These cards are often used for employee rewards, customer incentives, promotions, and corporate
              gifting, as they are perceived as secure and regulated.

      4.      Digital Platform–Issued Gift Cards:

              Digital platforms, including fintech apps, wallets, and loyalty or rewards platforms, issue gift cards that can be
                                                              185
               redeemed across multiple partner brands or categories. These cards are deeply integrated into apps, wallets, and
               super-app ecosystems, enabling instant issuance, storage, and redemption. They are commonly used in cashback
               programs, loyalty redemptions, peer-to-peer gifting, and promotional campaigns. This segment benefits from
               strong data integration, personalization, and real-time delivery, making it one of the fastest-growing areas in the
               digital gifting space.

               Each gift card segment serves a different role within the Indian digital gift card ecosystem, from brand-led
               retention tools to marketplace-driven flexibility, bank-backed security, and platform-enabled convenience.
               Collectively, these segments address diverse consumer and enterprise use cases, reinforcing gift cards as a
               preferred digital alternative to cash, discounts, and physical gifts in India.

5.3   Use cases

      The Indian digital gift card ecosystem thrives on use cases like corporate rewards, festival gifting, and personalized
      rewards, using workflows involving e-commerce platforms, APIs, AI recommendations, and integrated payments for
      seamless delivery, from virtual cards to physical products, driven by personalization, data analytics, and instant
      gratification in hybrid work settings. Key workflows include corporate procurement via ERP integration, consumer
      purchase with personalized notes/video, and influencer monetization via virtual gifts, all leveraging digital payments like
      UPI for efficiency.

      Use Cases in the Indian Digital Gift Card Market

      1.       Festival and Occasion-Based Gifting: Digital gifting is widely used for personal and semi-formal occasions
               such as birthdays, anniversaries, weddings, and festivals including Diwali, Raksha Bandhan, and New Year.
               Consumers and brands prefer e-gift cards, digital vouchers, and personalized digital or hybrid gifts due to last-
               minute purchase convenience, instant delivery via WhatsApp or email, and the ability to personalize messages or
               designs. This use case benefits from high seasonal spikes and impulse-led purchases.

      2.       Customer Acquisition, Loyalty, and Promotions: Brands deploy digital gift cards and vouchers as incentives
               for customer acquisition, referrals, first transactions, repeat purchases, and win-back campaigns. Custom-branded
               gift cards issued by platforms such as Amazon or Flipkart are commonly embedded into loyalty programs and
               promotional campaigns. The flexibility and perceived value of digital gifts make them more effective than
               traditional discounts, while also enabling better tracking of campaign ROI.

      3.       Corporate Gifting and Incentives: Corporate gifting is the largest and most mature use case for digital gifting
               in India. Enterprises use digital gift cards, vouchers, prepaid cards, and curated experiences for employee rewards,
               sales incentives, channel partner recognition, and promotional giveaways. These solutions are especially popular
               during festivals like Diwali, annual performance cycles, onboarding milestones, and large-scale events, as they
               offer instant delivery, compliance-friendly formats, and easy scalability across distributed workforces and partner
               networks.

      4.       Instant Refunds, Store Credits, and Compensation: E-commerce, retail, and fintech players increasingly use
               digital gift cards and store credits to process refunds, cancellations, or goodwill compensations instantly. Instead
               of waiting for bank reversals, customers receive immediate digital credits that can be reused within the same
               ecosystem. This improves customer satisfaction, reduces operational costs, and encourages faster repeat
               purchases.

      5.       Luxury and Premium Gifting: Digital gifting has expanded access to premium and luxury products beyond
               metro cities by enabling online discovery, rich visual merchandising, and virtual consultations. High-value gift
               cards, premium brand vouchers, and experiential gifts such as travel or fine dining are increasingly used for
               aspirational gifting, especially among affluent and corporate buyers.

      6.       Influencer, Creator, and Virtual Gifting: On live-streaming and social platforms, virtual gifting enables fans
               to purchase digital tokens, coins, or gifts for creators during live sessions. These gifts translate into instant
               recognition, shoutouts, or visibility, creating real-time engagement and monetization opportunities. This use case
               thrives on micro-transactions, impulse behaviour, and social validation.

5.4   Type of Gift cards

      The Indian digital gift card ecosystem spans four primary gift card types, each catering to distinct use cases. Retail /
      Consumer e-Gift Cards are widely used by individual consumers for gifting across retail stores, restaurants, and
      marketplaces. Corporate / B2B gifting cards are designed for business use, supporting client engagement, partner rewards,
                                                             186
      promotional campaigns, and festive corporate spending through compliant digital platforms. Employee rewards &
      incentives focus on digitally delivered vouchers and reward credits used for recognition, performance incentives, and sales
      motivation. Experiential & services gifting centres on experience-based offerings such as travel vouchers, event tickets,
      and curated activities. Collectively, these formats address consumer, corporate, and employee gifting needs while
      balancing issuer control with recipient choice.

      1.       Retail / Consumer e-Gift Cards: These include retail gift cards sold directly to consumers for use at retail
               merchants, restaurants, and online marketplaces. They are commonly purchased at retail checkouts or gifted at
               the point of sale, making them popular for personal gifting.

      2.       Corporate / B2B Gifting: Gift cards purchased by businesses for clients, channel partners, promotional
               giveaways, and festive or bulk corporate spending. These are often issued through specialized digital gifting
               platforms that support compliance, customization, and large-scale fulfilment.

      3.       Employee Rewards & Incentives: Digital vouchers and reward credits used by organizations for employee
               recognition, sales incentives, performance rewards, and service or milestone awards. These are typically delivered
               digitally for ease of distribution and tracking.

      4.       Experiential & Services Gifting: Digital gift cards focused on experiences and services rather than physical
               products, including event tickets, curated experiences, travel vouchers, and entertainment or wellness passes sold
               as digital gifts.

      Together, these gift card types address a wide spectrum of gifting objectives—from brand-driven retention and customer
      engagement to flexible, choice-led corporate incentives and experiential rewards—cementing gift cards as a core pillar of
      India’s digital gifting and loyalty ecosystem.

5.5   Macro & Demand Drivers

      India’s digital gift card market is booming, driven by widespread smartphone and internet penetration, massive e-
      commerce growth (Amazon, Paytm), rising disposable incomes, and a cultural shift toward convenient, cashless, and
      personalized gifting. Festive occasions like Diwali, Rakhi, and Christmas, along with corporate needs for employee
      rewards and client engagement, further fuel demand. Government-backed digital initiatives, including UPI and GST, have
      created a conducive environment, opening significant B2C opportunities in gaming and OTT, as well as B2B potential in
      employee incentives, with a growing preference for flexible and sustainable gifting solutions.

      Macro Drivers (Economic & Societal)

      1.       Digital Penetration: Rapid expansion of smartphones, internet access, and digital payment platforms (UPI,
               PhonePe, Paytm) makes digital gifts widely accessible.

      2.       E-commerce Growth: Integration of gift cards by major online retailers broadens reach and convenience.

      3.       Rising Disposable Income: Higher spending power drives demand for premium and personalized gifting.

      4.       Urbanization & Tech-Savvy Consumers: Younger urban demographics prefer digital, convenient, and varied
               gifting options.

      5.       Government Initiatives: Digitization efforts and MSME support foster a favourable digital economy.

      6.       Sustainability Trends: Growing preference for eco-friendly and customizable options shapes product
               development.

      Demand Drivers (Consumer & Corporate Behaviour):

      1.       Discounts, Cashback & Value Savings: Attractive discounts, cashback offers, user rewards, and bonus value
               on digital gift cards act as a strong demand driver among both consumers & corporates. Price-sensitive buyers
               are increasingly motivated to purchase gift cards when they offer immediate savings or higher perceived value.
               For corporates, discounted bulk purchases make digital gifting a cost-efficient rewards and incentives tool, while
               for consumers, such offers encourage self-gifting, impulse buying, and repeat usage—significantly boosting
               overall demand.

      2.       Festive Occasions: Major festivals drive spikes in gifting demand, efficiently met through digital solutions.

                                                             187
      3.         Convenience & Accessibility: Digital cards are easy to purchase, store on mobile devices, and redeem instantly.

      4.         Personalization: High demand for customized gifts reflecting individual preferences.

      5.         Self-Gifting & Utility: Consumers purchase gift cards for personal use, including gaming, OTT subscriptions,
                 and digital services.

      6.         Corporate Gifting: Companies use digital rewards to retain employees (notably in IT/BPO sectors) and
                 strengthen client relationships.

      7.         Variety & Choice: Platforms like Amazon offer access to multiple brands and categories (food, fashion, digital
                 services).

      8.         Innovation: AI-driven designs, customizable solutions (like Pine Labs Ltd.), and new formats such as reusable
                 boxes enhance appeal.
