OUR STRATEGIES

Below are our strategies, which have been approved by way of a resolution passed by the Board of Directors in their meeting
held on October 6, 2026.

    1. Continue to expand our user base across all of our offerings

As digital financial inclusion deepens and consumers look for smarter, controlled ways to transact, the prepaid and Direct to
Consumer spend management ecosystem is becoming a key pillar in India’s everyday retail economy combining convenience
with financial discipline (source: F&S Report, page 45).

The Indian digital gift card market has grown rapidly over the early 2020s, driven by increasing digital adoption, e-commerce
expansion, and rising use in both personal and corporate gifting (source: F&S Report, page 43). In terms of GTV, the market,
                                                               222
valued at USD 6.75 billion in the early 2020s, expanded to USD 10.67 billion by 2023, reflecting broadening consumer and
corporate adoption (source: F&S Report, page 43). By Calendar Year 2025, it was estimated to reach USD 15.10 billion,
establishing a strong base for continued growth (source: F&S Report, page 43). From Calendar Year 2025 to Calendar Year
2030, the market is projected to grow at a robust CAGR of 17.4%, reaching approximately USD 33.65 billion by Calendar Year
2030 (source: F&S Report, page 43). This rapid expansion is supported by the convenience and flexibility of digital gift cards,
wider corporate adoption for employee rewards and client engagement, increasing personalization, e-commerce penetration,
and sustained festive demand (source: F&S Report, page 43).

India’s digital gift card market is surging, propelled by e-gift cards’ instant delivery and flexibility, replacing physical gifts for
consumers and corporates alike (source: F&S Report, page 40). India’s rewards and loyalty ecosystem is witnessing rapid
growth, with the market estimated to reach USD 5.09 billion by Calendar Year 2025 and expected to expand significantly
through the latter half of the decade to reach USD 10.57 billion at a CAGR of 15.8% from Calendar Year 2025-2030, in terms
of revenue (source: F&S Report, page 40). The market is evolving into a highly digital, mobile-first, and data-driven
ecosystem, with a strong focus on personalization, real-time engagement, and cross-industry partnerships (source: F&S Report,
page 29). Brands are increasingly leveraging loyalty platforms and marketplaces to deliver meaningful value and differentiated
customer experiences (source: F&S Report, page 29).

To take advantage of these significant growth opportunities we plan to grow our business through the following initiatives:

a) Continue to spend on customer acquisition and retention incentives – We plan to increase the amount we spend on (a)
customer acquisition and retention incentives paid to Ecosystem Partners for referring users and corporate customers to our
offerings (b) incentives offered to users to promote usage of the Prepaid Cards and Gift Cards we distribute, drive issuance and
spending volumes, and increase overall monetisation per user. Additionally, we plan to introduce loyalty, rewards, and
incentive-based programs to enhance user engagement and repeat usage. Cashbacks, instant incentives and funded promotional
rewards act as a major demand and revenue driver in India’s digital gift card ecosystem (source: F&S Report, page 45).
Attractive discounts, cashback offers, user rewards, and bonus value on digital gift cards act as a strong demand driver among
both consumers & corporates (source: F&S Report, page 43). Further, we will incentivise Ecosystem Partners to refer clients
for our DevStack and Rewards and Loyalty business by offering them customer acquisition incentives. For more details in
relation to incentives for Ecosystem Partners, see paragraph (d) of this strategy titled “Increase in tie-ups with additional
Ecosystem Partners” and “Objects of the Offer” on pages 223 and 95 respectively. The table below sets forth our user acquisition
and retention expenses and such expenses as a percentage of our revenue from operations for the periods and Fiscal Years

     2. Enhance our technology and infrastructure

We plan to continue to invest in artificial intelligence (“AI”) / machine learning (“ML”) based capabilities by investing in (i)
scalable cloud and compute infrastructure to enable faster deployment and scaling of agentic tools, (ii) strengthening model
research and ML Operations frameworks to enhance the reliability, security and governance of automated systems, and (iii)
undertaking focused investments in talent acquisition and upskilling to improve productivity and operating leverage. In parallel,
we intend to deepen the use of AI-driven fraud detection and compliance solutions, strengthen risk controls and ensure the
responsible and safe deployment of AI across our digital gifting ecosystem. For more details in relation to (i) and (iii), see
“Objects of the Offer” on page 95.

We will continue to leverage our proprietary platforms and technology reusability and scalability through a multi-tenant, white-
labelled system under DevStack for corporate rewards and loyalty management.

     3. Enhance our existing products and develop new products and services to address a broader set of use cases

Our services operate on a technology platform that has been conceptualised, designed and developed in-house by us. We have
developed our core offerings: (1) SpendPro; (2) RewardOn; (3) yayyy.shop; and (4) DevStack. We plan to create a dedicated
team to enhance our existing products and services and to develop new solutions addressing a broader range of use cases. For
further details, see “Objects of the Offer” on page 95.

In order to enable us to expand our relationships with Ecosystem Partners, we plan to enhance and upgrade our platforms to
enable us to integrate our offerings with their platforms. We aim to strengthen our competitive position and serve a wider
market by collaborating with Ecosystem Partners that have established user bases. We seek to leverage the reach and
distribution capabilities of such partners by offering technology solutions, including the conceptualisation, development and
implementation of platforms aligned with partner-specific requirements. We plan to identify and target Ecosystem Partners in
new segments whose offerings can be enabled and offered on our Gift Card and Prepaid Card rails, allowing us to leverage
such partners’ existing capabilities, distribution strengths and established user bases.

                                                                            224
Additionally, we plan to invest in the development of agentic and AI-native solutions and pursue new use cases, and prepaid
foreign exchange instruments, as well as enterprise-oriented support tools. For further information on our strategy on agentic
and AI-native solutions, see “– Our Strategies – Enhance our technology and infrastructure” on page 224.

Other use cases include incentives and promotions, meal/expense cards, digital wallets, travel/forex cards, mobile wallets with
stored value, cross-border remittance cards, prepaid instruments linked to the Automated Permanent Academic Account
Registry (“APAAR”) which is “One Nation, One Student ID”, a unique 12-digit digital identifier for students in India and the
National Common Mobility Card (“NCMC”), which enables seamless contactless payments across metro systems, buses, tolls,
and retail merchants, integrating transport and retail payments on a single platform (source: F&S Report, page 21). Giftcards
(gift/fuel/retail/multi-brand prepaid) cards account for a significant share of issuance, while Prepaid cards (bank-issued Visa,
Mastercard, RuPay) dominate high-value spends (source: F&S Report, page 21). Each use case reflects innovative ways to
engage customers and control spend: gift cards acquire new shoppers and capture loyalty data, corporate cards streamline
employee spending, digital wallets embed payments into super apps, APAAR cards facilitate payroll and subsidy
disbursements, and NCMC simplifies daily commuting while promoting cashless transactions (source: F&S Report, page 21).
RBI-driven expansion of acceptance, including UPI integration and IoT payments, has further broadened the total digital
payment volume opportunity (source: F&S Report, page 21). Recent changes under India’s income tax rules (2026) have
increased the tax-exempt limit on meal cards and prepaid instruments, enhancing their attractiveness for salaried consumers
and expanding their usage in everyday spend categories (source: F&S Report, page 21). This structurally strengthens the
prepaid ecosystem by driving higher adoption, transaction volumes, and consumer familiarity with stored-value instruments
(source: F&S Report, page 21). For platforms operating in prepaid cards, spend management, and digital engagement, this
creates a larger addressable base and accelerates mainstream adoption of prepaid-led use cases across retail consumption
(source: F&S Report, page 21).

Additionally, the formalization of gift PPIs and the introduction of co-branding arrangements enable scalable distribution and
expansion of digital gifting solutions. Overall, these regulatory changes are anticipated to accelerate adoption of prepaid
instruments, enhance trust in digital payment platforms, and support the development of integrated, scalable fintech ecosystems
(source: F&S Report, page 21).

Furthermore, Securities and Exchange Board of India consultation paper dated 24th March 2026, proposes to enable mutual
fund gifting through prepaid payment instruments (PPIs), marking a significant expansion of digital gifting use cases into
financial products (source: F&S Report, page 21). By allowing PPIs to be used for investment gifting, the regulation broadens
the utility of prepaid instruments beyond consumption into wealth creation (source: F&S Report, page 21). This is expected to
deepen consumer engagement with digital gifting platforms and reinforce prepaid infrastructure as a scalable distribution layer,
benefiting companies operating in rewards, gifting, and prepaid ecosystems (source: F&S Report, page 21).

We offer bill payments through Bharat Connect. Bharat Bill Payment System, now branded Bharat Connect acts as the
interoperable national backbone for recurring bill payments across categories such as electricity, gas, water, telecom, DTH,
FASTag, loan repayment, insurance, municipal taxes, and more recently credit card bills (source: F&S Report, page 51). Bill
payments are no longer confined to direct bank channels or standalone utility apps (source: F&S Report, page 51). They are
increasingly being facilitated through consumer payment apps, merchant ecosystems, assisted commerce networks, API
platforms, and embedded fintech journeys (source: F&S Report, page 51). According to Bharat Connect platform data, bill
payment volumes increased sharply from around 1.1 billion transactions in Financial Year 2023 to 3.1 billion transactions in
Financial Year 2026 (source: F&S Report, page 51). Over the same period, transaction value expanded from ₹1.9 trillion in
Financial Year 2023 to ₹15.5 trillion in Financial Year 2026, reflecting continued acceleration in recurring bill categories,
credit card bill payments, utilities, and other digitally enabled payment flows (source: F&S Report, page 51).

We also plan to enable new fintech build use-cases through our technology stack through focused research and development
initiatives.

    5. Enhance the visibility of the “Paramotor” brand

To differentiate ourselves from our competitors and capture the interest of potential new users, we plan to implement a
multifaceted marketing strategy. As our platforms are primarily direct-to-consumer platforms, it is particularly important that
we establish strong brand presence and engagement across digital channels. This involves reaching out to large and targeted
user segments through localised brand-building initiatives executed in collaboration with referral partners and Ecosystem
Partners. In addition, we plan to undertake organic digital outreach through social media channels, supported by targeted public
relations initiatives to enhance brand visibility and recall.

Our proposed marketing initiatives may include creation of marketing assets and digital content designed to communicate the
functionality and benefits of our platforms, which may include platform/product explainer videos, customer testimonials and
other marketing creatives that support our brand communication and enterprise outreach initiatives. For instance, this may
entail advertisements on television and over-the-top channels. We also intend to deploy performance media (advertising)
strategies focused on measurable customer acquisition, lead generation and conversion optimisation across digital channels.
Customer engagement and awareness are further proposed to be strengthened through brand promotion campaigns, media
outreach activities and corporate communication programs designed to increase brand recognition and improve market
visibility. For example, this may entail advertisements on newspapers and print media, airport digital screens, or key locations
such as metro stations. Further, we plan to participate in curated industry events and undertake sponsorships to strengthen our
positioning within the fintech, corporate rewards and prepaid ecosystem segments.

We intend to focus our marketing strategies towards participation in industry events, conferences, and sponsorship initiatives
that allow us to interact with corporate clients, Ecosystem Partners and other participants in the fintech and digital rewards and
gifting ecosystem. Through these forums, we intend to target differentiated marketing initiatives aligned to distinct use cases
across multiple industries and ecosystems, enabling adoption and implementation by enterprises and Ecosystem Partners, and
translating such engagement into revenue-generating opportunities for the Company.

MARKET OPPORTUNITIES

PPI Program Management and Distribution business

India’s Prepaid Cards market has been experiencing accelerated growth, primarily driven by the cards’ multifaceted utility of
both reloadable and non-reloadable prepaid instruments that seamlessly fits into diverse aspects of daily financial life and
business operations (source: F&S Report, page 16). These cards offer secure, convenient, and pre-funded solutions, appealing
to both urban consumers and digitally transitioning users (source: F&S Report, page 16).

Prepaid cards are increasingly used as specialized financial tools for managing spending (source: F&S Report, page 22). They
appeal particularly to consumer segments seeking controlled financial behavior such as students, gig economy workers,
households managing budgets, deal-seekers using event-based purchase cards (source: F&S Report, page 22).
                                                                 226
The Indian digital gift card market has grown rapidly over the early 2020s, driven by increasing digital adoption, e-
commerce expansion, and rising use in both personal and corporate gifting (source: F&S Report, page 43). In terms of GTV, the
market, valued at USD 6.75 billion in the early 2020s, expanded to USD 10.67 billion by 2023, reflecting broadening consumer
and corporate adoption (source: F&S Report, page 43). By Calendar Year 2025, it was estimated to reach USD 15.10 billion,
establishing a strong base for continued growth. From Calendar Year 2025 to Calendar Year 2030, the market is projected to
grow at a robust CAGR of 17.4%, reaching approximately USD 33.65 billion by Calendar Year 2030 (source: F&S Report,
page 43). This rapid expansion is supported by the convenience and flexibility of digital gift cards, wider corporate adoption
for employee rewards and client engagement, increasing personalization, e-commerce penetration, and sustained festive
demand (source: F&S Report, page 43).

Rewards and Loyalty business

India’s Rewards and Loyalty ecosystem is witnessing rapid growth, with the market estimated to reach USD 5.09 billion by
Calendar Year 2025 and expected to expand significantly through the latter half of the decade to reach USD 10.57 billion at a
CAGR of 15.8% from Calendar Year 2025-2030, in terms of revenue (source: F&S Report, page 29). The growth of the Indian
rewards and loyalty ecosystem is fuelled by digital transformation, increasing smartphone and internet penetration, changing
consumer preferences, and the widespread integration of rewards into everyday spending categories such as retail, banking,
travel, food delivery, and e-commerce (source: F&S Report, page 29). The acceleration of digital transformation across online
shopping and payment ecosystems—driven by UPI, digital wallets, in-app commerce, and seamless checkout experiences—has
further embedded rewards and loyalty programs into routine consumer transactions (source: F&S Report, page 29).

The market is evolving into a highly digital, mobile-first, and data-driven ecosystem, with a strong focus on personalization,
real-time engagement, and cross-industry partnerships (source: F&S Report, page 29). Brands are increasingly leveraging
loyalty platforms and marketplaces to deliver meaningful value and differentiated customer experiences (source: F&S Report,
page 29), which we are well positioned to capitalise.

DevStack

The Fintech Software Development Market in India was valued at approximately USD 0.14 billion in 2020 and has grown
steadily to reach an estimated USD 0.53 billion in 2025, nearly a fourfold increase in five years (source: F&S Report, page
47). This expansion is driven by rising demand for custom fintech platforms across payments, lending, card management,
loyalty systems, analytics dashboards, and embedded finance infrastructure (source: F&S Report, page 47). Between 2025 and
2030, the market is expected to grow at a robust CAGR of approximately 32.3%, underscoring increasing investments in API-
first architectures, cloud-native financial systems, compliance-driven technology upgrades, and enterprise digitization (source:
F&S Report, page 47), which we are well positioned to capitalise.

OUR PRODUCTS AND SERVICES

PPI Program Management and Distribution business

Prepaid Cards

We act as a program manager, business correspondent and distribution agent for Prepaid Cards, which are non-reloadable PPIs
with a maximum value of ₹10,000. Direct-to-consumer prepaid platforms are designed to address the gap in retail-focused
spend management solutions by combining instant card issuance, budgeting tools, transaction analytics, and spending controls,
offering retail users functionality that mirrors corporate expense management capabilities (source: F&S Report, page 22).

As at June 30, 2026, we acted as a (i) program manager for six PPI Issuers, and (ii) the distribution agent for two program
managers of Prepaid Cards. We refer to the PPI Issuers for whom we act as a program manager and the program managers for
whom we act as a distribution agent as our PPI Partners. These partnerships enable us to distribute Prepaid Cards issued across
three prominent payment networks, including Visa, RuPay and Mastercard, ensuring broad merchant acceptance and access to
network-specific offers (source: F&S Report, page 54).

We earn revenue from acting as a program manager, business correspondent and distribution agent for Prepaid Cards from our
share of interchange fees generated on spends on Prepaid Cards at merchant outlets (at physical stores and online), comprising
(i) our agreed share of the interchange fees with the PPI Partners, including NSDL Payments Bank Limited, and (ii) income
from a third-party service providers including Monepeak Fintech Private Limited that provide transaction switching services
to banks in the form of incentives to promote issuer specific programs. We entered into a co-brand agreement with Mastercard
Asia Pacific Pte. Ltd. in March 2026 for Prepaid Cards co-branded with us. These Prepaid Cards will be issued by one or more
of our PPI Partners. We are entitled to receive incentive based income in consideration for the promotion of network-specific
                                                                227
programmes for Prepaid Cards from a network provider.

Interchange fees earned are usually charged as a percentage of the transaction amount and can be as high as 2.2% of the value
of spend incurred by users on Prepaid Cards at offline and/or online merchant outlets (source: F&S Report, page 23).
Interchange fees are decided by the payment networks of Rupay, Mastercard, and Visa in accordance with contractual
arrangements between the Payment Networks and the PPI Issuers, and is broadly influenced by the industry of the merchant
where the card is used, the merchant category and transaction value (source: F&S Report, page 23). A program manager
negotiates a share of the interchange fees with the issuer of the Prepaid Cards. There are also arrangements where there is an
incentive (share of interchange) paid to the Program manager by the Card network and the Switch service provider (source:
F&S Report, page 26). Interchange fees vary across types of merchants, the percentages of which are set by the third-party
payment networks (the “Payment Networks”), such as Mastercard, Visa, and Rupay and are generally driven by: (i) the
merchant’s business segment; (ii) applicable merchant category codes; (iii) transaction size (source: F&S Report, page 26).
Interchange fees are not levied directly on the consumer but are paid by the merchant’s bank (acquiring bank) to the card-issuing
bank to process transactions every time any customer uses a card to make purchases from a merchant’s store (source: F&S
Report, page 23).

We choose to promote the Prepaid Cards based on our commercial arrangements with PPI Partners, including the interchange
fee sharing structures agreed with them.

Users of the Prepaid Cards issued by our PPI Partners can use our SpendPro platform, which serves as the spend management
platform, enabling users to access virtual cards, track real-time transaction feeds, receive real-time alerts, manage stored-value
limits, allowing users to monitor spends and check applicable spending limits, and instant card controls, such as, instant freeze
of the card. We currently do not charge fees for using SpendPro.

SpendPro case study

In Fiscal 2026, a user purchased and activated a virtual Prepaid Card with a load value of ₹10,000. The Prepaid Card functions
as a self-contained spending instrument with a preloaded amount enabling controlled spending, unlike payment methods such
as UPI, where transactions may be debited directly from the user's bank account. Confining expenditures to the amount loaded
on the Prepaid Card enabled the user to control his spending and manage his budget more effectively.

Gift Cards

We distribute Gift Cards which are non-reloadable brand gift cards issued by merchants, to users through our yayyy.shop
website and mobile application available on a well-known application marketplace, which were launched in second and fourth
quarters of Fiscal 2026, respectively. Our yayyy.shop website and our mobile application support the prompt digital delivery
of Gift Cards through instant messaging and email, providing a streamlined gifting experience. These Gift Cards can be spent
offline at the respective brand’s physical stores or online through the brand’s website or mobile application (if applicable). We
earn commission income from Gift Card Aggregators for facilitating the distribution of Gift Cards to users.

As at June 30, 2026, we act as a distribution agent for Gift Cards for three Gift Card Aggregators. As at June 30, 2026, we
offered a catalogue of 234 Gift Cards covering national and international brands across fashion, electronics, dining, travel, and
e-commerce platforms.

yayyy.shop case study

In January 2026, a user purchased a Gift Card valued at ₹7,500 from a grocery / daily essential brand listed on yayyy.shop
website. The Gift Card selected offered 3% wallet points upon completion of the purchase.

Upon completion of the Gift Card purchase, the user earned 225 reward points (3% of ₹7,500), which were credited to his
reward points wallet.

The user could then redeem the Gift Card with the relevant brand in accordance with the applicable Gift Card brand specific
terms and conditions. In addition, the 225 reward points could be applied towards future Gift Card purchases on yayyy.shop.
For instance, if the user were to return to the platform and purchase another Gift Card worth ₹7,500, he could apply those
reward points to reduce the payable amount to ₹7,275, while also earning fresh reward points on that subsequent eligible
purchase.

This case demonstrates yayyy.shop as a digital marketplace where users can purchase Gift Cards for various needs, earn reward
points on eligible purchases and utilise such points towards future purchases, thereby creating a recurring value proposition
                                                                 228
and encouraging repeat purchases on yayyy.shop.

Rewards and Loyalty Business

Our rewards and loyalty business comprises: (i) reward points and our own reward points card, the “yayyy Reward Points
Card”, which can be purchased directly through our digital marketplace on the yayyy.shop website and mobile application and
used to redeem Gift Cards and Prepaid Cards available on our marketplace; and (ii) our RewardOn platform, a comprehensive,
end-to-end digital rewards and incentives platform that enables corporate customers to design, manage, and distribute reward
points to end-user beneficiaries, which can be redeemed digitally through a configurable rules engine integrated with a
customised catalogue of Gift Cards, Prepaid Cards and the yayyy Reward Points Card.

Users can purchase reward points or our own reward points card, the “yayyy Reward Points Card”, directly through our digital
marketplace on the yayyy.shop website and mobile application (available on a well-known application marketplace). The
reward points can be used to redeem Gift Cards and Prepaid Cards available on our marketplace. Our yayyy Reward Points Card
is particularly suitable for those who wish to give a gift but leave the choice of which Gift Card(s) to give to the recipient. The
yayyy Reward Points Card is non-reloadable. Our yayyy.shop website and mobile application support the prompt digital
delivery of Gift Cards and Prepaid Cards through instant messaging and email, providing a streamlined gifting experience for
the recipient. As at June 30, 2026, we offered a catalogue of Prepaid Cards and 234 Gift Cards on yayyy.shop covering national
and international brands across fashion, electronics, dining, travel, and e-commerce platforms, thereby providing recipients
with a wide range of redemption choices.

Our RewardOn platform, which was launched on August 1, 2025, is a comprehensive, end-to-end digital rewards and incentives
platform that enables corporate customers to design, administer, and deliver structured reward, recognition, and engagement
programs for employees, channel partners, distributors or other beneficiaries. RewardOn provides corporate customers with the
flexibility to tailor reward programs to their specific objectives. We had six and five corporate customers for our RewardOn
platform during the three months ended June 30, 2026 and Fiscal 2026, respectively. Through the RewardOn platform, reward
points are purchased by the corporate customers and are allocated to users (beneficiaries), who redeem reward points for Gift
Cards across categories, such as fashion, electronics, dining, travel, and e-commerce platforms through a catalogue available
and Prepaid Cards (if applicable) for each rewards and loyalty program. Corporate customers can curate and select specific
Gift Cards they want to make available for redemption from the entire catalogue of Gift Cards available, which also includes
yayyy Reward Points Card, which can be redeemed only on our yayyy.shop website. As at June 30, 2026, we offered Prepaid
Cards and a catalogue of 234 Gift Cards covering national and international brands across fashion, electronics, dining, travel,
and e-commerce platforms on the RewardOn platform.

Our RewardOn platform operates through web-based dashboards for the corporate customers and the users and digital reward
point wallets or redemption interfaces for the users.

We are responsible for end-to-end program management including configuration and administration, the provisioning of Gift
Cards and Prepaid Cards, maintenance of technology infrastructure, creating management reports, user support and grievance
redressal.

Revenue from reward points is recognised upon redemption of reward points for Gift Cards/Prepaid Cards by users rather than
at the time of sale of the reward points, and is recorded on a gross basis. Margins are derived through discounts negotiated with
Gift Card Aggregators and Gift Card Dealers, with key margin drivers, the redemption mix across categories and brands, and,
where contractually permitted and subject to applicable laws, revenue attributable to reward points that are not exercised within
the validity or redemption period.

We also offer our RewardOn platform as a white-label solution for companies to run their own rewards and loyalty programs,
which is offered under our DevStack business.

RewardOn Case study

In Fiscal 2026, a corporate customer (“Client N”) engaged our Company to run a rewards and loyalty program for its customers
under its incentive or engagement programs. Our Company deployed our white-labelled rewards and loyalty platform,
RewardOn, customised to Client N’s requirements, including a curated catalogue of Gift Cards.

Client N purchased reward points and allocated them to its customers. Customers receiving reward points could redeem them
against Gift Cards available on the RewardOn platform.

DevStack

Through our DevStack business, which we launched in the first quarter of Fiscal 2026, we offer technical and platform
development services designed for the creation of customised enterprise software applications. Built on the technology
infrastructure that powers our other platforms, RewardOn, and yayyy.shop, DevStack enables clients to leverage market-tested,
production-ready components, reducing the time and effort of undertaking ground up development and lowering
implementation risk. As at June 30, 2026, we had five corporate customers for DevStack.

The DevStack platform provides a comprehensive Application Programming Interface (“API”) and Software Development
Kit (“SDK”) layer that enables integration of core functionalities, including KYC onboarding, card management system and
wallets as per different use cases. It additionally offers configurable workflows and customisable user interface components
that integrate directly with users’ existing mobile and web experiences, reducing development complexity and implementation
delays attributed to undertaking ground up development.

The underlying architecture supports multiple tenants through a central “tenant-as-a-service” framework, enabling distinct
brands and partners to operate on shared infrastructure, while maintaining independent configurations, branding, and user
management (source: F&S Report, page 54). This technology led approach supports efficient scaling of transaction volumes
while maintaining reliability, security, and compliance (source: F&S Report, page 54).

Beyond its core technical offerings, DevStack supports platform, development and technical build services, including tailored
ready-to-deploy solutions built on our architecture that can be adapted and white-labelled to meet the specific requirements of
customers.

We generate revenue from DevStack through Platform Fee/Service Fee for our technical development services offered through
DevStack.

DevStack Case Study

In Fiscal 2026, we entered into a platform enhancement and modernisation engagement for an Indian company providing
expense management segment (the “Client”). The engagement involved upgrading the Client’s business-critical corporate
expense management platform while maintaining continuity of live operations. The scope included technology architecture
modernisation, automation enablement using AI-based components, and enhancement of compliance, analytics and security
features. The project was delivered through an agile execution framework with phased deployment and post-implementation
support, resulting in an upgraded platform with improved scalability, automation and user experience, aligned with the Client’s
operating requirements.

DATA PROTECTION AND PRIVACY

Our platforms are built on the foundation of privacy and security. We ensure that users are informed of our data practices and
about how their data is utilized. Our privacy policy is designed to safeguard the personal and financial information of our users,
ensuring that we collect, use, disclose, transfer, store, retain, and process information in compliance with applicable laws and
regulations to reinforce confidence in our data protection practices, we hold third-party security certifications which include:

    •    ISO certification 27001 – for information security management systems; and
    •    ISO certification 9001 – for quality management systems.

Our data protection and privacy policies are focused on ensuring that: (i) our collection of personal data is conducted in
accordance with applicable laws and regulations; (ii) personal data we collect are reasonable for the purposes for which they are
collected; and (iii) our users are informed of the purposes for which their personal data are collected and used and their rights
with respect to such data. In addition, to minimize the risk of data loss or leakage for yayyy.shop and RewardOn, we conduct
internal periodic vulnerability assessments and penetration testing. We are subject to various laws and regulations, including
the Information Technology Act, 2000 and Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. For further information, see “Key
Regulations and Policies in India” on page 238.

TECHNOLOGY, RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT

Our products and services function on a technology that has been conceptualised, designed and developed in-house by us. Our
R&D team, which is a combination of internal and external resources, has developed SpendPro, (our D2C spend management
platform), yayyy.shop (our D2C digital marketplace), and RewardOn (our B2B2C rewards and loyalty platform). These
platforms are designed to function independently or in combination, forming a vertically integrated ecosystem that supports
spend management, rewards and loyalty programs, and digital gifting.

Our platforms are built as secure, multi-tenant, API-driven infrastructure, designed for reliability at scale. We operate an
ecosystem-driven model built on integrations with external stakeholders which enable incorporation of third-party offerings into
our platforms. Our three core platforms, SpendPro, yayyy.shop and RewardOn, are integrated with relevant third-party systems
for issuance, redemption, and settlement, enabling real-time synchronization and automation across the value chain. Our
DevStack business uses this architecture to empower enterprises to launch customized platforms and software applications with
minimal development effort and faster go-to-market timelines.

Our platforms rely on the following core pillars:

Microservices-based Platforms

We have built and operate in-house, microservices-based technology platforms, including SpendPro, yayyy.shop and
RewardOn. The technology framework is structured around reusable service blocks and integrations, enabling core
functionalities, such as KYC onboarding, card management systems and wallets, to operate independently and be integrated
as per different use cases. By leveraging reusable service blocks and integrations, our technology framework enables
configurability, interoperability and rapid deployment across use cases, while supporting integration with enterprise customers
and Ecosystem Partners. This enables us to manage increases in activity across our platforms, while maintaining operational
resilience and providing a streamlined experience for users.
                                                                 232
Scalable Cloud-Native Architecture Supporting User and Transaction Growth

Our cloud-native architecture enables us to handle growth in users and transaction volumes, while maintaining operational
reliability and performance, and supports quick configuration and integration with third-party systems and customers. The
scalability of our technology platforms is evidenced by their ability to support a large and growing transacting user base. During
the three months period ended June 30, 2026, our platforms supported 634,316 transacting users, compared to 107,403
transacting users during the corresponding previous period.

Multi-Tenant Architecture for Enterprise-Facing Solutions

RewardOn, our rewards and loyalty platform, operates through web-based dashboards for corporate customers and users, and
digital reward point wallets or redemption interfaces for users. We undertake end-to-end programme management on
RewardOn, including configuration and administration, provisioning of Gift Cards and Prepaid Cards, maintenance of
technology infrastructure, preparation of management reports, user support and grievance redressal.

RewardOn is built on architecture that supports multiple tenants through a central “tenant-as-a-service” framework, enabling
distinct brands and partners to operate on shared infrastructure, while maintaining independent configurations, branding and
user management. This architecture enables management of various programmes, workflows and user experiences, including
reward issuance, allocation to user wallets and redemptions, across different customers and use cases on a common technology
infrastructure, while supporting efficient scaling of transaction volumes while maintaining reliability, security, and compliance.

API and SDK-Based Integration Frameworks

Our yayyy.shop, RewardOn, and SpendPro platforms are integrated with relevant third-party systems for issuance, redemption
and settlement, enabling synchronisation and automation across the value chain.

Through our DevStack vertical, we provide an API and SDK layer that enables enterprise customers to integrate core
functionalities and components into their existing platforms. It also offers configurable workflows and customisable user
interface components that integrate directly with users’ existing mobile and web experiences, reducing development
complexity and implementation delays associated with ground-up development.

INSURANCE

We have obtained a burglary insurance policy in respect of computer and computer equipment and office equipment at each of
our offices, and a Bharat Sookshma Udyam Suraksha insurance policy in respect of computer and computer equipment,
furniture, fixtures and fittings, and office equipment at each of our offices. The Bharat Sookshma Udyam Suraksha insurance
excludes losses caused by labour unrest, deprivation of use or value of property due to actions by any government authority,
and damages caused by chemical or biological contaminants. The burglary insurance policy provides for exclusions, such as
larceny and terrorism. For details on our offices, see “– Properties” on page 235.

We have obtained a Directors and Officers Liability Insurance policy, which covers claims made against our Company’s
directors and officers for alleged wrongful acts in their managerial capacity. This policy includes coverage for legal
representation.

We have obtained a cyber and data protection insurance policy which covers third-party liability including privacy and data
breaches, network security claims, media liability claims, regulatory costs and fines, e-payment / contractual penalties, as well as
first party business interruption and crime coverage, such as business interruption loss and restoration costs, and hacker theft and
cyber extortion.

As part of our employee welfare initiatives, we provide comprehensive health insurance coverage to our employees under a
group policy.

We have obtained a vehicle policy which covers risks arising from the use of the company vehicle, including self-caused damage
to the vehicle and third-party liability arising from accidents involving the vehicle, subject to the terms, conditions, and exclusions
and limits of the policy.

Each of the above policies has been structured with sub-limits and deductibles as per standard industry practices.

While we believe that the level of insurance we maintain would be adequate to cover the normal risks associated with the
operation of our business, we do not have insurance policies to cover all possible risks. For risks in relation to our insurance, see
“Risk Factors – 23. Our insurance coverage may be inadequate to protect us against all potential losses, which could have an
adverse effect on our business, financial condition, results of operations and cash flows. In particular, we have not obtained
insurance policies to cover us for losses resulting from business interruption, commercial general liability except to the extent
covered by our cyber and data protection insurance, and any such losses would have to be borne by us, which could have an
adverse effect on our business, financial condition, results of operations and cash flows” on page 39.

                                                                             237
                                       KEY REGULATIONS AND POLICIES IN INDIA

The following description is an overview of certain laws and regulations in India, which are relevant to the business and operations
of our Company, as of the date of this Updated Draft Red Herring Prospectus – I. The information in this section has been obtained
from various legislations, including rules, regulations and policies promulgated by regulatory and statutory bodies, which are
available in the public domain. The description of laws, regulations and policies set out below is not exhaustive and is only intended
to provide general information to investors and is neither designed nor intended to be a substitute for professional legal advice.
The statements below are based on the current provisions of Indian law and the judicial and administrative interpretations thereof,
which are subject to change or modification by subsequent legislative, regulatory, administrative or judicial decisions. For details
regarding the registrations and approvals obtained by our Company under applicable laws and regulations see, “Government and
Other Approvals” on page 367.

Laws in relation to our business

The Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 (“PSSA”)
The PSSA regulates and supervises the payment systems in India and designates the RBI as the authority for that purpose, and for
matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. Under the PSSA, a “payment system” has been defined as a system that enables
payment to be effected between a payer and a beneficiary, involving clearing, payment or settlement service or all of them. A
“payment system” includes systems enabling credit card operations, debit card operations, smart card operations, money transfer
operations or similar operations, but does not include a stock exchange. Under the PSSA a “system provider” means a person who
operates an authorised payment system.
Under the PSSA, it is mandatory to secure authorisation from the RBI for commencement and/or operation of a payment system.
An authorisation may be revoked by the RBI for any contravention of the provision of the PSSA or the regulations thereunder, or
for any failure to comply with the directions of the RBI, or operates the payment system contrary to the conditions based on which
the authorisation was issued. The PSSA provides that the RBI shall give the system provider a reasonable opportunity of being
heard before revocation of authorisation, however, the same is not applicable when the RBI considers it necessary to revoke the
authorisation in the interest of the monetary policy of the country, or for other reasons which it may specify in the order. The RBI
is also empowered to lay down the standards regarding the format of payment instructions, and the size and shape of such
instructions, timings to be maintained, manner of transfer of funds within the payment systems membership criteria, and other
standards. The RBI is also empowered to call for returns, documents, and other information from the system provider, and to inspect
the premises and access the equipment and documents of the provider.
The PSSA casts a duty on system providers to disclose the terms and conditions, including charges and limitations of liability under
the payment system to existing and prospective system participants. It is also mandatory for system providers to keep the documents
in the payment system confidential.

Payment and Settlement Systems Regulations, 2008 (“PSS Regulations”)
The PSS Regulations were enacted to give effect to the provisions of the PSSA. The PSS Regulations contain the instructions
regarding the manner in which applications and authorisations under the PSSA are to be made. They provide that an application for
grant of an authorisation certificate for commencing or carrying on a payment system must be made to the Chief General Manager
of Department of Payment and Settlement Systems, RBI at Mumbai. The Regulations also make it mandatory for every system
provider to submit returns, documents and other information as the Bank may require, to the Department of Payment and Settlement
Systems, Central Office, Mumbai. Further, it is mandatory for each system provider to furnish a copy of its audited balance sheet
together with a copy of the profit and loss account for the year and a copy of the auditor's report, within three months from the date
on which its annual accounts are closed and balanced.

Reserve Bank of India Framework for Outsourcing of Payment and Settlement-related Activities by Payment System Operators,
2021 (“PSO Framework”)
In August 2021, the RBI introduced the PSO Framework for outsourcing of payment and settlement-related activities by payment
system operators (“PSOs”), to put in place the minimum standards to manage risks in outsourcing of payment and/or settlement-
related activities (including other incidental activities like on-boarding customers, IT based services, etc.). The PSO Framework is
applicable to non-bank PSOs insofar as it relates to their payment and / or settlement-related activities. It is now essential that the
PSO, which is outsourcing its activities, ensures that it exercises due diligence, puts in place sound and responsive risk management
practices for effective oversight, and manages the risks arising from such outsourcing of activities, and that outsourcing
arrangements do not impede its effective supervision by RBI. Further, the PSOs shall not outsource core management functions,
including risk management and internal audit and compliance and decision-making functions such as determining compliance with
KYC norms. However, while internal audit function itself is a management process, the auditors for this purpose can be appointed
by the PSO from its own employees or from the outside on contract. In addition, to outsource any of its payment and settlement-
                                                                 238
related activities, the PSO shall have a board-approved comprehensive outsourcing policy, which incorporates, inter-alia, criteria
for selection of such activities and service providers; parameters for grading the criticality of outsourcing; delegation of authority
depending on risks and criticality; and systems to monitor and review the operation of these activities.
Reserve Bank of India Master Directions on Prepaid Payment Instruments, 2021 (“MD-PPIs”)
Pursuant to the powers under Section 18 read with Section 10(2) of the PSSA, the RBI has issued the MD-PPIs. Prepaid Payment
Instruments (“PPIs”) are instruments that facilitate purchase of goods and services, including financial services, remittances
facilities, etc., against the value stored in such instruments, and are classified under two types: Small PPIs, which are issued by
banks and non-banks after obtaining minimum details of the PPI holder, and are used only for purchase of goods and services, and
do not permit fund transfer and cash withdrawal; and Full-KYC PPIs, which are issued by banks and non-banks after completing
KYC of the PPI holder, and may be used for purchase of goods and services, fund transfer, and cash withdrawal. PPI Issuers operate
or participate in a payment system for issuing PPIs to individuals or organisations. No entity is allowed to set up and operate
payment systems for issuance of PPIs without prior approval or authorisation of RBI. Non-banks that comply with the eligibility
criteria, including those stipulated by the respective regulatory department of RBI, shall be permitted to issue PPIs after obtaining
authorisation from RBI. Non-banks, regulated by any of the financial sector regulators, seeking authorisation from the RBI under
the PSSA shall apply to the Department of Payment and Settlement Systems (DPSS), Central Office (CO), RBI, Mumbai along
with a ‘No Objection Certificate’ from their respective regulator, within 30 days of obtaining such clearance.
PPI issuers are required to follow the know your customer, anti-money laundering, and combating financing of terrorism guidelines
issued in the Master Direction – Know Your Customer Direction, 2016, ensure compliance with the provisions of the Prevention
of Money Laundering Act, 2002, and maintain a log of all the transactions undertaken using the PPIs for at least 10 years. This data
shall be made available for scrutiny to RBI, or any other agency/agencies as may be advised by the RBI. The PPI issuer shall also
file suspicious transaction reports to Financial Intelligence Unit – India. PPI issuers are mandated to disclose all important terms
and conditions in clear and simple language to the holders while issuing the instruments, including expiry period, terms and
conditions, pertaining to expiration of the instrument, and all charges and fees associated with the use of the instrument. For PPIs
issued by bank and non-bank PPI issuers, the customers have recourse to the Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021, as amended,
for grievance redressal. All non-bank entities seeking authorisation from RBI under the PSSA shall have a minimum positive net
worth of ₹50 million as per the latest audited balance sheet at the time of submitting the application. Thereafter, by the end of the
third financial year from the date of receiving final authorisation, the entity shall achieve a minimum positive net worth of ₹150
million which shall be maintained at all times.
PPI issuers are also required to have a board approved policy for achieving PPI interoperability, through UPI (where PPIs are issued
in the form of wallets), or cards (physical or virtual), where the cards shall be affiliated to the authorised card networks. PPI issuers
shall ensure adherence to all guidelines/requirements of card networks/ UPI in terms of reconciliation of positions at daily / weekly
/ monthly or more frequent basis, as the case may be, and shall adhere to all dispute resolution and customer grievance redressal
mechanisms as prescribed by the card networks/ NPCI. Further, the MD-PPIs lays down conditions that PPI issuers must follow
with respect to validity and redemption, deployment of money collected, handling of refunds, and customer protection and grievance
redressal framework.
Further, as part of the Vendor Risk Management, PPI issuers shall adhere to the relevant legal and regulatory requirements relating
to geographical location of infrastructure and movement of data out of borders. PPI issuers shall put in place a formal, publicly
disclosed customer grievance redressal framework, including designating a nodal officer to handle the customer complaints /
grievances, the escalation matrix and turn-around-times for complaint resolution. In case of co-branding arrangements between a
bank and non-bank entity, the bank is the PPI issuer. The role of the non-bank entity is limited to marketing or distribution of the
PPIs or providing access to the PPI holder to services that are offered by the PPI issuer. PPI issuers are mandated to disclose all
important terms and conditions in clear and simple language to the holders while issuing the instruments, including expiry period,
terms and conditions, pertaining to expiration of the instrument, and all charges and fees associated with the use of the instrument.

Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Know Your Customer) Directions, 2025 (“KYC Directions”)
The RBI issued the KYC Directions (as amended from time to time) to ensure that inter alia PSOs adhere to certain customer
identification procedures while undertaking transactions exceeding specified thresholds, and to monitor customer transactions in
order to ensure the regulated entities’ compliance with the PMLA (defined below), PMLA Rules (defined below) which aim to
ensure integrity and stability of the financial system by preventing banks and other financial institutions from being used as a
channel for money laundering / terrorist financing.
The KYC Directions requires regulated entities to, inter alia, adopt a board-approved KYC policy and implement necessary
programmes to combat money laundering and terror financing. Primarily, the KYC policy framework adopted must include (i)
customer acceptance and customer identification policies which ensure that appropriate due diligence measures are undertaken to
identify customers at the time of commencement of an account based relationship with the customer and on an ongoing basis; (ii)
a risk management policy for risk-based categorisation of customers; (iii) robust record management systems to ensure compliance
with the KYC Directions; and (iv) a transaction monitoring mechanism to ensure that transactions are consistent with the entity’s
                                                                  239
knowledge of the customer, their business and risk profile, as well as to enable monitoring of specific categories of transactions as
mandated by the KYC Directions. The KYC Directions are applicable to entities including payment system providers/system
participants and prepaid payments instrument issuers.


The Information Technology Act, 2000 (the “IT Act”)
The IT Act seeks to (i) provide legal recognition to transactions carried out by various means of electronic data interchange
involving alternatives to paper-based methods of communication and storage of information, (ii) facilitate electronic filing of
documents and (iii) create a mechanism for the authentication of electronic documentation through digital signatures. The IT Act
provides for extraterritorial jurisdiction over any offence or contravention under the IT Act committed outside India by any person,
irrespective of their nationality, if the act or conduct constituting the offence or contravention involves a computer, computer system
or computer network located in India. Additionally, the IT Act empowers the Government of India to direct any of its agencies to
intercept, monitor or decrypt any information in the interest of sovereignty, integrity, defence and security of India, among other
things. The Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009
specifically permit the Government of India to block access of any information generated, transmitted, received, stored or hosted
in any computer resource by the public, the reasons for which are required to be recorded by it in writing.
The IT Act facilitates electronic commerce by recognizing contracts concluded through electronic means, protects intermediaries
in respect of third-party information liability and creates liability for failure to protect sensitive personal data. The IT Act also
prescribes civil and criminal liability including fines and imprisonment for computer related offences including those relating to
unauthorised access to computer systems, tampering with or unauthorised manipulation of any computer, computer system or
computer network and, damaging computer systems and creates liability for negligence in dealing with or handling any sensitive
personal data or information in a computer resource and in maintaining reasonable security practices and procedures in relation
thereto.
The IT Act empowers the Government of India to formulate rules with respect to reasonable security practices and procedures and
sensitive personal data. In exercise of this power, the Department of Information Technology, Ministry of Electronics and
Information Technology, Government of India (“DoIT”), in April 2011, notified the Information Technology (Reasonable Security
Practices and Procedures and Sensitive Personal Data or Information) Rules, 2011 (the “IT Security Rules”) which prescribe
directions for the collection, disclosure, transfer and protection of sensitive personal data by a body corporate or any person acting
on behalf of a body corporate. The IT Security Rules require every such body corporate to provide a privacy policy for handling
and dealing with personal information, including sensitive personal data, ensuring security of all personal data collected by it and
publishing such policy on its website. The IT Security Rules further require that all such personal data be used solely for the
purposes for which it was collected, and any third party disclosure of such data is made with the prior consent of the information
provider, unless contractually agreed upon between them or where such disclosure is mandated by law.

The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (the “DPDP Act”)
The Parliament passed the DPDP Act on August 9, 2023, and certain provisions of the DPDP Act have become enforceable from
November 13, 2025 (“Enforcement Date”). The DPDP Act will replace the data protection provision contained in Section 43A of
the IT Act, 18 months from the Enforcement Date. The DPDP Act and the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, notified
by the Government of India, under the DPDP Act, vide a notification dated November 13, 2025 (“DPDP Rules”) provide for the
processing of digital personal data in a manner that recognises both the rights of individuals to protect their personal data and the
need to process personal data for lawful purposes and matters incidental thereto. The DPDP Act and the DPDP Rules provides that
personal data may be processed only for a lawful purpose after obtaining the consent of the data principal to whom the personal
data relates, or for certain legitimate uses. A notice must be given before seeking consent. It further imposes certain obligations on
data fiduciaries including (i) ensuring the accuracy, consistency and completeness of personal data processed, (ii) building
reasonable security safeguards to prevent a data breach, (iii) informing the Data Protection Board of India (the “DPB”) and affected
persons in the event of a breach, and (iv) unless retention is necessary for compliance with any law, personal data is to be erased
upon the data principal withdrawing consent or as soon as the purpose has been met and retention is not necessary for legal purposes
(storage limitation). In case of government entities, storage limitation and the right of the data principal to erasure will not apply.
The Central Government will establish the DPB. Key functions of the DPB include: (i) monitoring compliance and imposing
penalties, (ii) directing data fiduciaries to take necessary measures in the event of a data breach, and (iii) hearing grievances made
by data principals. The DPB members will be appointed for two years and will be eligible for re-appointment. The Central
Government will prescribe details such as the number of members of the DPB and the selection process.

Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (“PMLA”)
The PMLA was enacted to prevent money laundering and to provide for confiscation of property derived from, or involved, in
money laundering, and for incidental matters connected therewith. Section 12 of the PMLA inter alia casts certain obligations on
reporting entities (as defined under the PMLA) in relation to preservation of records and reporting of transactions. The Prevention
of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005 (“PMLA Rules”) were framed under the PMLA to implement
                                                                 240
provisions that help combat money laundering in India. The aim of PMLA Rules is to ensure that certain entities and financial
institutions maintain comprehensive records of their transactions and client details in order to prevent money laundering activities
and facilitate the enforcement of anti-money laundering laws.

The Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act, 2006
The Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act of 2006 (“MSMED Act”) regulates the classification, development,
and enhancement of micro, small, and medium enterprises (“MSMEs”) in India. The MSMED Act specifies the criteria for
classifying enterprises based on investment and turnover and outlines the prerequisites for obtaining registration to avail of benefits
under the MSMED Act. Moreover, it mandates that all registered enterprises maintain comprehensive records subject to inspection
by relevant authorities. Any breaches of the MSMED Act, including those related to misrepresentation of enterprise size or failure
to comply with specified regulations, are subject to fines, penalties, or both. The MSMED Act also lays down the functions of the
Micro and small Enterprises Facilitation Council, established to promote and support MSMEs. Registration under the MSMED Act
is required to access various incentives and support schemes, with application details outlined in the MSMED Act.

Consumer Laws
The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (the “Consumer Protection Act”)
The Consumer Protection Act, which repeals the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, was designed and enacted to provide for timely
and effective administration and settlement of consumer disputes. It seeks, inter alia, to promote and protect the interests of
consumers against deficiencies and defects in goods or services and secure the rights of a consumer against unfair trade practices,
which may be practiced by manufacturers, service providers and traders. The definition of “consumer” has been expanded under
the Consumer Protection Act to include persons who buy goods or avail services by offline or online transactions through electronic
means or by tele-shopping or direct-selling or multi-level marketing. It provides for the establishment of consumer disputes
redressal commissions for the purposes of redressal of consumer grievances.
The Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020, issued under the Consumer Protection Act apply to, among other things,
goods and services bought or sold over digital or electronic networks, all models of e-commerce and all forms of unfair trade
practice across e-commerce models. The rules specify the duties of sellers, duties and liability of e-commerce entities and inventory
ecommerce entities.

Intellectual Property Laws
The Trade Marks Act, 1999 (the “Trade Marks Act”)
The Trade Marks Act provides for the application and registration of trademarks in India. The purpose of the Trade Marks Act is
to register trademarks applied for in India and to provide for better protection of trademark for goods and services and also to
prevent use of fraudulent marks. Application for the registration of trademarks has to be made to Trade Marks registry by any
person or persons claiming to be the proprietor of a trade mark, whether individually or as joint applicants, and can be made on the
basis of either actual use of intention to use a trademark in the future. The Trade Marks Act prohibits any registration of trademarks
which are identical/similar to other trademarks or commonly used name of chemical compound among others. It also provides for
penalties for falsifying and falsely applying trademarks and using them to cause confusion among the public. The Trade Marks Act
provides for civil remedies in the event of infringement of registered trade marks or for passing off, including injunction, damages,
account of profits or delivery-up of infringing labels and marks for destruction or erasure.
In March 2017, the Trade Marks Rules, 2017 (“Trade Mark Rules”) were notified. The Trade Mark Rules provide that renewal
of a trade mark may be made at any time not more than one year before the expiration of the last registration of the trademark. The
Trade Mark Rules provide that hearing for any proceeding under the Trade Marks Act may also be held through video-conferencing
or through any other audio-visual communication devices.

Copyright Act, 1957 and the rules thereunder
The Copyright Act, 1957, along with the Copyright Rules, 2013 protect literary, dramatic works, musical and artistic works
including photographs and audio-visual works (cinematograph films and video). Software, both in source and object code,
constitutes a literary work under Indian law and is afforded copyright protection and the owner of such software becomes entitled
to protect his works against unauthorised use and misappropriation of the copyrighted work or a substantial part thereof.

Laws governing foreign investments
Foreign investment in India is governed by the provisions of Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999, as amended, along with
the rules, regulations and notifications made by the RBI thereunder, and the consolidated FDI Policy Circular of 2020 (No.
5(2)/2020) dated October 15, 2020, as amended, issued by the Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion, Ministry of
Commerce and Industry, Government of India, and any modifications thereto or substitutions thereof, issued from time to time.
                                                                 241
Labour related regulations
Shops and establishments legislations

Under the provisions of local shops and establishment legislations applicable in the states in which establishments are set up,
establishments are required to be registered under the respective legislations. These legislations regulate the condition of work and
employment in shops and commercial establishments and generally prescribe obligations in respect of, among others, registration,
opening and closing hours, daily and weekly working hours, rest intervals, overtime, holidays, leave, health and safety measures,
termination of service and wages for overtime work. There are penalties prescribed in the form of monetary fine or imprisonment
for violation of these legislations.

Labour Codes

In order to rationalize and reform labour laws in India, the Government of India had framed four labour codes (“Labour Codes”),
which (barring certain provisions) have been brought into effect, through a notification, from November 21, 2025, namely:

    a)   The Code on Wages, 2019
    The Code on Wages, 2019, provides for subsumption of 4 (four) legislations, namely, the Payment of Wages Act, 1936, the
    Minimum Wages Act, 1948, the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 and the Equal Remuneration Act, 1976. It provides for a new
    definition of ‘wages’ and minimum wages to be notified for all employees in all industries, based on the categories of employees
    and/or geographical locations and other conditions of service, which shall be equal to or above the rate of floor wages set by
    the Central Government, and further mandates fixation of wage period and timely wage payment. It also requires that pay
    parity should be ensured for all genders, and provides for payment of annual bonus, and normal working hours to be prescribed
    (with the requirement to pay overtime at twice the normal pay rates in the event an employee works beyond the normal working
    hours). Employers must pay wages within prescribed timelines (daily, weekly, fortnightly or monthly), observe authorized
    deductions (capped at 50% of wages), and comply with labelling, records, returns, wage slips, and notice display requirements.
    There is no standalone “license” under the Code on Wages; however, employers must maintain prescribed registers and notices,
    issue wage slips, and adhere to bonus provisions (eligible employees receive at least 8.33% of wages, up to 20%, subject to
    notified thresholds).

    b) The Industrial Relations Code, 2020
    The Industrial Relations Code, 2020, subsumes 3 (three) legislations inter alia the Trade Unions Act, 1926, and the Industrial
    Disputes Act, 1947. The objective of the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, is to promote industrial harmony whilst balancing
    worker protection with business flexibility. The key provisions include (i) recognition of negotiating union (51% membership)
    and negotiation council (union with at least 20% support), (ii) specific recognition of fixed-term employment with equal
    benefits including parity in wages, working hours, and allowances with permanent workers, (iii) definitions of key terms
    including ‘employee’ and ‘worker’, (iv) conditions for lay-offs, retrenchment and closure, including increase in the headcount
    threshold from 100 (one hundred) to 300 (three hundred) workers for applicability of certain special provisions of retrenchment,
    lay-off and closure to factories, mines and plantations, (v) constitution of a grievance redressal committee with equal employer
    and employee representatives, (vi) mandatory notice requirements for strikes and lock-outs in all industrial establishments,
    (vii) provision of notice to workers prior to change in certain conditions of service; (viii) prohibition of identified unfair labour
    practices, (ix) adoption and certification of standing orders, and (x) dispute resolution through conciliation, labour courts and
    industrial tribunals.

    c)   The Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 (“Occupational Safety Code”)
    The Occupational Safety Code subsumes 13 (thirteen) legislations such as the Factories Act, 1948, the Contract Labour
    (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970, the Inter-State Migrant Workmen (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of
    Service) Act, 1979, and the Building and Other Construction Workers (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service)
    Act, 1996, among others. It applies broadly to establishments employing at least 10 workers, and to all mines and docks, with
    certain core health, safety, welfare, hours-of-work and leave provisions extendable to all employees.

    The Occupational Safety Code provides for definitions of key terms including ‘contract labour’, ‘contractor’, ‘principal
    employer’ and ‘establishment’, annual leave with wages and prescription of working hours and rest intervals, special provisions
    on employment of women in night shifts, and prescription of health and safety obligations and provision of welfare facilities.
    The Occupational Safety Code provides for a common registration to be obtained by establishments (including factories and
    commercial establishments), licence for contractors supplying contractor labour, and scope for prescription of requirement for
    factories to obtain specific licences, etc. The Occupational Safety Code also regulates the employment of contract labour
    including inter-state migrant workers in certain establishments including with respect to prohibition of engagement of contract
                                                                  242
     labour in core activities, and provisions for welfare and health of contract labour.

     d) The Code on Social Security, 2020
     The Code on Social Security, 2020 provides for subsumption of 9 (nine) social security related legislations, inter alia the
     Employee’s Compensation Act, 1923, the Employee’s State Insurance Act, 1948, the Employees’ Provident Funds and
     Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952, the Maternity Benefit Act, 1961, and the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972. The Code on
     Social Security, 2020 provides for a common registration to be obtained, social security provisions including on provident
     fund, pension, and employees’ deposit-linked insurance, employees’ state insurance coverage and benefits including sickness
     benefit, disablement benefit, etc, compensation to be paid to employees for workplace injuries/occupational diseases, maternity
     benefits, gratuity payments including to fixed-term employees, and prescription of social security benefits including for
     building and other construction workers, unorganised workers, gig workers and platform workers. Employers are required to
     obtain necessary registration and make necessary contributions/payments as prescribed.

The Labour Codes prescribe penalties in the form of monetary fine or imprisonment or both for violations of the provisions provided
therein. In furtherance of the implementation of the Labour Codes, including requirements relating to registration and other
procedural compliances, the Ministry of Labour and Employment notified the Industrial Relations Code (Central) Rules, 2026, the
Code on Wages (Central) Rules, 2026 and the Social Security Code (Central) Rules, 2026 on May 8, 2026, and the Occupational
Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code (Central) Rules, 2026 on May 9, 2026.

In addition to Labour Codes and shops and establishments legislations, certain other labour and employment-related legislations
(and rules issued thereunder) that may apply to our operations, from the perspective of protecting the workers’ rights, reporting and
other compliances, and the requirements that may apply to us as an employer, such as:

     •   The Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986;
     •   Labour welfare fund legislations; and
     •   Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013.

Laws relating to taxation

may be applicable to the operations of our Company include:

laws and regulations imposed by the central and state governments, RBI, and other authorities for its day-to-day operations.

Corporate Information

Paramotor Giftbrandz Private Limited (“Giftbrandz”) was incorporated on July 8, 2025, as a private company limited by shares
under the Companies Act, 2013. Its corporate identification number is U82990MH2025PTC452098. The registered office of
Giftbrandz is located at 433, 4th Floor, Laxmi Plaza, Laxmi Industrial Estate, New Link Road, Andheri, Mumbai 400 053,
Maharashtra, India.

Giftbrandz is authorized under its memorandum of association, to carry on the business of providing digital payment solutions
including the issuance and operation of prepaid payment instruments, acting as a payment aggregator and payment gateway for
processing electronic transactions, operating as a Bharat Bill Payment Operating Unit under the Bharat Bill Payment System, and
offering mobile wallet services for the storage and transfer of digital funds. It shall also provide services related to UPI, facilitate
cross-border payments including inward and outward remittances, and perform permitted activities in compliance with applicable
laws and regulations prescribed by the RBI, NPCI, and other competent authorities and carry on other business or activities which
are directly or indirectly necessary for the furtherance of the objects of the Giftbrandz.
