Brief profiles of our Directors

Sonia Pankaj Asher is one of our Promoters and the Executive Chairperson and Whole-time Director on the Board of our Company.
She is responsible for the strategic vision and long-term growth of our Company. She has a bachelor’s degree in commerce from
University of Mumbai. She has over 24 years of experience across the fields of banking and payments with multinational banks
and institutions in leadership roles. She has previously worked with Global Payments Asia - Pacific India Private Limited as the
regional account and partners channel manager. She has also worked with the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation
Limited as the sales relationship manager in the merchant services department, and with Standard Chartered Bank as a personal
financial consultant. She has been awarded the Woman Super Achiever of the Year at the 7th Future Tech Congress & Awards 2026
and has been recognised as CEO of the Year at the 24th Global Edition and 9th Indian Edition: Business Leader of the Year, 2026.
She has also been recognised in the Fintech: Excellence under 40 at the 10th Payment Industry Awards, 2023. She has been
recognised as one of the Most Influential 50 Payments Professionals by World Payments Congress & Awards, 2020, and has been
awarded the Women in Tech, Entrepreneur of the Year – FinTech at the Women Leadership Influencer Awards in 2020. She has also
been recognised in SuperSheroes: Women Power in Payments awarded at the 11th Payment Industry Awards. She is also the winner
of the Women in FinTech Demo Day conducted by Paisabazaar.com Fintegrate Zone 2019. She was also part of the panel discussion
at the event titled “Global Fintech Fest, 2026” on the topic “The Future of PPIs: Regulation, Innovation & Emerging Use Cases”.

Rahul Anand is one of our Promoters and the Managing Director on the Board of our Company. He is responsible for managing
the overall business operations driving growth, implementing strategies, and ensuring achievement of our Company’s business
achievements. He has over 17 years of work experience including as a management consultant and in the field of e - commerce &
digital payments. He has been previously associated with Dreamland Innovative Solutions Private Limited as a director. He has
been recognised as the Business Super Achiever at the 19th Edition of the Stars of the Industry Awards, 2026. For further details,
please see “Risk Factors – 44. The documents evidencing certain educational qualifications of Rahul Anand, the Promoter and
Managing Director of our Company, are not traceable. Accordingly, we have not included the disclosure of his educational
qualifications in this Updated Draft Red Herring Prospectus-I.” on page 51.

Kunal Sharma is a Non – Executive Director on the Board of our Company. He has been associated with our Company as director
since September 22, 2025. He holds a bachelor’s degree of technology in electrical engineering from Kurukshetra University and
holds a master of business administration from Punjab University with specialisation in telecommunications and information
technology. He has over 15 years of experience in the field of real estate sales and strategy through leading his proprietorship firm
Kunal Realty. He has received certificate of appreciation for contribution as a speaker at TEDx Kothari International School, Noida
Youth under the theme “From Barriers to Bridges - Redefining Possibilities”.

Meeta Sanjay Mukherjee is an Independent Director on the Board of our Company. She has been associated with our Company
as a director since January 21, 2026. She holds a bachelor’s degree in commerce from University of Bombay and holds an
international diploma in computer programming and applications moderated by the National Computing Centre (U.K.) from the
Apple Information Technology Division. She has over 26 years of experience across the fields of branch administration, banking
operations, client relationship management and team leadership. She has previously worked with the Hongkong and Shanghai
Banking Corporation Limited as the AM premier services, premier service manager, AVP deputy branch manager, as premier service
manager with HSBC Bank Middle East Limited, and with Standard Chartered Bank as a personal financial consultant.

Prasanna Babanrao Lohar is an Independent Director on the Board of our Company. He has been associated with our Company
as a director since January 21, 2026. He holds a bachelor’s degree of engineering in computer science and engineering from Swami
Ramanand Teerth Marathwada University, Nanded. He has over 20 years of experience across the fields of information technology,
                                                                   254
banking, innovation and consulting sectors. He is currently associated with Union Bank of India as an external expert for the
Innovation Centre at its department of information technology. He has been associated with the Ernst and Young LLP as a project

Limited, as a senior manager and technical architect at Atos Wordline India Private Limited (pursuant to the acquisition of Venture

The Nomination and Remuneration Committee was constituted by way of resolution passed by our Board on February 14, 2026.

The terms of reference of the Nomination and Remuneration Committee are in accordance with the applicable provisions of the
Companies Act and the SEBI Listing Regulations, and its terms of reference are as disclosed below:

  (a) formulation of the criteria for determining qualifications, positive attributes and independence of a director and recommend
       to the board of directors of our Company (“Board”) a policy relating to the remuneration of the directors, key managerial
       personnel and other employees (“Remuneration Policy”). The Nomination and Remuneration Committee, while
       formulating the Remuneration Policy, should ensure that:
         (i) the level and composition of remuneration be reasonable and sufficient to attract, retain and motivate directors of the
               quality required to run our Company successfully;
         (ii) relationship of remuneration to performance is clear and meets appropriate performance benchmarks; and
         (iii) remuneration to directors, key managerial personnel and senior management involves a balance between fixed and
               incentive pay reflecting short and long term performance objectives appropriate to the working of our Company and
               its goals.
    (b) for every appointment of an independent director, the Nomination and Remuneration Committee shall evaluate the balance
         of skills, knowledge and experience on the Board and on the basis of such evaluation, prepare a description of the role and
         capabilities required of an independent director. The person recommended to the Board for appointment as an independent
         director shall have the capabilities identified in such description. For the purpose of identifying suitable candidates, the
         Committee may:
         (i) use the services of an external agencies, if required;
         (ii) consider candidates from a wide range of backgrounds, having due regard to diversity; and
         (iii) consider the time commitments of the candidates.
    (c) formulation of criteria for evaluation of performance of independent directors and the Board;
    (d) devising a policy on Board diversity;
    (e) identifying persons who are qualified to become directors of our Company and who may be appointed in senior
         management in accordance with the criteria laid down, and recommend to the Board their appointment and removal;
    (f) whether to extend or continue the term of appointment of the independent director, on the basis of the report of performance
         evaluation of independent directors;
    (g) recommend to the Board, all remuneration, in whatever form, payable to senior management; and
    (h) carrying out any other activities as may be delegated by the Board and functions required to be carried out by the
         Nomination and Remuneration Committee as provided under the Companies Act, 2013, the SEBI Listing Regulations or
         any other applicable law, as and when amended from time to time.”

The Nomination and Remuneration Committee shall perform such functions as are required to be performed by the compensation
committee under the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Share Based Employee Benefits and Sweat Equity) Regulations,
2021, as amended, including the following:
    (a) administering the employee stock option plans of our Company, as may be required;
    (b) determining the eligibility of employees to participate under the employee stock option plans of our Company;
    (c) granting options to eligible employees and determining the date of grant;
    (d) determining the number of options to be granted to an employee;
    (e) determining the exercise price under the employee stock option plans of our Company; and
    (f) construing and interpreting the employee stock option plans of our Company and any agreements defining the rights and
         obligations of our Company and eligible employees under the employee stock option plans of our Company, and
         prescribing, amending and/or rescinding rules and regulations relating to the administration of the employee stock option
         plans of our Company.

The declaration and payment of dividends on our Equity Shares, if any, will be recommended by our Board to the Shareholders
for their approval, at their discretion, subject to compliance with the Articles of Association and provisions of the Companies
Act, including the rules made thereunder and other relevant regulations, if any, each as amended.

Further the Board shall also have the absolute power to declare interim dividend in compliance with the Act. The dividend
distribution policy of our Company was approved and adopted by way of a resolution dated April 18, 2026 passed by the Board
of Directors (“Dividend Policy”).

In terms of the Dividend Policy, the dividend, if any, will depend on a number of internal factors including but not limited to,
retained earnings, current and projected cash balances, our liquidity position, past dividend trends, profit earned, capital
expenditure requirements, financial commitments, business expansion plans, cost of fund raising from alternate sources, other
corporate actions and any other factor which is deemed fit by our Board, and external factors, including but not limited to
applicable laws and regulations, regulatory changes and changes in macro-economic environment or any other external factors
which may deemed fit by our Board.

There is no guarantee that any dividends will be declared or paid in the future. For details in relation to risks involved in this
regard, see “Risk Factors – 42. We cannot assure payment of dividends on the Equity Shares in the future” on page 51.

fulfilled and the corresponding obligation has crystallised, is measurable and is enforceable as at the reporting date.
Amounts invoiced in respect of which the relevant customer acquisition and card issuance conditions have not been fulfilled as at the reporting date are considered as
uncrystallised commercial amounts and are recognised as recoverable and adjustable commercial balances, and resulting into the excess amount of Rs.9.48 million has been
recognised as a recoverable commercial advance under Other Financial Assets, to be adjusted against future commercial entitlements as and when the applicable contractual
conditions are fulfilled.
The Company has accounted for the arrangement based on its substance and in accordance with the applicable requirements of Ind AS relating to recognition, measurement and
presentation of the relevant expenses, assets and liabilities.

Bonus Share
Pursuant to approval by the Board of Directors, meeting held on 10 October 2025 bonus share were issued in the ratio of 3,523 new equity shares for every 1
existing equity share by capitalizing a sum of Rs. 388.09 million from free reserves of the Group. The Equity share issued upon allotment rank pari-passu in all the
respects with the existing equity shares of the Group.

Nature and purpose of the reserve
Securities premium
Securities premium reserve is used to record the premium on issue of shares. The reserve can be utilized only for limited purposes in accordance with the
provisions of the Companies Act, 2013.
Retained earnings
Retained Earning is created from time to time by way of transfer of profits for appropriation purposes. Retained earnings represent the amount of accumulated
earnings of the Group. Retained earnings represent the cumulative undistributed profits of the Group and can be utilized in accordance with the provisions of
the Act. Retained Earnings is not an item of other comprehensive income.
Other Comprehensive Income
Remeasurements are not reclassified to the statement of profit and loss in subsequent periods. Re-measurement, comprising of actuarial gains and losses and
the return on plan assets (excluding amounts included in net interest on the net defined benefit liability), are recognized immediately in the balance sheet with a
corresponding debit or credit to retained earnings through OCI in the period in which they occur.

Note 32 - Earnings per share

Basic EPS is calculated by dividing the profit for the year attributable to equity holders of the Company by the weighted average number of equity shares outstanding during the period/year.

Diluted EPS is calculated by dividing the profit attributable to equity holders of the Company by the weighted average number of equity shares outstanding during the year plus the weighted
average number of equity shares that would be issued on conversion of all the dilutive potential equity shares into equity shares of the Company.

i) Earnings per share is computed in accordance with Ind AS 33 with taking the retrospective effect of the Bonus shares of the Company approved in the Board of Directors meeting held on
October 10, 2025 whereby bonus share was issued in the ratio of 3523 new equity shares for every 1 existing equity share each and number of Shares has been considered after taking the above
effect for calculating the Earnings per Share.

Valuation Principle
Fair value is the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction in the principal (or most advantageous) market at the measurement date under
current market conditions (i.e., an exit price), regardless of whether that price is directly observable or estimated using a valuation technique.

Fair value Hierarchy
This section explains the judgments and estimates made in determining the fair value of the financial instrument that are (a) recognized and measured at fair value and (b) measured at amortized
cost and for which fair values are disclosed in the financial statements. To provide an indication about the reliability of the inputs used in determining fair value, the Group has classified its financial
instruments into three levels prescribed under the accounting standard. The Group uses the following hierarchy for determining and disclosing the fair value of the financial instruments by
valuation techniques:
Level 1 : Level 1 hierarchy includes financial instruments measured using unadjusted quoted prices in active markets that the Group has the ability to access for the identical assets or liabilities. A
financial instrument is classified as a Level 1 measurement if it is listed on an exchange. This includes listed equity instruments, traded bonds and mutual funds that have quoted price. The fair
value of all equity instruments which are traded in the stock exchanges are valued using the closing price as at the reporting period. The mutual funds are valued at the closing NAV.

Level 2 : The fair value of financial instruments that are not traded in active markets is determined using valuation techniques which maximize the use of observable market data either directly or
indirectly, such as quoted prices for similar assets and liabilities in active markets, for substantially the full term of the financial instrument but do not qualify as Level 1 inputs. If all significant inputs
required to fair value an instrument are observable the instrument is included in level 2.
Level 3 : If one or more of the significant inputs is not based in observable market data, the instruments is included in level 3. That is, Level 3 inputs incorporate market participants’ assumptions
about risk and the risk premium required by market participants in order to bear that risk. The Group develops Level 3 inputs based on the best information available in the circumstances.

Financial instruments valued at carrying value
The respective carrying values of certain on-balance sheet financial instruments approximated their fair value. These financial instruments include cash in hand, balances with Banks, financial
institutions, accrued interest receivable, accrued interest payable, and certain other assets and liabilities that are considered financial instruments. Carrying values were assumed to approximate
fair values for these financial instruments as they are short-term in nature and their recorded amounts approximate fair values or are receivable or payable on demand.

Note 40 - Financial risk management
The Group's board of directors has overall responsibility for the establishment and oversight of the Group's risk management framework. The major risk to which the Group
is exposed are described below:

A. Credit risk
Credit risk is the risk of financial loss to the Group if a customer or counterparty to a financial instruments fail to meet its contractual obligations. The Group is exposed
mainly to credit risk arises from cash and cash equivalents, deposit with banks and outstanding trade receivables.
(a) Trade Receivables
The Group extends credit to customers in normal course of business. The Group considers factor such as credit report of customer, industry practice, payment record etc.
The Group evaluates the concentration of risk with respect to trade receivables and unbilled revenue as low.
(b) Cash and cash equivalent and Bank deposits
The Group considers factors such as track record, size of institution, market reputation, credit institution with high credit ratings and service standards to select the banks
with which balances and deposits are maintained. The balance and fixed deposits are generally maintained with the banks with whom the Group has availed the credit
facilities. Further, the Group does not maintain significant cash in hand other than those required for its day to day operations. Considering the same, the Group is not
exposed to expected credit loss of cash and cash equivalent and bank deposits.
B. Currency Risk
The Group does not have material revenues, expenses, assets or liabilities denominated in foreign exchange and hence the Group is not subject to foreign currency
fluctuation.

Note 40 - Financial risk management

C. Liquidity risk
Liquidity risk is the risk that the Group will encounter difficulty in meeting the obligations associated with its financial liabilities that are settled by delivering cash or
another financial asset. The Group's approach to managing liquidity is to ensure, as far as possible, that it will have sufficient liquidity to meet its liabilities when they are
due, under both normal and stressed conditions, without incurring unacceptable losses or risking damage to the Group's reputation.

Note 47 - Re-audit of Financial Statements

The financial statements of the Company for the financial year ended March 31, 2025 were previously audited by the
predecessor statutory auditors. In connection with the Company’s proposed initial public offering and in accordance
with the requirements of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements)
Regulations, 2018, the Company has undertaken a re-audit of the financial statements for the limited purpose of
issuance of audit reports by the current statutory auditors, who hold a valid peer review certificate issued by the Peer
Review Board of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, as required under the applicable regulations.

During the course of the re-audit, based on additional information and reassessment of underlying obligations, the
Company has recognized additional provisions towards certain expenses. The Company has also recognized the
corresponding deferred tax impact on such adjustments in accordance with the applicable Indian Accounting
Standards.

Note 48 - Discontinued operations
Pursuant to a resolution passed at the meeting of the Board of Directors held on 15 April, 2025, the Company approved the discontinuation of its Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) / Point of Sale
(POS) services business with effect from 01 April, 2025, as part of its strategic decision.

Accordingly, the MDR/POS business qualifies as a discontinued operation in accordance with Ind AS 105. During the year ended 31 March, 2026, the Company has recognized the following in
relation to the discontinued operation write-off of fixed assets amounting to Rs. 0.50 million (gross carrying value with net carrying value of Rs 0.16 million as on 1 April, 2025) and write-off of
trade receivables amounting to Rs. 0.01 million. The financial impact of the above has been included under “Profit/(Loss) from discontinued operations” in the Statement of Profit and Loss


Further, in accordance with Ind AS 105, the Company has restated the comparative financial information for all periods presented. Accordingly, the Statement of Profit and Loss for the three
month ended 30 June, 2026 and 30 June, 2025, and the financial years ended March 31, 2026, March 31, 2025, and March 31, 2024 have been re-presented to reflect the MDR/POS business as a
discontinued operation.

   Note 49 - First Time Adoption of Ind AS & Reconciliation of audited financial statement with restated financial information:

   First Time Adoption of Ind AS

   Company had prepared financial Statement as at & for the financial year ended 31 March 2023, 31 March 2024, 31 March 2025 and 31 March 2022 in accordance with accounting standards notified under section 133 of the Companies Act
   2013, read together with paragraph 7 of the Companies (Accounts) Rules, 2014 (Previous GAAP- Indian GAAP). These financial statements were audited by previous statutory auditors of respectively years. The Standalone special purpose
   financial statements, as at and for the financial year ended 31 March 2023, were the first financial statements of the Company prepared in accordance with Ind AS. In preparing the first Ind AS financial statements, the Company's Ind AS
   opening balance sheet was prepared as at April 01, 2022, the Company’s Statutory date of transition to Ind AS.
   The Special Purpose March Audited Standalone Ind AS Financial Statements as at and for the year ended 31 March 2023, 31 March 2024 and 31 March 2025 have been prepared after making suitable adjustments to the accounting heads from
   their Indian GAAP values following accounting policies and accounting policy choices (both mandatory exceptions and optional exemptions availed as per Ind AS 101) consistent with that used at the date of transition to Ind AS (April 01, 2022)
   and as per the presentation, accounting policies and grouping/classifications including revised Schedule III disclosures followed as at and for the thee months period ended 30 June, 2026.


    Exemptions and exceptions availed
    Set out below are the applicable Ind AS 101 optional exemptions and mandatory exceptions applied in the transition from previous GAAP to Ind AS.
a) Ind AS optional exemptions
 i) Deemed cost
    Ind AS 101 permits a first-time adopter to elect to continue with the carrying value for all of its property, plant and equipment as recognized in the financial statements as at the date of transition to Ind AS, measured as per the previous GAAP
    and use that as its deemed cost as at the date of transition. This exemption can also be used for intangible assets covered by Ind AS 38 Intangible Assets. Accordingly, the Company has elected to measure all of its property, plant and
    equipment and intangible assets at their previous GAAP carrying value.
ii) Lease accounting
    Ind AS 116 requires an entity to assess whether a contract or arrangement contains a lease. In accordance with Ind AS 116, at the inception of the contract, an entity shall assess whether the contract is, or contains, a lease. Ind AS 101 provides
    an option to make this assessment on the basis of facts and circumstances existing at the date of transition to Ind AS, except where the effect is expected to be not material. The group has elected to apply this exemption for such
    contracts/arrangements. The Company has opted for exemption for short term leases provided in Ind AS 116.

b) Ind AS mandatory exemptions
    The Company has applied the following exceptions from full retrospective application of Ind AS as mandatorily required under Ind AS 101:
 i) Estimates
    An entity’s estimates in accordance with Ind AS at the date of transition to Ind AS shall be consistent with estimates made for the same date in accordance with previous GAAP (after adjustments to reflect any difference in accounting policies),
    unless there is objective evidence that those estimates were in error. Ind AS estimates as at 1 April 2022 are consistent with the estimates as at the same date made in conformity with previous GAAP. The Company has made estimates
    relating to impairment of financial assets based on expected credit loss model and amortization of processing fees over the average period of loan in accordance with Ind AS at the date of transition. These estimates were not required under
    previous GAAP.
 ii) Initial recognition of financial asset
     An entity may apply the requirements in paragraph B5.1.2A (b) of Ind AS 109 prospectively to transactions entered into on or after the date of transition to Ind AS.
iii) Classification and measurement of financial assets
     Financial assets like security deposits received and security deposits paid, has been classified and measured at amortized cost on the basis of the facts and circumstances that exist at the date of transition to Ind AS. Since, it is impracticable for
     the group to apply retrospectively the effective interest method in Ind AS 109, the fair value of the financial asset or the financial liability at the date of transition to Ind AS by applying amortized cost method, has been considered as the new
     gross carrying amount of that financial asset or the financial liability at the date of transition to Ind AS.


c) Statement of restatement adjustment & reconciliations between previous GAAP and Ind AS
   Ind AS 101 requires a first time adopter to reconcile equity, total comprehensive income and cash flows for prior periods. The following tables represent the reconciliations from previous GAAP to Ind AS.

  d) Notes for restatement of GAAP to IND AS
  (I) Other comprehensive income
      Under Ind AS, all items of income and expense recognized during a period are required to be included in profit or loss for that period, unless a specific standard requires or permits their recognition in other comprehensive income (OCI).
      Accordingly, certain items, such as remeasurements of defined benefit plans, are recognized in OCI and presented separately in the statement of profit and loss. The concept of OCI did not exist under the previous GAAP and, therefore, such
      items were recognized in profit or loss in earlier periods.
 (II) Security deposits paid
      Under the previous GAAP, interest-free security deposits, refundable in cash upon completion of the contract, were recognized at their transaction value. Upon transition to Ind AS, such financial assets have been recognized at fair value.
      The difference between the transaction value and the fair value of these security deposits has been adjusted against the related expenditure. This difference is subsequently amortized over the tenure of the deposit using the effective interest
      rate method and recognized as interest income. Accordingly, interest income has resulted in an increase in profit of Rs. 0.04 million for the year ended March 31, 2025, Rs. 0.02 million for the year ended March 31, 2024, and Nil for the year
      ended March 31, 2023. Correspondingly, rent expense has been recognized, leading to a reduction in profit of Rs. 0.40 million, Rs. 0.25 million, and Rs. 0.09 million for the years ended March 31, 2025, 2024, and 2023, respectively.



(III) Remeasurements of post-employment benefit obligations
      Under Ind AS, remeasurements of defined benefit plans, comprising actuarial gains and losses and the return on plan assets (excluding amounts included in net interest on the net defined benefit liability), are recognized in Other
      Comprehensive Income rather than in profit or loss. Accordingly, a gain of Rs. 0.15 million has been recognized in Other Comprehensive Income for the year ended March 31, 2025, Nil for the year ended March 31, 2024, and a loss of Rs. 0.18
      million for the year ended March 31, 2023.
(IV) Lease :
     Operating Lease
     Under the previous Indian GAAP, lease rentals were recognized as an expense on a straight-line basis based on invoices received. On transition to Ind AS, the Company has applied Ind AS 116 and recognized a lease liability measured at the
     present value of the remaining lease payments. Correspondingly, a right-of-use (ROU) asset has been recognized at an amount as if the standard had been applied since the commencement of the lease, but discounted using the lessee’s
     incremental borrowing rate as at April 1, 2022. Accordingly, the Company has recognized a right-of-use asset of Rs. 1.11 million and a corresponding lease liability of Rs. 1.21 million. The resulting net impact of Rs. 0.08 million has been
     adjusted against retained earnings on the date of transition. Further, the principal portion of lease payments is presented under cash flows from financing activities. On adoption of Ind AS 116, the nature of expenses has changed from lease
     rental expense recognized under previous GAAP to depreciation expense on the right-of-use asset and finance cost on the lease liability.


  (V) Deferred Tax
      Deferred tax have been recognized on the adjustments made on transition to Ind AS, provision for expenses and impact of accounting policy.
 (VI) Retained Earnings
      Retained earnings as at April 1, 2022 has been adjusted consequent to the above Ind AS transition adjustments, provision for expenses and impact of accounting policy.
(VII) Regrouping the Financial Statement from GAAP to IND AS
      The Financial Statement have been prepared after incorporating adjustments for the changes in accounting policies, first time adoption of IND AS, material errors, Restatement on account of discontinued operations and
      regrouping/reclassifications retrospectively as at and for the financial years ended March 31, 2026, 2025, 2024 and 2023, to reflect the same accounting treatment as per the accounting policy and grouping/classifications followed as at and for
      the three months ended 30 June, 2026 and 30 June, 2025 pursuant to adopted new accounting policy by Board of Directors dated December 02, 2025.

Note 51 - New Labour Law
The Government of India, vide notification dated November 21, 2025, has notified the Code on Wages, 2019, the Industrial
Relations Code, 2020, the Code on Social Security, 2020, and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code,
2020 (collectively referred to as the "New Labour Codes"), which consolidate and replace twenty-nine existing central labour
laws into an unified framework governing employee benefits during employment and post-employment. The New Labour
codes, amongst other things introduced changes, including a uniform definition of wages for statutory purposes.

Further, the Ministry of Labour & Employment, issued draft Central Rules and FAQs to facilitate assessment of the financial
impact arising from the New Labour Codes. In accordance with the requirements of Ind AS 19 - Employee Benefits, changes
to employee benefit plans arising from legislative amendments constitute a plan amendment, requiring immediate
recognition of the resultant impact as past service cost in the period in which the amendment is notified.

The management has assessed and disclosed the pursuant to the amendment in the Labour Code relating to gratuity
applicability based on actuarial valuation reports obtained for March 31, 2025 and March 31, 2026, based on the
information available as at the reporting date, in a manner consistent with the guidance issued by the Institute of Chartered
Accountants of India (ICAI). Accordingly, the resultant impact has been recognised in the respective reporting periods in the
Statement of Profit and Loss in accordance with the applicable accounting standards on employee benefits.

The Company will continue to monitor further developments including the finalization of the central and state rules under
the New Labour Codes, which are yet to be notified and shall evaluate and give effect to any consequential accounting
adjustments, if any arising therefrom in future periods, as and when required.

Increases in Program Fees

We act as a program manager, business correspondent and distribution agent for non-reloadable prepaid payment instruments
(“PPIs”) with a maximum value of ₹10,000 issued by banks and RBI licensed issuers (which we refer to as “PPI Issuers” and
such cards, “Prepaid Cards”) and act as a distribution agent for non-reloadable brand gift cards (PPIs) issued by merchants
(which we refer to as “Gift Cards”). We refer to these activities as our “PPI Program Management and Distribution”
business. We began distributing Gift Cards, through our yayyy.shop website, which is our digital gifting marketplace, in the
second quarter of Fiscal 2026 and through our yayyy.shop mobile application in the fourth quarter of Fiscal 2026. For more
details, see “Our Business – Our Products and Services – PPI Program Management and Distribution Business” on page 227.

We earn revenue from acting as a program manager, business correspondent and distribution agent for Prepaid Cards from our
share of interchange fees generated on spends on Prepaid Cards at merchant outlets (at physical stores and online), comprising

                                                                    324
(i) our agreed share of the interchange fees with the PPI Partners, including NSDL Payments Bank Limited, and (ii) income
from third-party service providers that provide transaction switching services to banks in the form of incentives to promote
issuer specific programs, including Monepeak Fintech Private Limited. We entered into a co-brand agreement with Mastercard
Asia Pacific Pte. Ltd. in March 2026 for Prepaid Cards co-branded with us. These Prepaid Cards will be issued by one or more
of our PPI Partners. We are entitled to receive incentive based income in consideration for the promotion of network-specific
programmes for Prepaid Cards from a network provider.

In May 2026, we entered into an Ecosystem Partner agreement for the marketing and distribution of Prepaid Cards and Gift
Cards. Pursuant to this agreement, we will provide incentives to the Ecosystem Partner to promote card spends on Prepaid
Cards and Gift Cards distributed under this agreement. The agreement remains in force for an initial period of 12 months and
automatically renews for the same term. The agreement may be terminated at will with 30 days’ notice in writing. In July 2026,
we entered into a mutual referral agreement with TransBnk Solutions Private Limited, our Ecosystem Partner, where we agreed
to refer potential clients to each other, facilitate introductions and exchange information. The agreement remains valid until
terminated by either party at will, with or without cause, by giving no less than 90 days’ prior written notice to the other party
or in limited circumstances, upon 45 days of written notice.

Interchange fees are decided by the payment networks of RuPay, Mastercard, and Visa in accordance with contractual
arrangements between the Payment Networks and the PPI Issuers, and is broadly influenced by the industry of the merchant
where the card is used, the merchant category and transaction value (source: F&S Report, page 22). A program manager
negotiates a share of the interchange fees with the issuer of the Prepaid Cards. There are also arrangements where there is an
incentive (share of interchange) paid to the Program manager by the Card network and the Switch service provider (source:
F&S Report, page 25). Interchange fees vary across types of merchants, the percentages of which are set by the third-party
payment networks (the “Payment Networks”), such as Mastercard, Visa, and RuPay and are generally driven by: (i) the
merchant’s business segment; (ii) applicable merchant category codes; (iii) transaction size (source: F&S Report, page 25).
Interchange fees are not levied directly on the consumer but are paid by the merchant’s bank (acquiring bank) to the card-
issuing bank to process transactions every time any customer uses a card to make purchases from a merchant’s store (source:
F&S Report, page 22). As on the date of this Updated Draft Red Herring Prospectus–I, the interchange fees on Prepaid Cards
are not subject to any regulatory limits. However, the RBI has implemented regulations limiting interchange fees payable on
debit card transactions, including the ceiling on the merchant discount rate applicable for debit card transactions, and if any
similar regulations are extended to Prepaid Cards in the future it could have a material adverse effect on our business, financial
condition, results of operations and cash flows. Further, the National Payments Corporation of India has implemented limits on
merchant discount rate (“MDR”) fees applicable on UPI transactions paid by merchants to banks and payment service providers,
which includes interchange fees.

Historically, Program Fees have been one of the significant components of our revenue from operations. The table below sets

Growing demand for Prepaid Cards

Digital payment transactions in India have risen from 21 billion transactions in Fiscal Year 2017-2018 to a substantial 187
billion transactions in Fiscal Year 2023-2024 and 228 billion in Fiscal Year 2024-2025, growing at a CAGR of 40.6 percent
from Fiscal Year 2018 to Fiscal Year 2025 (source: F&S Report, page 20). This growth has become a defining feature of the
country’s economic landscape, driven by a confluence of factors (source: F&S Report, page 12). Government-led initiatives
such as Digital India have built robust digital infrastructure, expanding access across urban and rural areas (source: F&S Report,
page 12).

India’s prepaid cards market represents a dynamic pillar of the nation's burgeoning digital payments landscape, enabling
financial inclusion for millions through versatile, reloadable and non-reloadable instruments tailored for retail, corporate, and
gifting needs (source: F&S Report, page 16). Prepaid cards, including reloadable and non-reloadable variants, have become
integral to modern consumer behaviour, with total prepaid transactions in India estimated to reach 2.0 billion in Calendar Year
2025 and ₹700.9 billion in terms of transaction value reflecting broad adoption across categories such as retail, travel, and
everyday purchases (source: F&S Report, page 16). Growth is expected to remain consistent over the next five years, with total
prepaid transactions in India projected to reach 4.5 billion and ₹1,028.9 billion in value by Calendar Year 2030, reflecting
strong acceptance of the prepaid card model (source: F&S Report, page 16).

India’s Prepaid Cards market has been experiencing accelerated growth, primarily driven by the cards’ multifaceted utility of
both reloadable and non-reloadable prepaid instruments that seamlessly fits into diverse aspects of daily financial life and
business operations (source: F&S Report, page 16). These cards offer secure, convenient, and pre-funded solutions, appealing
to both urban consumers and digitally transitioning users (source: F&S Report, page 16). Consumers increasingly turn to
Prepaid Cards for hassle-free transactions on popular e-commerce platforms, where they provide a secure, pre-funded
alternative to linking bank accounts, minimizing fraud risks during online shopping sprees for everything from groceries to
electronics (source: F&S Report, page 16). In merchant stores, ranging from neighbourhood Kirana shops to large retail chains,
these cards facilitate quick contactless payments at point of sales (“POS”) terminals, appealing to urban shoppers seeking speed
and convenience over cash handling (source: F&S Report, page 16).

India’s D2C spend management and prepaid cards landscape is evolving rapidly, driven by rising digital adoption among retail
consumers, expanding acceptance infrastructure, and regulatory support for seamless, secure payments (source: F&S Report,
page 21). Prepaid cards, both physical and virtual, are increasingly being used by individuals for everyday purchases, online
shopping, travel, gifting, and personal budgeting (source: F&S Report, page 21). Market directionally, prepaid instruments
continue to carve out a specialized role even as UPI dominates everyday payments (source: F&S Report, page 21). In 2024,
outstanding prepaid cards witnessed a 34% growth year-on-year (source: F&S Report, page 21).

A key trend in India’s digital gift card market is the increasing use of attractive discounts, cashbacks, user rewards, and bonus
value to drive customer engagement and adoption (source: F&S Report, page 39). Digital gift cards are often offered at
discounted prices or bundled with platform rewards, making them a value-driven purchase rather than just a gifting instrument
(source: F&S Report, page 39). This strategy strongly appeals to India’s price-sensitive consumers, encouraging impulse
purchases, higher redemption rates, and repeat usage (source: F&S Report, page 39). For platforms and brands, discount-led
gifting helps boost transaction volumes, acquire new users, and stimulate incremental spending when gift card values are
redeemed—creating a win-win ecosystem for consumers, merchants, and intermediaries alike (source: F&S Report, page 39).

Festive occasions such as Diwali, Raksha Bandhan, Christmas, and weddings significantly boost digital gifting activity (source:
F&S Report, page 40). During these peak periods, platforms and brands often run high visibility offers and thematic campaigns,
which further amplify demand (source: F&S Report, page 40). Digital gift card volumes typically spike during major festive
and sales events, with platforms reporting millions of transactions in these seasons (source: F&S Report, page 40). For example,
network gift cards launched on India’s ONDC platform recorded around 1.2 million transactions during a recent festive period,
indicating growing penetration across cities and categories (source: F&S Report, page 40).

The industry is experiencing significant growth, and new use cases continue to emerge. For further details, see “Our Business
– Our Strategies – Enhance our existing products and develop new products and services to address a broader set of use cases”.
As we enhance our existing products and develop new products and services to address a broader set of use cases, the rate of
market adoption will be a significant factor influencing our results of operations in the future.

We operate within a vertically integrated ecosystem. Redemption of reward points against Gift Cards or Prepaid Cards may
also generate Program Fees with such fees being recognised separately based on the nature and substance of the underlying
transaction. Evaluating the Rewards and Loyalty business in isolation would not capture the holistic economics of the overall
transaction and the end-to-end customer journey. This is also consistent with the segment reporting adopted by our Company
under Indian Accounting Standard 108 — Operating Segments (“Ind AS 108”). As disclosed in Note 44 of the Restated
Financial Information, the Chief Operating Decision Maker does not review the performance of our revenue streams separately,
nor are operating costs, assets and liabilities are not allocated among such revenue streams.

Our results of operations may be influenced by the adoption and scalability of our recently launched Rewards and Loyalty
business. As this offering is relatively new, its contribution to our revenue and profitability in the future will depend on our
ability to increase transaction and redemption volumes on our platforms. While our technology infrastructure is designed to
support scalable deployment, the pace at which these offerings scale may vary and may require continued investments in
technology development, partner integrations, marketing and personnel. Accordingly, the growth trajectory of this new offering
may affect our future revenue mix, cost structure and overall results of operations.

Decrease in Brand & Business Promotion Expenses

Our brand and business promotion initiatives are designed to support both corporate customer outreach and user engagement.
Typically, while corporate customers access our platforms through direct relationships and Ecosystem Partners, users are
onboarded, in part, through digital engagement initiatives such as social media advertisements and promotional campaigns.

We have engaged third-party agencies to assist us in our efforts to increase brand awareness through media publications and
for providing services pertaining to search engine optimization, website content review and optimization, digital clean-up and
accuracy enhancement, social media and performance marketing services, and contextual online monitoring. For instance, in
the past, we engaged The Blind Spot Media, to provide organic public relations, news and press dissemination services to help
build media authority and search engine visibility. Further, we also engaged Alphacret Studio to provide services pertaining to
social media content creation and performance marketing. Examples of our past brand and business promotion initiatives
include social media content and advertisements for our offerings such as yayyy.shop, communication campaigns around
occasions such as Women’s Day, New Years’, informational blog posts on our Company’s website. We have participated in
and were one of the sponsors of an industry-focused event titled the Global Fintech Fest, 2026. We also participated in a fintech
focused event titled “Afinatics 3.0” held at Chitkara University, Punjab, India as an “Industry Partner”.

financial performance or as an indicator of our financial condition, results of operations or cash flows.

Basis of Preparation & Presentation

The Restated Consolidated Financial Information of the Company and in the applicable period/year, its subsidiary (the
Company and its subsidiary together referred to as the “Group”), which comprises:

     • the restated consolidated statement of assets and liabilities of the Group as at June 30, 2026 and the restated consolidated
       statement of profit and loss (including other comprehensive income), the restated consolidated statement of changes in
       equity and the restated consolidated statement of cash flows for the three months ended June 30, 2026, derived from
       the audited special purpose consolidated financial statements of the Group as at and for the three months ended June
       30, 2026;

     • the restated consolidated statement of assets and liabilities of the Group as at March 31, 2026 and the restated
       consolidated statement of profit and loss (including other comprehensive income), the restated consolidated statement
